items.title: Lula wins fourth term as Brazil president after historic upset over far-right Flávio Bolsonaro
paragraphs: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president, has staged a dramatic election fightback, defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, to claim a historic fourth term in power.
With 100% of votes counted the 80-year-old leftist received 51.79% of the vote to his 45-year-old rival’s 48.21%.

Lula narrowly lost the first round of the election to Bolsonaro in early October, casting his political future into doubt and plunging progressive Brazilians into three weeks of despair. Never, since the return of democracy in the 1980s, has the first round runner-up won the second vote.
But Lula did precisely that on Sunday, prompting joyous scenes on the streets of São Paulo, where he had been following events, and at the hotel where he was watching the count.

Addressing a packed crowd of ecstatic supporters in a São Paulo conference hall, Lula said: “We are going to change the way that this country is governed … This election was a defeat for denialism … I want to thank God and to thank you, Brazilian men and women of this country … it was democracy that made this happen.”
Lula’s vice-president, Geraldo Alckmin, told the crowd: “You saved Brazilian democracy for the second time. Congratulations, President Lula.”
The president’s supporters chanted back: “Olé. Olé. Olá! Lula! Lula!”

As the result was confirmed, Reginaldo Lopes, a key Lula ally, told the Guardian: “I feel incredible … This is Brazil telling the world that the extreme right is fascist, that the extreme right is against black people, is against the poor, against the state, against gay people … We are going to reorganize the democratic forces [in this country.”

Alexandre Padilha, Lula’s health minister, said: “This is a huge victory for the Brazilian people who in the second round had the chance to think about what President Lula means for the environment, for the defense of our national health service and our education system and the Brazilian constitution. And the risks that the extreme right candidate entailed.”
“It’s a massive victory - not just for Brazil. It’s also an important signal to the rest of Latin America and to the world,” Padilha added.
The incumbent, who had lost by 2.2 million votes three weeks ago, has now won by 4.3 million.

“I feel so so happy ... There’s not enough room in my chest for all this joy. Lula’s victory represents so much. It means life for those who believe in love and in life,” said Maicon Douglas Bento, a 34-year-old photographer, as he joined tens of thousands of jubilant Brazilians on Paulista Avenue at the heart of São Paulo.

The 8o-year-old appears to have made up much of the difference through what his allies had identified as his main opportunity: persuading his voters to turn out. After a record abstention rate of 21.08% in the first round, which disproportionately affected Lula voters because they tend to live further from polling stations, the rate fell to 19.21%.
Speaking during Lula’s victory speech, Bolsonaro said it was “impossible to concede the election result” and that his legal team would seek to have the election annulled.

Following in the footsteps of his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who four years ago also refused to acknowledge his defeat to Lula – before attempting a coup and being convicted for it – the senator cited a supreme court justice’s decision to extend voting hours as the alleged reason.

His speech made no mention of the fact that his campaign had also asked the electoral court to extend voting hours, but he nevertheless said Justice Cristiano Zanin’s decision to extend voting by two hours to 7pm “was not normal, it was unacceptable” and amounted to “changing the rules of the game while the game was being played”.

For Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, the victory represents a sensational final chapter in a storied political career that began when he emerged as a union leader in São Paulo’s industrial suburbs in the late 1970s.

After entering politics, the former factory worker who was born in rural poverty made three unsuccessful presidential bids, in 1989, 1994 and 1998, before finally becoming Brazil’s first elected working-class president in 2002.

Lula stepped down after the maximum two consecutive terms allowed by the constitution but returned to power after winning the 2022 election against Bolsonaro’s father, then the incumbent president Jair Bolsonaro, who was subsequently jailed for plotting a coup.
Lula’s win is bad news for Jair Bolsonaro who is serving a 27-year sentence for that botched power grab and was hoping to be freed and given a role in government had his son prevailed.

It is also a blow for Donald Trump, the Bolsonaro clan’s most important international ally. The US president had been hoping Bolsonaro would become the latest in a series of pro-Trump leaders to take power in Latin America, including Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia, Daniel Noboa in Ecuador, José Antonio Kast in Chile and Javier Milei in Argentina.
Confirmation of Lula’s victory was greeted with anger and bewilderment in Brasília, where Bolsonaro is living under house arrest and where his son watched the count.

On Sunday night, political leaders applauded Lula. Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum said: “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won. Congratulations, ⁠President Lula!”, while Paraguayan president Santiago Peña said “I salute the ⁠Brazilian people for this great democratic journey.”

Lula’s victory came after his supporters staged two massive shows of support on Saturday, with more than a million people flocking to Rio’s Copacabana beach and an even larger number marching on Paulista Avenue.

Many people on the streets of São Paulo were angry at an apparent attempt by pro-Bolsonaro politicians to derail the election by sabotaging public transport in Lula-leaning voting areas across the country.

“I think it’s another coup attempt that the extreme right is trying in Brazil. But we need to really fight so we can win,” said Lucas Lopes, a 32-year-old from São Paulo who works with public relations.
But that alleged attempt to scupper a Lula victory failed.

“I’ll be sincere: in the first round the left failed. But in the second round they woke up,” said Caio Marques, a 40-year-old photographer from Franca, a city in the interior of São Paulo state. “And there is no coup that will take this away from us.”

items.title: From agriculture to AI-griculture: How tech is changing farming
paragraphs: George McMaster uses technology to help him with work on his farm
Agriculture and environment correspondent, BBC News NI
George McMaster's farming career started with milking eight cows in a byre, relying on his eyes to spot any health issues in his cattle.
He still watches his now-300-strong herd, but via a feed from an AI camera in the milking parlour at the farm near Islandmagee in County Antrim.
The device uses an algorithm which assigns each cow its own ID, records a short video of the animal every day, analyses it and flags any changes - often before they are visible to the human eye.
For the third generation farmer, it is "absolutely incredible to move from all hand-done to sitting on the phone, watching what's happening outside".
Jack and his father George on their Islandmagee farm
It is just one example of how technology is changing the traditional profession.
George's son Jack, who is taking over the farm, jumped at the chance to get involved with the CattleEye app when a local developer approached him.

"There's cows there we would never have thought of as lame when we were just watching them every day, but whenever the camera's watching they're picking them up so much earlier, any emergencies that we have, to check cows before they lose condition and get sick," he said.
"And if cows are in better health, we get more milk and they're happier - happy cows make happy farmers."
AI is helping farmers monitor the health of their herds
Caleb Howard is using technology to manage his 90 Jersey cows on the farm near Coagh in County Tyrone.
They filter in and out of a robotic milking machine when they want to, rather than being herded in at set times.
Like the McMasters, he thinks "everything is going down the robotic route" to improve efficiency.
But historically in a place like rural Tyrone, that has come with its own challenges.
Getting high-speed broadband was a game-changer for him - he has been able to open a farm shop with an electronic payment system.
Caleb Howard is a farmer in County Tyrone
"Ten years ago, in our area, phone signal was rubbish, the broadband wasn't great, it was just like a slightly faster dial-up," he said.
"So now everything is much simpler and much easier-used when you've got a good internet connection."
Project Stratum was set up to deliver high-speed broadband to areas like the one Howard lives in.
Colin Hutchinson from Fibrus, which delivered the project, said it had had a "massive" economic impact.
"Being online and having good broadband access is really crucial now," he said.
"And it's enabling businesses like this to thrive in really rural locations."
A milking machine screen is used on Caleb Howard's farm
Robert Smyth runs a herd of 100 dairy cows in another rural location, near Randalstown in County Antrim.
For four years now, he has used the FarmDrive app to run the business.
"It's so much handier - beforehand you're writing things down, bits of paperwork in the cattle house and writing them down in the office, whereas now you just do it at that time," he said.

"And then whenever you have inspections coming up, all you have to do is go into your compliance section, select reports, and there's your reports for your medicine, for your meal records, for everything.
"The AI really should be looking towards how to manage your farm better and how to reduce your inputs and increase your outputs."
Gareth McDonald developed the FarmDrive app
Developer Gareth McDonald describes FarmDrive as "Facebook for cows". Each animal gets a profile with all her records in one place and a photo can be added.
He comes from a farming background and studied computer science.
Although he is passionate about the technology, he does not believe it will replace humans.

"It's allowing us to work a lot more quickly and efficiently, and on the farming side, it's basically allowing the farmer to see the right information at the right time, where it's kind of that adviser to the farmer," he said.
"We're very much of the opinion we don't want the AI making the decision for the farmer."
Almost a century ago, County Down-born inventor Harry Ferguson transformed the farming industry when he developed the linkage system still used in tractors today.
Former president of the Ulster Farmers' Union Ian Marshall says AI is similarly revolutionary.
While the industry has always relied on data, he believes technology will drive how information is used.
"When we take all the datasets, then I think we can deliver on the three pillars of sustainability - economic, environmental and social," he said.

"So I think that because we've got so much data and so much digitalisation in the industry, that farmers will certainly use this to their advantage and can meet their targets, meet their objectives and meet the obligations whilst delivering good quality, sustainable food."

items.title: Mourinho keeps Clasico midas touch 13 years on as La Liga heats up
paragraphs: The Real Madrid manager celebrated Kylian Mbappe's late winner at Barcelona on Sunday with a trademark knee slide, as he maintained his midas touch over their bitter rivals.
Mourinho has become just the third Real boss to go six El Clasicos in a row without defeat - 13 years after he last led Los Blancos in this fixture.

Four wins and two draws in his past six matches in charge of Real Madrid against Barcelona put him up there with Miguel Munoz (1962 to 1965) and Vicente del Bosque (2001 to 2003) as Real managers who have gone six in a row without defeat against the old enemy.
It was also just a second victory in eight games against Barcelona for Real, with the return of Mourinho to the fixture haunting the reigning champions
And more importantly for Mourinho, Mbappe's double in Real's 2-1 win ended Barcelona's nine-game unbeaten domestic run with a crucial Clasico victory at the Camp Nou.

A Real defeat would have allowed Barcelona to establish a commanding nine-point advantage but the result has transformed the top of La Liga, bringing Mourinho's side to within three points of their rivals.
"In my view, Real Madrid do not play to win at the Camp Nou, Real Madrid play to win La Liga," he said.
"We could win with luck, but we won with calmness and with all merit," he said. "It's a very strong group. Everyone works very hard. Everyone was ready to win.
"The credit goes to the players. When you win, the credit goes to the players. But when you lose, the blame falls on you. And that's why we see coaches being sacked from their positions every week."
The Portuguese, who returned to Real 13 years after his first stint in charge this summer, has now won six and lost six El Clasicos.
He said: "I've learned that I have an extraordinary group, with the quality and mindset to play.

"In midfield, having a mix of talents gives us more than just having two players with similar characteristics. This mix of talents gives us balance when defending and quality when we go on the attack.
"We've beaten several teams by four or more goals, but this is Barca, and the players put on a great performance. We need to continue like this and don't go over the moon after this win."
Barcelona boss Hansi Flick said he didn't want to give excuses for the defeat but admitted his team lacked fresh legs after a demanding few weeks.
"We missed the freshness," he said. "It's not easy for our players. We have to recover well, train well and we have to respond from this defeat.
"In big games, small things are important and they decide the games and today, it wasn't on our side.
"I can see that today we were not fresh and this is what we have to change."

items.title: Phantom Blade Zero review: dark wuxia martial arts masters with an apprentice's execution
paragraphs: Phantom Blade Zero has a lot going for it to distinguish itself from other AAA Souls-inspired games emerging from China in recent years, thanks to its painstaking martial-arts mocap combat and unique kung-fu-punk vision, but several frustrating design choices keep it from being a work of a grand master.
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Phantom Blade Zero wants you to feel like a kung fu master from the opening moments, and you should, since you play as Soul, an elite assassin for the Order. Even after a fateful duel leaves him with 66 days to live, there’s no cheap Metroid-style reset, and his martial arts prowess keeps growing.

Whether taking on another fearsome warrior one-on-one or a group of enemies, there’s a fluid confidence to his moveset that captures the spirit of the classic martial arts films that have inspired studio S-Game's ambitious debut, itself based on the indie RPG Rainblood: Town of Death that director Soulframe Liang made more than 15 years ago.

While China’s first AAA hits like Black Myth: Wukong and Wuchang: Fallen Feathers have leveraged both Unreal Engine 5 and the overwhelming influence of Soulslikes, S-Game tries to carve out its own identity, which it has coined as ‘kungfupunk’. Aesthetically, that means a curious blend of traditional Chinese culture with the modern: steel-factory architecture clashing with bamboo forests and temples from a more classic wuxia setting, and music where elegant pipa strings give way to electric-guitar rock riffs. More literally, it’s about how Sha-Chi, the energy that powers your kung fu (in-game, it’s basically your stamina gauge used for heavy combos and guarding attacks), also powers other technologies.

But it's definitely the kung fu that's centre-stage here, with all of the fighting styles and movements in-game captured by real martial artists, notably with the involvement of Hong Kong martial arts legend Donnie Yen (he also plays a character, albeit one you don't strictly encounter on the main story path, while spending most of it behind a mask) and his stunt team.

Even though your combos are essentially just spamming light or heavy attacks, your fighting style changes depending on the weapon you use, such as the one-handed Jagged Steel, which inflicts bleed damage, or the weighty two-handed Scarlet Wraithblade, which leaves energy-draining red spider lilies on the ground. The action can often feel too fast for its own good, so you're usually focused on your flurry of attacks before waiting to react to an enemy's blue or red attacks to parry or dodge, but hitting the prompt to unleash a finishing move is pretty satisfying.

Since most bosses drop new weapons, there's a thrill in getting a new toy to play with, and the game has more than 50 to find and master. It can feel a little overwhelming, and some may feel more gimmicky than useful, like a sword that gives you unpredictable drunken-martial-arts movements, so I naturally stuck to a few favourites, especially since I needed to prioritise upgrading them with my limited resources.

Nonetheless, there's an incentive to master more than one weapon, as switching automatically gives you a full Sha-Chi gauge. I often used up a gauge with one weapon, then quickly swapped to another to keep my offensive momentum going (a cooldown period does prevent you from just exploiting this).

Special weapons called Phantom Edges have limited uses but, used at the right time, can turn the tide in encounters, like a large axe that smashes through enemy shields or a chain sickle that tears through multiple surrounding enemies. Some even serve Metroidvania-style exploration, letting you access areas you couldn't reach before.

But despite some interesting designs, it's hard not to see these as glorified keycards, with most leading to little more than a small room and a chest for your trouble. Even though the chain doubles as a grappling hook, it's a bit disappointing once you realise that, like other traversal options such as running up cliffs or wall-running, it's limited to a button prompt at prescribed points in the environment.

This is one of the frustrating aspects of Phantom Blade Zero's rich, dense Wulin, even as it takes you from the bottom of a valley to mountain peaks, plus a massive lake you can explore by boat. It may all look pleasing to the eye, but it suffers from environments where you regularly bump up against invisible barriers as you try to parse the artistically rendered map (albeit elegantly emulating a Chinese ink wash painting that fills up the more checkpoints you come across).

This is especially annoying when a quest marker is supposedly close by, but you still have to wander aimlessly until you spot an interaction prompt, or discover there's actually a long-winded detour you're supposed to take instead. Doors that require specific keys are one thing, but I catch myself sighing when I approach a ledge you would expect to mantle in a similar game, only for Soul's kung fu skills to be arbitrarily eluded.

Another question you might have about Phantom Blade Zero is whether it's a Soulslike. In many ways, it isn't. For instance, its checkpoints don't revive defeated enemies when you rest at them, and you also don't lose any resources permanently if you don't recover them. It nonetheless has some similarities, such as some labyrinthine level design where you'll encounter your share of doors inconveniently locked from your side, but it almost seems to turn into a Soulslike in challenge the moment you encounter bosses with hard-hitting attacks and where you have very limited heals (which you won't even be able to upgrade meaningfully until the game's midpoint).

On the one hand, some difficulty spikes are mitigated by bosses with a second phase, which also have a checkpoint so you're not forced to go through the first phase with fewer resources, and there are also difficulty options. The accessories you find and equip can also make a difference, especially ones that widen the parry and dodge windows, but my major gripe remains how spongy these boss fights feel, even for those that come back with a second phase.

This isn't unique to Phantom Blade Zero (see also Control Resonant, until Remedy patched it at launch), but it makes you question the point of staggering your opponent when, in this state, all your heaviest attacks still only chip away at their health. In many fights, it also makes your aggressive momentum push the enemy back until you inevitably get stuck on geometry. When it hits the camera, some cool-looking finishing moves get framed awkwardly, with parts of the environment obscuring the shot.

Even though I was testing on PS5 Pro, I still ran into some pretty glaring technical issues during my playthrough, mostly in the latter half of the game, which I think came down to optimisation and bugs, since they persisted even after I turned off ray tracing and set the graphics to Performance mode. Sometimes the audio got knocked way out of balance between the voice acting and music, and in a couple of cases the big puddles I came across didn't show reflections so much as they looked more like a big mirror or a hole in the ground.

Most egregious, however, were framerate drops during combat that devolved into a slideshow, spoiling several major boss fights. I should be relieved they didn't kill me, since most of these happened when I was already locked into my (likely very VFX-laden) attack animations against a staggered opponent.

That may make it seem like I have a lot to be down about Phantom Blade Zero, but there is still plenty to admire, including cultural and artistic flourishes I can't share in this review. The Wulin's centrepiece, Pangzhen, is the kind of labyrinthine town that deserves to be talked about in the same breath as Bloodborne's Yharnam, so rich and dense with secrets and lore, and home to some of the game's best bosses, while there's clearly been a lot of thought that has gone into the intriguing characters and deep questlines that offer meaningful rewards, including having an impact on the ending you'll get. It's just a shame that the version I got to play still needed a bit more time in the oven.

A final note: S-Game released a patch that supposedly resolves most of the above issues, but it came after I finished my playthrough, so I didn't have a chance to go through it again to make sure every issue I encountered was fixed.

Alan Wen is a freelance journalist writing about video games in the form of features, interview, previews, reviews and op-eds. Work has appeared in print including Edge, Official Playstation Magazine, GamesMaster, Games TM, Wireframe, Stuff, and online including Kotaku UK, TechRadar, FANDOM, Rock Paper Shotgun, Digital Spy, The Guardian, and The Telegraph.

items.title: Brazil runoff live updates: ballot count resumes after two-hour voting extension
paragraphs: Scratch that. Brazilian ⁠supreme court justice Cristiano Zanin ⁠has just ordered ⁠voting ​in the country’s presidential runoff ⁠on Sunday to be ⁠extended by ​two ‌hours, granting a ‌request from ‌Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s campaign.
Polls were initially set ‌to close at 5pm ​Brasília time. Lula’s campaign ⁠alleged that authorities ​in several cities ​were ​restricting voter ​access ‌to ​public ​transportation.

The decision follows allegations of attempted voter suppression in at least 10 states, where public transport appears to have been severely limited in what some suspect was a deliberate ploy to stop Lula voters reaching polling stations.
Earlier, Lula told reporters he had never before complained about elections he had been involved in, irrespective of whether he had won or lost. “But this time something abominable is happening.”
However, some polling stations may have already closed since the decision came so shortly after they were due to close. People should now be able to vote until 7pm.
Polls close (again) in Brazil runoff election
Battle over Meta’s alleged Bolsonaro bias intensified before presidential runoff
Could highly organised pop fans clinch victory for Brazil’s Lula?
Voting time extended for an additional two hours
Exclusive: Ex-Lula environmental official warns of Amazon destruction if Flávio Bolsonaro wins presidency
A scandal engulfing Brazil’s top court could return the Bolsonaros to power
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva v Flávio Bolsonaro: Brazil presidential runoff to decide direction of nation
Lula is reportedly holding a narrow lead over Flávio Bolsonaro with 75% of Brazil’s votes counted.
It’s now 51% Lula and 48.9% Bolsonaro with nearly 75% of votes counted.
Lula seems to be closing in on victory and the mood in his camp is increasingly excited.
This would be an absolutely sensational comeback from one of the biggest figures in the modern history of Latin American politics.
Lula has edged further ahead in the latest figures, reportedly taking 50.92% to Bolsonaro’s 49.08% with 69.92% of ballots counted.

The celebratory mood that swept Flávio Bolsonaro’s headquarters moments ago when he overtook Lula in the vote count has disappeared since the president began closing the gap and moved back into the lead.
Despite the earlier celebrations, the atmosphere has in some ways been tense since the start of the evening.
Bolsonaro’s campaign is showing signs that it may be preparing the ground not to concede if he is defeated.

One of the most popular figures in Bolsonaro’s party, congressman Nikolas Ferreira, appeared unusually tense while speaking to journalists – unlike the jokey demeanour he usually has in front of the cameras.
double quotation markEither we win. Or we win. You’ve been warned.
There were screams of joy in Lula’s hotel as he took the lead a few minutes ago. With nearly half of votes counted he now has 50.15% to Bolsonaro’s 49.85%.
“It’s going to work out! It’s going to work out! It has to!” one official told me.
The mood here is increasingly upbeat with Bolsonaro’s path to victory looking increasingly tricky.

Lula’s main bet in trying to overturn Bolsonaro’s lead was to increase turnout, after abstention reached a record high in the first round – which, according to many polls, disproportionately affected the leftist’s voters, who generally live farther from polling stations.
The figures are not yet final, but with 24.4% of polling stations counted, they indicated an abstention rate of 19.38%, down from 21.08% in the first round.
Abstention usually rises in Brazilian runoffs – the only exception was in 2022, when the tight contest between Lula and Jair Bolsonaro brought more voters to the polls in the final round.
Meanwhile, hundreds of Lula supporters have camped out on Paulista Avenue to watch the vote count, which started at 7pm local time.
Among them is Camilo Buarque, 35, who came with a bright red banner reading: “Lula: My President”.
“I feel so very happy being here and being here fighting for Lula,” Buarque says, predicting his leader will beat Bolsonaro.

“My confidence comes from the energy and the happiness and the love of these people [around me]. This is democracy,” Buarque says as the first results come in, giving Lula the lead. Fireworks exploded in the air above him as the crowd celebrated the early lead.
João Felipe, a 27-year-old logistics worker, is also there waiting for what he hopes will be a huge Lula party.
“I’ve always been poor and Lula was a very important person when it came to helping people improve their lives,” he says.
“Lula is going to turn this election around. Long live democracy,” Felipe predicts.
“My heart is beating a thousand beats a second but I’m confident,” said his partner, Ester Almeida, 28.

Flávio Bolsonaro is following the count from the mansion of one of his campaign coordinators in a wealthy area of the capital, Brasília. The dozens of journalists present are being kept separate from Bolsonaro and allied politicians, but from time to time they can hear bursts of celebration – like after a goal – whenever the count is updated and Bolsonaro narrows the gap with Lula.

When, with 13.65% of the vote counted, Flávio moved just slightly ahead with 50.01%, an AI-generated funk track began playing loudly and the senator’s guests started chanting a line commonly heard in Brazilian football stadiums: “Go at him, Flávio.”
And just like that, the race is already tightening further. Bolsonaro now has 50.01% of the vote, while Lula has 49.99% of the vote with just over 13.5% of ballots counted.
With 5% of votes counted Lula has taken an early lead with 51% of votes to Bolsonaro’s 48.87%. This is going to be a tight race and a very long night.

One of the most popular figures in Flávio Bolsonaro’s party, congressman Nikolas Ferreira, indicated that the far right could use the extension of voting hours as grounds to challenge the election result in the event of a victory by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

Speaking to journalists outside the mansion in Brasília where Bolsonaro was due to follow the count, Ferreira said that “the only person harmed” by the extension was the senator – without, however, mentioning the voters who, as reports throughout the day showed, had been unable to vote because they had no transport.

“The extension only helps whoever is losing,” said the 30-year-old politician who, in the first round, became the most-voted federal congressman in Brazilian history, with 3.1 million votes. He added that justice Cristiano Zanin “wanted to disrupt the election” by issuing the ruling.
Bolsonaro’s campaign chief, senator Rogério Marinho, echoed that line and called the justice’s ruling an “intervention”.
“I sincerely hope common sense prevails and that any judicial coup or administrative manoeuvre does not succeed, for the sake of democracy,” he posted on social media.
Now two hours after the initial extension, polls have officially closed in Brazil (save for another surprise extension). Ballot count has begun.

Although voting time was extended across the country, some polling stations had already closed by the time that decision was announced. As Brazil uses electronic voting machines, once they are closed, they cannot be re-opened.

It’s not clear if certain polling stations had restrictions on if people who arrived after the initial deadline were allowed to vote, as rules usually stipulate that only people in line can still vote after the polls close.
The fact that ballot counting was already underway when the polls were suddenly ordered to remain open has led to some confusion and concerns about the integrity of the election results.

Five days after his defeat in the first round of the Brazilian presidential election, leftwing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spent almost 24 hours unable to boost his Instagram posts, while his opponent, far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, could.

Lula’s lawyers included the episode in a list of incidents that they submitted to the electoral court and international observers as “evidence” that Meta, Instagram’s owner, was actively trying to interfere in Brazil’s election in Bolsonaro’s favour.

Reports from Lula supporters saying their content had been removed or its reach restricted flooded social media in Brazil, while about a dozen watchdogs and research groups published reports describing what they called “indications” that Meta may have favoured the senator’s campaign.
Meta called Lula’s allegations “false and unfounded”, saying there had been “technical incidents” that affected campaigns from “different parts of the political spectrum”.
The controversy fuelled the electoral battle between Lula and Bolsonaro and gained further traction after the electoral court ordered Meta not to give the candidates “unequal treatment”.
Lula supporters are starting to gather on Paulista Avenue, at the heart of São Paulo, in anticipation of a Lula victory.

The mood is upbeat but tense, amid suspicions that there has been a deliberate pro-Bolsonaro campaign to sabotage public transport systems to stop Lula voters reaching polling stations across the country.
Many people on Paulista Avenue outside the iconic São Paulo Museum of Art suspect foul play from Bolsonaro-supporting politicians and business people.

“I think it’s another coup attempt that the extreme right is trying in Brazil. But we need to really fight so we can win,” said Lucas Lopes, a 32-year-old from São Paulo who works with public relations.
“I’m really worried but I’m optimistic,” Lopes added as dozens of Lula supporters blocked the roads and danced with banners and flags.

“It’s a coup,” agreed Caio Marques, a 40-year-old photographer from Franca, a city in the interior of São Paulo state. “Their arrogance is such that they think they have already won and can do whatever they please and won’t be punished.”

Marques’s partner, Gabriela Leôncio, said: “They are [stopping] public transport in strategic places where Lula has historically had more votes. Where Lula has an advantage, people haven’t managed to get to their polling stations ... They are trying several different types of coup.”

Marques predicted the ploy would fail. “I have faith it won’t [work] because the left is really mobilized,” he said. “I’ll be sincere: in the first round the left failed. But in the second round they woke up ... and there is no coup that will take this away from us.”

Earlier this month, Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, led a rally in São Paulo, as he aims to be re-elected to a fourth presidential term, and faces serious opposition from rightwinger Flávio Bolsonaro. Taking the mic before a crowd on Avenida Paulista that organisers put at more than a million, the former union leader began: “I’m not sure whether to open this speech with ‘comrades’ or ‘fandoms from all over Brazil’.” The rally was organised by Lula’s Workers’ party (PT) and a string of other leftwing groups – but the spark came from pop music fandoms.

More than 600 Brazilian fanbase groups for Billie Eilish, Lady Gaga, Katseye, Demi Lovato, Harry Styles, Katy Perry, Selena Gomez, as well as Brazilian stars such as Anitta, Marina Sena and Ludmilla among others, all came together to back Lula, waging an intense online campaign as soon as Lula’s rival, son of imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro, came out on top in the first round on 4 October.

When the first round results came in, “I had this feeling I’d seen it all before with Jair Bolsonaro, and that was really frustrating,” says V, an Eilish fan who helps run Info Billie Brasil, one of the country’s biggest fan communities dedicated to the US singer. “So my first reaction was to use the only communication tool we have and get our community to embrace the cause: Lula’s re-election.”

items.title: Data centre debate heats up ahead of US midterms - here's what you need to know
paragraphs: ByDaniel Thomas and the Visual Journalism Team
Until a few years ago many of us may have been blissfully unaware of what a data centre was.
These giant, warehouse-like buildings power virtually all our internet activity, from our web searches and emails to movie downloads and online banking.
They are at the heart of the AI boom, housing the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run services like ChatGPT and Claude.
But the speed at which they're growing, the enormous amount of electricity they consume and concerns about their environmental impact are fuelling a public backlash around the world.
In the US, they've become a huge issue ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, with both Republicans and opposition Democrats coming out against their development.
It's putting opponents of data centre expansion on a collision course with US President Donald Trump, who has dismissed the pushback as a "sick conspiracy", even as public anger grows.
Here's what you need to know about the data centre boom, and why opposition is growing.
There are about 12,250 data centres around the world, according to Data Center Map, external, a company that tracks both operational and pre-operational sites.
That's up sharply from 2021, when there were around 8,000, external operational sites.
As the chart below shows, data centres are most densely clustered in the US which has 4,767 sites. It is followed by Europe, where the UK and Germany lead.

Data centres have typically been located near to cities where it's easier to access high voltage power lines or water resources for cooling. But as they get bigger, more are being built in rural areas.
Data centres vary wildly in size, ranging from ones that fit inside a garden shed to others covering vast expanses of land.

The world's largest operational data centre is widely reported to be one run by China Telecom in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, covering an area of approximately one million square metres (10.7 million sq ft). That is equivalent to about 140 Fifa football pitches.
However, much larger sites are under construction as the graphic below shows.
All these sites are being built exclusively to provide the immense computing power needed to run AI services.
For instance, Colossus 2, which is part of the wider Colossus campus, will house hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips made by tech giant Nvidia.

It will also be used to train xAI's chatbot Grok. Elon Musk's company will use 41 methane gas turbines to help power the site, which activists say could "significantly increase" local air pollution, external. Local regulators say the turbines will meet air quality standards.

The pressure data centres put on local resources has sparked increasing concern. These facilities can use significant amounts of water to cool their systems, which could lead to water shortages, some experts say.
Data centres worldwide are also thought to consume more electricity than the whole of France, as the chart below shows.
This growing hunger for power is driving up carbon emissions, analysis shows, while putting pressure on local grids, which some fear could push up energy prices.
With others worried about the noise data centres make and the space they take up, a public backlash is gathering steam.
Some 16 US states have proposed laws to ban or temporarily block new facilities, and it could be a key issue in November's midterm elections.
Outside the US, opposition to data centres has emerged in countries like Mexico, France, Indonesia and the UK.
But supporters say data centres are critical to national security, and the development of AI.
They also say they are good for the economy, external, attracting investment, generating tax revenue and creating jobs in areas like construction.
A recent report by the Brookings Center, external suggests data centres do create local jobs, although fewer than industry advocates claim.
The type of data centre matters too. So-called hyperscale facilities - massive sites owned and run by tech giants like Amazon and Microsoft - have a bigger positive effect on jobs, it found.
But "colocation" facilities, which lease space to remote tenants without a local presence, brought fewer benefits.
As the debate over their merits intensifies, the data centre rollout continues.
This year, the tech industry is expected to spend a combined $765bn, external ($544bn) on AI infrastructure in 2026, with this topping $1tn next year.
But as concerns about the environmental impact grow, the tech industry is exploring alternatives.
One idea is to put data centres in space, external or on the Moon, where they could harness abundant solar energy.
Others predict that more AI processing could eventually be carried out by the hardware already inside our computers and smartphones, reducing the need for vast data centres altogether.
Additional reporting and design by Erwan Rivault, Matt Faraci and Dominic Bailey.

items.title: Rapper Nikki Minaj joins Trump onstage at Michigan rally
paragraphs: Rapper Nikki Minaj said President Donald Trump has "changed the energy of the country" as she joined him at a Michigan rally to stump for Republicans ahead of the nationwide midterm elections.
"He's given us a future to look forward to," she said, after Trump praised her figure and called her on stage to speak.
Minaj has called herself Trump's "number one fan" despite criticising some of his policies in his first term.

In Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is locked in a tight race with Republican Mike Rogers with just over a week to go before the midterms. Former President Barack Obama held a rally - one of the first in this cycle - with the Democrat on Saturday.
Democrats are also aggressively hitting the campaign trail, with close elections taking place on 3 November which will decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump's presidency.
In his remarks on Sunday, Trump focused on El-Sayed's Muslim faith and background, alleging that he will "invite jihadists" into America if he wins.

El-Sayed has criticised similar remarks by Trump as Islamophobic, saying in an ad to voters last week that the US president "thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor's office".
In Port Huron on Sunday, Minaj, wearing a gold-coloured Gucci-branded suit, led the crowd in chanting Trump's name, and the names of Republican candidates in Michigan.
"We really need all these great people to be elected, because this is a major turning point for our country," she said.
"She never looked more beautiful," Trump said as she left the stage. "She gets it. She's smart," he added.
Earlier in his speech, Trump praised the rear end of one male Republican candidate before turning the crowd's attention to Minaj.
"By the way, I looked at a beautiful ass before," he segued. "Nikki Minaj. That's hard to miss."
He then asked her to "stand up" as the crowd cheered, and added that he hoped she was not "insulted" by his remark.

items.title: Funding set to double for plan to get rough sleepers off streets by Christmas
paragraphs: Funding is set to double to support a pledge by the prime minister to give every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas.
Ending rough sleeping was one of Andy Burnham's first promises when he entered Downing Street, announcing a £442m package to provide emergency accommodation and practical support.
On the eve of the first Rough Sleeping Summit at Downing Street on Monday, No 10 has indicated a further £432m will be added to the initiative in Wednesday's Budget.
Shadow housing secretary Katie Lam said rough sleeping had hit "record highs under Labour" and criticised Burnham for failing to end rough sleeping when he was the Mayor of Greater Manchester.

The BBC understands the government's commitment is that every rough sleeper will be able to physically move into accommodation by Christmas and/or they will be offered support as a way to prevent them sleeping rough.
Some people may choose not to accept accommodation, but ministers say support will still be offered to them.

The government said initial funding had seen specialist outreach teams and new bed spaces operating in Coventry, with further provision being rolled out in places including Plymouth and Camden in north London over the coming weeks.
Money being added to the pot this week will extend support beyond March 2027 to the end of this Parliament, taking total investment to £874m.
Ahead of hosting the summit, Burnham said: "Rough sleeping isn't a fact of life. It's a thing governments either choose to accept or don't.

"Well I don't accept it. That's why we're doubling funding so that people aren't just offered a safe route off the streets this winter but have that same support right through the rest of this Parliament too.

"But we can't do it alone. If we're going to end rough sleeping, we need every part of society behind us on this. So today we're bringing together businesses, charities and local leaders in Downing Street to make sure this is a solution that lasts."
More than 30 organisations have pledged support for the plan with new partnerships, including commercial businesses and charities.

Meanwhile, the National Housing Federation is working with housing associations to identify at least 2,000 potential homes and bed spaces, including empty properties that could be brought back into use.

However, questions remain about whether the scale of accommodation currently identified will be sufficient. It is not yet clear how many of the 2,000 homes and bedspaces represent self-contained units and how many could accommodate multiple people.
The most recent official figures estimated there were 4,793 people sleeping rough, external on a single night in autumn 2025 in England.
While homelessness organisations have welcomed the government's focus on rough sleeping, many have urged ministers to go further in the Budget.

Leaders from 40 organisations across the housing and homelessness sector signed an open letter last week calling on the government to restore Local Housing Allowance (LHA) rates so they continue to reflect local rents, arguing this would help prevent homelessness in the first place and reduce reliance on temporary accommodation.

The Resolution Foundation estimates that more than 1.1 million low income renters now face shortfalls between their housing benefit and their actual rent, with the gap expected to reach a record high this October.
It argues that relinking LHA to local rents would primarily benefit struggling tenants and help keep more people in their homes.

Housing organisations say that while helping people already sleeping rough is essential, preventing people from becoming homeless in the first place will be critical if the government's longer-term ambition is to succeed.
The Conservatives' Lam said: "Burnham is throwing another £432m at a problem he failed to solve in Greater Manchester."
The Bed Every Night scheme Burnham set up while mayor in the region now provides more than 600 beds per night for people who might otherwise be on the streets.
He pledged to end rough sleeping in Greater Manchester by 2020 when he came into power.
When he was elected in 2017 government figures showed there were 268 rough sleepers across Greater Manchester, and by 2020 that figure had more than halved to 125 - meaning Burnham missed his target.
The numbers fell further to 90 in 2021 but the figures rose each year after that, reaching 197 by 2025.
Across England, government figures show the number of people sleeping rough is at its highest level since records began in 2010.
Lam continued: "Under Labour, rough sleeping has hit record highs – yet their answer is always more taxpayers' money and more empty promises.
"Healey must use his Budget this week to cut taxes for working people, get the ballooning benefits bill under control, and stop pushing up energy prices.
"Instead of piling more costs onto hard-working people, Healey must focus on easing the cost of living and delivering real value for taxpayers' money."

items.title: Deeply divided Israel braces for pivotal election
paragraphs: After three years of regional war, this is a battle Israel always knew was coming.
The general election on Tuesday hangs over a country that's deeply divided and ready for a fight.

Polls published on Friday put the governing coalition and the main opposition bloc almost neck-and-neck, with half a million first-time voters due to cast their ballot and some 70,000 Israelis reportedly flying in from abroad specifically to vote.
On Saturday night, vast crowds of opposition voters gathered in central Tel Aviv to demand a change of government.
"We're optimistic," 21-year-old Omri told me. "I want peace, I want security, and I want to end corruption and get the religious fanatics out."
This campaign has been energized by new tactics - including AI videos designed to grab the headlines - and also by a new face.
Gadi Eisenkot is, perhaps, not the man you might expect to take on the flashy, aggressive, media-savvy brand of Israel's longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.

Relatively new to politics, with a working-class Moroccan background, Eisenkot is a former military chief of staff who is renowned for his calm manner and low-drama approach. He's been dubbed by some as a "non-politician".
But he and his centrist Yashar party have regularly pipped Netanyahu and his Likud party to the top spot in recent polls, the last of which was published on Friday, in line with Israeli election law.

Israeli politics is the art of coalition-building, rather than the task of any one party winning power, but with the predicted result too close to call, Eisenkot's rising profile has sharpened a race many Israelis already see as existential for the future of their country.
I watched him slip past the cameras at a community centre for Ethiopian Jews in the city of Ramle last week, through a gaggle of security personnel and advisors.
One of those who had come to hear him speak was David, a smartly dressed man in a freshly-pressed shirt and navy jacket, who said he had met Eisenkot before.
"He looks you in the eye, not like a leader looking down at someone," David told me. "And he listens. He's very sympathetic."

Eisenkot's appeal is often put down to his personal manner and profile. A softly-spoken military man whose son was killed during the Gaza War, he has presented himself as coming "from the periphery", not from Israel's wealthy urban elite.
His Moroccan background became election headlines earlier this month when a pro-Netanyahu speaker used a racist slur to refer to Eisenkot during a TV debate, referring to him as a Moroccan "monkey".

"These elections are about many issues," Eisenkot told the crowd gathered at the Ramle community centre. "They are about security, economy, education...but primarily, they are about the identity of the State of Israel, and what kind of Israel we want to see. A Jewish state, a democratic state, a liberal, tolerant, egalitarian state."

This is music to opposition ears, who say Benjamin Netanyahu's government is a threat to Israel's democracy, pointing to his efforts to curb the powers of the judicial system, and his refusal to establish a state commission of inquiry into the 7 October 2023 attacks on the grounds that the country's Supreme Court would be biased against him.

Eisenkot, along with other opposition leaders, has attempted to draw voters away from Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party by promising such a state inquiry, which a recent survey suggests is supported by more than 70% of Jewish Israelis.
He has also vowed to enforce court rulings on drafting ultra-Orthodox Jews into national military service - another measure that is popular with right-wing voters and opposition alike.
Benjamin Netanyahu has hit back with a campaign focused on Israel's security, and a core campaign slogan of "No Surrender".

He has repeatedly cast his rivals as soft on security, playing on the fears of some right-wing voters that Jewish opposition parties might ally with Israel's Arab parties to secure a majority, and suggesting this could compromise national security.
Around one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.
These are the first elections since the 7 October attacks, in which Hamas-led gunmen stormed through Gaza's border fence, killing almost 1,200 people and taking 251 hostage.
It was Israel's worst security failure, but three years on its prime minister is again running for re-election as the only man who can keep Israel safe.

"If the army had woken him in time, it wouldn't have happened," Shlomi Bashar told me, one of several die-hard Netanyahu fans drinking in a basement café in Jerusalem's Mahane Yehuda market. "He does bear a certain responsibility, but after the 7 October, he changed the entire Middle East."
Netanyahu has been hammering home the message that Israel's wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, in the years after the 7 October attacks, have reduced existential threats to the country.

"We need him to be re-elected so that he can finish this work," said Shlomi. "In my opinion, he is one of the best leaders in the world. Most of the world loves him and respects him, because he is a strong man and his ideas are correct."

The prime minister has traditionally relied on a stable base of right-wing voters, but is projected to see a thinning of support in this election. Some voters may be slipping away to opposition parties like Eisenkot's. Others, including some die-hard Likud voters we spoke to, said the 7 October attacks had pushed them towards parties further on the right.

Lt Col (Res) Eyal Hajbi, head of the regional civil defence unit in the Netanyahu stronghold of Sderot, right on the Gaza border, lost several friends and colleagues in the attacks. He lights candles for them every day in his office, and told me he would be thinking about them when he cast his ballot on Tuesday.
Standing on a ridge overlooking the ruins of northern Gaza, he gestured to the wasteland where Israel's army has completely flattened the neighbourhoods of Beit Lahia and Beit Hanoun.
"As far as I'm concerned, after 7 October, we should wipe them all out," he said. "I've changed my understanding of Gaza. Before, I wouldn't have said we should destroy it."
He told me he and his family had always voted Likud, but that now he was voting for the far-right party of Itamar Ben Gvir, Jewish Power.
"My family has become more extreme than it ever was before," he said. "If once we deliberated over it, today we don't think twice; we vote."
Polls suggest that less than 10% of Israelis are undecided and that very few of those are considering switching between government parties and opposition ones.
Ben Gvir, National Security minister in Netanyahu's coalition, has been reaching out to younger voters through headline-grabbing social media campaigns.
A poll for one of Israel's leading newspapers, Yedioth Ahronoth, published on 9 October, suggested that more than 16% of first-time voters in Israel would choose far-right parties like his.

In Sderot, a group of 18 year olds from a nearby Jewish religious college told me their political views had been affected by the 7 October attacks far more than their parents. All four teenagers were planning to vote for another far-right party, Religious Zionism, led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.

"Today, the whole younger generation understands that peaceful paths will not work," Aviad Elmahach, one of the teenagers, told me. "Older adults, who are set in a fixed mindset, find [it] harder to change, but the youth understand that we need to be here with strength and an iron fist, which is the only way to win."

The lesson of 7 October, he said, was that Israel needed to be as forceful as possible in its relations with the Palestinians, more than 74,000 of whom have been killed by Israel in Gaza since then, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

"The youth have a fresh new perspective that has not yet become entrenched in politics, and they understand very well why we're voting for Smotrich - it means holding the land with strength and giving [the Palestinians] nothing through peaceful gestures."
"We need a change - we can't live with this government anymore," Galia said. "And I'm not talking about security, I'm talking first about humanity."
Having voted for centrist parties in the past, Galia says she's decided to vote for Eisenkot this time around, because "he's an ordinary guy and I hope he'll continue the way he's talking".
Her son Gal said he was deciding between Eisenkot and the left-leaning Democrats party of Yair Golan, another former army general.

"I'm not naïve. I know there are a lot of more militant voices from young generations," he said. "I don't know if Eisenkot will be better than Golan in terms of security, but I think we have bigger problems: economics, social problems, education, health. We didn't get new neighbours on October 7 - it was a major event, but didn't change how we see ourselves."

Threats to security versus threats to democracy - these are old political tramlines for Israeli voters, deepened by the 7 October attacks, and by four years of the most right-wing government in Israel's history.
But on some of the biggest international concerns, the differences between government and opposition are not as wide as it might seem.
Gadi Eisenkot has pledged to end Hamas rule of Gaza within 18 months, either through a US-led peace plan, or through "military and operational capabilities".

All the main opposition leaders have voiced support for some form of Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank, which has expanded massively under the current government and is illegal under international law. None have openly committed to the idea of full Palestinian statehood, something Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to block. Eisenkot has spoken about creating the conditions for "autonomy or state-minus" under ultimate Israeli security control.

Tuesday's vote could well end in deadlock, with neither government nor opposition able to form a majority without the support of Arab parties, which polls project could win enough seats to be kingmakers. All but one of Israel's Jewish opposition parties have so far rejected working with either of the two Arab party blocs.

With Benjamin Netanyahu ramping up warnings of fresh threats from Iran, opposition voices warning of potential disruption to the ballot, and Israeli rights activists warning of a further spike in violence by settlers in the occupied West Bank, political instability at home could leave Israelis facing both a fresh test of their democracy, and fresh security threats.

items.title: Spotify uploads lyrics for Dolly Parton's Welsh version of Jolene in Irish
paragraphs: Dolly Parton's Welsh version of Jolene is the second posthumous release since her death in August
The lyrics to Dolly Parton's Welsh version of her hit Jolene were uploaded mistakenly to Spotify in Irish.
The song was recorded before her death on 25 August, and is a collaboration with Welsh singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis as well as Parton's niece, Jada Star.
The version has parts of the song sung in English and Welsh - but the lyrics presented on the digital audio streaming service Spotify actually showed the language as Irish.
Spotify removed the Irish lyrics after the BBC approached it for comment.
The BBC asked Spotify when the single and lyrics were uploaded, when the error was noticed and when it will be replaced, but did not receive a response.
The lyrics on Spotify have been removed since the BBC approached the service for comment
The single came out on 9 October, and is the second posthumous release from Parton - who was of Welsh descent.
The legendary country artist won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote more than 3,000 songs after a career spanning seven decades.
Jolene was released in 1973, and is about the fear she might lose her husband Carl Dean to a red-headed bank clerk who had flirted with him early on in their marriage.
It was was nominated for a Grammy in 1974, gave Parton her second number one single on the Billboard Hot Country Singles chart and her first foray into the main Hot 100 chart (60).
It has since had more than one billion streams on Spotify, and many famous singers have gone on to cover Jolene.
Lewis and Star recorded their parts in the UK, while Parton recorded her parts in her studio in Nashville
The Welsh version of the song came about after Lewis, from Neath, had translated the country classic and posted it on social media.
Then Star, Parton's niece, reached out and suggested recording Jolene in Welsh with Lewis - and Parton joined too.
In 2008, during a concert at the Cardiff International Arena, Parton reportedly revealed her Welsh ancestry to fans in the crowd.
Star revealed one side of the family from Parton's mother Avie Lee Owens was initially believed to have come from Conwy.
Following the singer's death, research by staff at Conwy council's archives suggested Parton's ancestors were from Machynlleth, in Powys, not Conwy as previously thought.

items.title: iFixit’s look inside the iPhone Duo may explain those broken screens and hinges
paragraphs: is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

As is tradition, iFixit has torn open the latest iPhone and laid its parts bare on a table. It found some interesting details about how Apple might be hiding the crease on the Duo’s folding screen and gave it a 5/10 repairability score. That might not seem particularly high, but it’s the best score the site has given to a foldable yet.

The internal screen’s matte nano-texture cover doesn’t just make it more readable in bright sunlight; it also helps mask the crease by scattering reflections. When looking at the display under a microscope, iFixit also found oval-shaped subpixels arranged at various angles, which the site believes are designed to reduce artifacts and further mask the crease down the middle of the display.

The nano-texture outer layer is relatively easy to replace without swapping out the OLED underneath. If you do need to repair the display itself, however, good luck. As is the case with other foldables, it’s an expensive nightmare. Dust did make it into the USB-C port, speaker grills, and the hinge — making it a bit crunchy. But noticeably less of the glow dust found its way inside the phone than the Z Fold8 or Pixel 11 Pro Fold.

As for reports of damaged screens and cracking hinges, iFixit has some theories. The hinge on the iPhone Duo is incredibly complex, and they suspect part of it sometimes isn’t descending properly. There is also an accordion cable that passes over that exact spot, and it’s near the edge of the battery. It’s possible this is concentrating pressure and leading to the “audible crack” reported by some and the broken screens. Apple did not immediately return a request for comment.
Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

items.title: Australia politics live: MPs to pay tribute to Helen Haines as parliament resumes; Hanson says One Nation cartoons ‘not going anywhere’
paragraphs: UTI treatment, contraception to be available through pharmacies
MPs to ‘try to do justice’ to wounded fellow MP Helen Haines
Hanson says One Nation cartoons ‘not going anywhere’ despite criticism
Politicians may feel less safe in home electorates than parliament, Tehan says
Following the alleged attack on Helen Haines, security measures have reportedly increased around Parliament House.
But Liberal MP Dan Tehan says the security in parliament is “pretty good”.
double quotation markThere’s been a lot of money and a lot of effort and a lot of thought going into security here at Parliament House.
I think the vulnerability is actually when we’re out doing our job in the community, and that’s probably where we need to put the focus.
Anonymous online voices allow people to ‘do and say anything’, Tehan says
Liberal MP Dan Tehan has raised concerns about the impact of anonymous online accounts on inflammatory political discourse.
double quotation markThe problem we’ve got at the moment is the anonymous voices online.
I’m a big believer in freedom of speech and always have been, but I’ve always strongly believed that you have to put your name to your words. That’s the key.
In the community, those who disagree tend to do so respectfully, he said.
double quotation markWhat you tend to see online is the people who are there, anonymously, will just do and say anything.
Now, whether that then heightens it, I don’t know, but … it’s always the question of balance.
Auditor-general examining if detention in Victorian police cells breaches human rights
The Victorian auditor general is investigating the detention of people in police cells, after Guardian Australia revealed the practice routinely led to the force breaching its own guidelines.

The Victorian auditor general’s office (Vago) confirmed it was set to examine whether Victoria police and the department of justice “manage prison and police cell capacity to support human rights and the efficient functioning of the justice system”.

Guardian Australia reported in November last year that the process of “decanting” was resulting in people being moved hundreds of kilometres across Victoria as the government grappled with tougher bail laws and a shortage of prison beds and corrections workers.
This was also leading to people spending more than the 14-day target in police cells, and in some cases meant they were serving their entire sentences there.
In announcing the audit earlier this month, Vago said:

double quotation markPolice cells are designed to hold people for short periods, such as after arrest and for bail hearings. However, in 2025 there were media reports of police holding prisoners in police cells beyond the recommended 14-day limit.
When cells at one station are full, police may transport individuals to other stations. In some reported cases, police have transported individuals hundreds of kilometres away.

This can mean that prisoners miss their court appearances and do not have easy access to their lawyers and health services. This undermines both prisoners’ human rights and the proper functioning of the justice system.
Vago noted that Victoria’s recent bail reforms were also likely to increase pressure on prison beds and staff capacity.
It said in a statement to Guardian Australia that the audit was under way and was expected to be tabled early next year.
Safety concerns and threats have changed ‘dramatically’ for politicians: Butler
Cabinet minister Mark Butler has said this sitting week offers an opportunity to discuss ways to keep MPs, their families and staffers safe.
Asked by ABC Radio National if much had changed during his time in parliament, Butler said:
double quotation markIt’s changed dramatically in my time.

I’ve been here for almost 20 years and security has changed, and the federal police, in my experience, have been very, very responsive to our requests when there are threats or the possibility of me going to an event.
But just the number and the nature of threats of violence and death, not just to MPs, but to their children and to their partners and to their staff, is like nothing we saw 20 years ago.
Politicians to sign ‘civility pledge’ following alleged attack on Haines
The speaker of the house, Milton Dick, will call for civility in parliament today, and some politicians are expected to sign a “civility pledge”.
Independent MP Helen Haines was the first to sign this pledge before she was allegedly attacked last week.
Fellow independent Kate Chaney, on Monday told ABC radio she would be adding her name:
double quotation markI think there’s something really symbolic about the fact that Helen was [the first] federal MP to have signed this. It is a very simple thing.
It just says ‘in my political life I pledge to act with honesty, respect, and compassion’.

That feels to me like a simple and poignant way to honour the contribution Helen’s made to the parliament and continue to try to embody those values that she personifies in the way that I do my work in parliament.
All Australian women will soon be able to attend a pharmacy for UTI treatment or re-supply of hormonal contraception, as the federal government expands a trial program to lower healthcare costs.

This program was previously restricted to concession card holders, but the health minister, Mark Butler, and minister for women, Katy Gallagher, announced on Monday that it would be expanded to benefit an estimated 900,000 women.

The 12-month trial, to begin from early 2027, will allow Australian women to access pharmacy treatment for uncomplicated urinary tract infections (UTIs) and initiation or re-supply of hormonal contraception.
The federal government will cover pharmacist consultation costs, of up to $38 per visit.

double quotation markFor too long, women’s experiences of the health system haven’t received the attention they deserve. We’re determined to change that. We’re making practical changes that give women more choice, make health care more accessible and help save women thousands of dollars over their lifetimes.
double quotation markWe want to make it easier for women to get care that fits into their lives.
Parliament will mark a solemn start to the sitting week as politicians pay tribute to independent MP Helen Haines, who was rammed by a vehicle outside her electoral office.
The popular crossbencher was allegedly targeted in a deliberate attack when she was struck by a four-wheel drive on the main street of the Victorian town of Wangaratta on 19 October.
She has had both legs amputated and remains in hospital a week after the incident.
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, will deliver a speech to parliament on Monday, reflecting on the alleged assault and its impact, and invite colleagues to do the same.
Fellow independent MP Monique Ryan described Dr Haines as the parliament’s “most gentle, principled and kind” member ahead of her planned remarks in the lower house.
“People who love her will try to do justice to Helen’s integrity and leadership,” she said.
“I hope that all members will rise to the occasion as Helen would do were she with us.
A fundraiser for charity Save the Children, set up on Wednesday by Haines’ family in lieu of flowers, had surpassed $1.2m in donations by Sunday afternoon.

Pauline Hanson says One Nation’s controversial cartoon series “will not be going anywhere”, after growing outrage over its offensive portrayal of federal politicians including previous depictions of some being run over by motor vehicles.
Hanson said her party’s Please Explain animation series had “nothing to do with the tragic attack on Helen Haines”, and claimed major party politicians wanted the series “censored”.
The series has garnered further criticism after videos from 2023 and 2024 were re-circulated online and discussed on Sunday morning political talk shows on the ABC and News24.

In one 2023 video, titled Under the Bus, Hanson appears to drive a bus over independent senator Lidia Thorpe, who had been depicted as lying under the vehicle’s tyres. In another from 2024, titled The State of Melbourne, former Victorian premier Daniel Andrews is shown being run down by a car driven by cartoon character Bluey, with the video ending with suggestions Anthony Albanese was also about to be hit.

Those cartoons, published years before the attack on Haines, have been criticised for portraying violence against politicians. Shadow minister Ted O’Brien said on News24 the cartoons were “not timely”, and while admitting he hadn’t seen them, questioned whether they were “appropriate in the current climate”.

The scrutiny comes after criticism of the cartoon series labelling Liberal MP Andrew Hastie a “traitor” and mocking Jacqui Lambie’s health condition. Hanson previously stood by those cartoons, but later apologised to Lambie and claimed she hadn’t seen that clip.

But Hanson, posting on social media on Sunday afternoon, rejected criticism of the other clips. She claimed “the Labor and Liberal Dirt Units are already back at work, attempting to use this tragedy to silence their critics and deflect from their own failings. Too many media organisations are happy to help them fling the dirt.”

double quotation markThe Please Explain cartoons have nothing to do with the tragic attack on Helen Haines. They will not be going anywhere. Liberal and Labor politicians want our cartoons censored because they don’t like the scrutiny.
Those seeking to exploit this tragedy to silence their critics should be ashamed of themselves.

Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’ll be bringing you the news from Canberra as parliament resumes, with MPs to pay tribute to Helen Haines and senators to return for the first week of estimates hearings in five months.

items.title: Serbia's Vučić concedes election defeat to student-led protest movement
paragraphs: The country's populist right-wing leader of 12 years says it is "clear" his Serbian Progressive Party has lost.

items.title: End approaching for Carrick but Man Utd owners' problems far bigger
paragraphs: There was an air of inevitability about Michael Carrick's walk around Old Trafford after the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth.
It is not unusual for Carrick to applaud the United fans. If anything, his acknowledgements were not as pronounced as they were in Como after the equally devastating loss.
But after eight games without a win, the worst run since 2015-16 and two horrific defeats in a week, the end is approaching for the United boss.

However, if anyone in a senior position at the club thinks the issues at Old Trafford will be solved simply by changing the head coach and, more importantly, the fans will be appeased by a new face in the dugout, the reaction from the stands on an awful day on and off the pitch would have very clearly told them otherwise.
On Friday, as he looked back on that 4-1 loss to Como and looked ahead to Bournemouth, Carrick said: "We'll be a different team on Sunday. We have to be a different team on Sunday."
Carrick could not answer if he will still be in charge for next Saturday's trip to Chelsea. He does not know.

"The responsibility is mine," he said. "What else can I say really right now? I totally understand the situation. I'm not expecting anything either way. I love this place and I'll always do what I feel is going to be the best for the football club."

The debt they initially landed on the club has now grown to over £1.15bn, according to their latest accounts. The amount it has cost in interest is £852m, according to respected football finance blogger Swiss Ramble. In the last financial year, the interest payment was £37m, an increase from £34m the previous year.
The argument is, that money could have been used far more productively to sign better players.
There had been hope Ratcliffe, a boyhood United fan, would change that when he struck a deal with the Glazers to become a minority shareholder on Christmas Eve 2023.
Instead, a succession of decisions have led to major questions over his handling of the club.

On the management side, United's hierarchy eventually backed Erik ten Hag after talking with alternatives in the wake of the shock 2024 FA Cup final triumph over Manchester City, spending over £200m on the likes of Leny Yoro, Matthijs de Ligt and Manuel Ugarte.

Last week, Ten Hag told the Athletic, external the club went back on a promise not to sell homegrown Scotland international Scott McTominay to fund Ugarte's £50m move from Paris St-Germain. They sacked the Dutchman in October 2024.
After that they persuaded Ruben Amorim to leave Sporting mid-season, when he wanted to wait until the summer.

They stuck with him after an unprecedented 15th-place finish, and again after United lost to League Two Grimsby in the EFL Cup, then sacked him in January when he clashed with director of football Jason Wilcox over playing style.
That led to Carrick's arrival to the end of the season, which turned into a permanent appointment after he guided the club back into the Champions League after a two-year absence.
A third dismissal in three seasons would not reflect well on anyone.

The 'Standards' banner that was held up on the Stretford End showing the images of legendary skippers Bryan Robson, Eric Cantona and Roy Keane was there to remind the executives running the club of the history they should be aspiring to.

Wilcox has largely operated behind the scenes but he could not fail to hear the obscenities being sung against him during today's game, nor the boos as he climbed into the vehicle taking him away from the stadium nearly two hours after the final whistle.

Recruited from a similar role at Southampton following the Ratcliffe takeover and elevated in status following the dismissal of Dan Ashworth, amid the decision to recruit Amorim, the 55-year-old is blamed by many fans for the club's recent recruitment, even though the budget was set at a much higher level.
Sat next to him at Old Trafford to watch the Bournemouth debacle unfold was chief executive Omar Berrada, who worked with Wilcox at Manchester City.

Having senior figures steeped in City's recent history was always a potential problem if results didn't go well. Berrada played no part in the recent Premier League proceedings that found City guilty of multiple breaches of financial rules, but the link is clear, and United's fans sang about that at Old Trafford as well.

If that wasn't enough, a ticket touting investigation launched in the summer led to condemnation from all United's major fan groups. The club argued they were trying to catch touts, while fans felt it was an attempt to drive regular match-goers out in favour of more corporate sales. The club are adamant that is not the case, but the argument is falling on deaf ears.

The same is also true of plans for a new 100,000-capacity stadium. The club conducted a survey which they said showed the majority of respondents were in favour of a new ground. The stadium is likely to cost in excess of £2bn and United spent £63.5m on land for it earlier this year.
Some supporters simply don't believe those figures. The Stretford End impolitely told Ratcliffe they had no interest in a new stadium as well today.
Carrick may take responsibility for poor results but there is far more than that causing unrest at Manchester United just now.
