items.title: Police using AI risks making discrimination worse, researchers warn
paragraphs: The growing use of AI in policing risks increasing discrimination against minority groups, researchers have warned.
Studies suggest that predictions of future crime hotspots may be based on biased data, which can magnify existing prejudice and create a dangerous feedback loop.
Experts are calling for the use of AI in policing to be reviewed with greater human oversight.

This would involve checking the data that forces use to find and remove any bias, according to Dr Carolyn McKay, an associate professor and researcher in digital justice at the University of Sydney Law School.
"The public functions of state policing ought to be subject to human oversight and scrutiny," she says.
The problem, according to McKay, is that AI systems are trained on data that already contains human bias, and this can lead to self-fulfilling prophecies.
Think of AI as a map-maker asked to draw a map of a city they have never visited. They are locked in a windowless room and can't go outside. All they have are maps that are 50 years old.

Anyone following the new map would find themselves stopping at walls that were knocked down years ago and looking for roads that no longer exist. The map-maker hasn't made anything new. They have only copied the old maps.
Now suppose the map-maker is handed a list of past crimes and where they took place, and asked to shade in where the next ones are likely to happen. Police then patrol the shaded areas.

More crime is recorded there simply because more officers are there to see it. Areas outside the shading appear to have less crime, because fewer people are looking. When the next map is drawn, the same areas are shaded even darker.
So the crime figures are not a full list of crimes. They are partly a record of where police have chosen to look.
The problem is as old as policing, but AI may be speeding it up.

Sarah Brayne, a sociologist at the University of Texas at Austin, spent time inside the Los Angeles Police Department studying how it uses big data. In her research paper, published in the American Sociological Review, she found that the force increasingly used data to predict crime, rather than only to respond to it.

She also found that the data fed into these systems was skewed. Crimes in public places were more likely to be seen and recorded, and police focus was disproportionately on black neighbourhoods. Once this goes into the system, she writes, "the predictions appear impartial".
The models, she says, create "a feedback loop in which they not only predict events such as crime or police contact, but also contribute to their future occurrence."

But that is a view challenged by Dr Dimitrios Kollias, an associate professor in multimodal artificial intelligence at the Queen Mary University of London (QMUL). He says that the technology has moved on to take the bias of historical data into account.
"The old-map analogy is useful for explaining how historical bias can be inherited, but it has its limits," he told BBC News.

"Modern AI systems do not simply retrieve or copy their training examples; they can combine learned information in new ways and generate outputs and solutions that were not explicitly present in those examples."
But those new insights pose a separate risk, Kollias adds.

"As AI systems become more capable of generating novel decisions and acting with greater autonomy, we need to ensure that their behaviour remains safe, reliable and under meaningful human control," he said.
But arguably a more intractable problem is dealing with the sometimes flawed information stored by authorities and which AI systems draw from.

Researchers at New York University said that many of their predictions may rely on what they call "dirty data". These are police records shaped, they say, by corrupt, biased or unlawful practices, including rigged crime figures and arrests of innocent people.
In their study, the researchers found that in nine of the 13 US areas they looked at, police data from periods of unlawful or biased policing was available to train these systems.

The system can't tell that this data is flawed, according to the researchers. It simply treats it as a pattern to repeat. It is as if the map-maker's compass points only to where crime has been recorded before. The map-maker thinks they have found a new crime hotspot, when all they have done is follow the bias of earlier officers.
McKay's answer is to have someone independent check the map before anyone uses it and rub out the lines that are wrong.

But cleaning up dirty data won't be easy. The mistakes aren't a few stray pencil marks. The whole map has been drawn on top of them. The New York University researchers say that technical fixes offered by the companies selling these systems aren't enough unless someone independently checks how the data was produced in the first place.
Because AI can see the world only through the data it is given, it can make serious mistakes which can harm people.

For example, a 2019 study in the journal Science looked at an AI system used in US healthcare to help decide which patients should get extra support. It did this by predicting whose care would cost the most. But there was an inherent bias in the data it drew from. Less was already being spent on black patients than on equally ill white patients, partly because of poorer access to care. By treating higher costs as a sign of greater need, the system unfairly favoured white patients.

It was as if the map-maker had been told to mark the sickest parts of the city but had marked the places where the most money was spent instead. When the researchers changed the system to predict how ill patients were, rather than how much their care would cost, the bias largely disappeared. The share of black patients picked for extra help would have risen from about 18% to 47%.
Kollias acknowledges that AI bias from dirty data is "an important concern".
"But this does not mean that bias is inevitable." he says.
"We can test systems for unfair outcomes, improve the data and objectives they use, and introduce safeguards to reduce these effects."

One improvement would be to provide additional data that provides context. What if the map-maker were given more than a list of crimes? They could also be shown which areas have been neglected - places with broken streetlights, little funding and missing public services. That could show whether the local environment plays a part. Instead of sending police cars to the shaded areas, councils might send money to fix the lighting, support the community and repair the area itself.
Yet even this may not be enough, according to McKay.
"The target environments are still intimately linked with their inhabitants," she says. "They might (continue to) be over-policed and marginalised."
She points to systems which were designed to use information about places rather than people. Even so, critics raised concerns that they still led to over-policing.

It is as if the map-maker promised to stop writing people's names on the map and to mark only the streets and buildings. But those streets were shaded because of years of neglect and heavy policing, so rubbing out the names changes very little.

AI has no beliefs or personality of its own. Like the map-maker in the windowless room, it knows only what it is told. If the person describing the city holds a grudge against one neighbourhood, that grudge ends up on the map.

But ultimately the problem is the human bias that fed the AI. People decide what a suspicious person looks like on CCTV, or what counts as a risky loan, and they bring their own cultural, educational and political biases with them. So perhaps AI can be part of the solution rather than a magnifier of the problem, says Kollias.
"A carefully designed and independently evaluated AI system can make some of these patterns more measurable and visible, giving us an opportunity to identify and reduce them."

But humans too have to play their part. The healthcare study shows that those choices can be checked and changed. That is why researchers argue that people must stay in the loop. Otherwise, like a map-maker inking over old pencil lines, AI risks leaving us all in a windowless room, permanently trapped in yesterday's mistakes.

items.title: Google’s AI search changes upended online publishing
paragraphs: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more about AI’s impact on the web, follow Emma Roth. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

The digital publishing industry has relied on Google for a very long time. Many outlets spent time and money optimizing their webpages to show up at the top of the search engine, with the goal of getting readers to click on their articles or discover their websites for the first time. For years, the relationship between Google and publishers was largely reciprocal; online publishers filled out Google’s search index with content, while Google supplied publications with exposure and traffic.

But that relationship has changed. The launch of Google’s AI search features — coupled with changes to the way it ranks search results — has made it harder for publishers to survive on traffic from Google alone. In 2024, Google rolled out AI Overviews, a feature that slots an AI-generated search result summarizing pages from across the web at the very top of Google Search, with links to sources its AI system determines to be the most useful placed below the summary. Instead of vying for clicks on the first page of Search, publishers became beholden to an AI system that regurgitates results, with no guarantee that users will actually click on the source of that information.

Though Google’s AI Overviews got off to a shaky start, the feature immediately raised concerns among publishers, with the News/Media Alliance saying it will be “catastrophic” to web traffic. A 2024 investigation from the Press Gazette found that Google’s AI Overviews appeared for almost a quarter of news-related searches in May 2024. By August, the outlet found that AI Overviews had begun impacting the visibility of publishers by replacing media sites that previously held the top spots on Google’s search engine for certain queries.

A future where Google could eventually stop sending traffic to outside sites on the web has only gotten closer as the company builds out its vision for an AI-powered search. In May 2025, it launched AI Mode, a feature that replaces Google’s standard search engine with a chatbot-like interface that provides detailed summaries from results on the web.

The concerns raised by the News/Media Alliance were real: Traffic to online publishers tanked following the launch of Google’s AI search features. A June 2025 report from The Wall Street Journal revealed how traffic to Business Insider, The Washington Post, HuffPost, and the WSJ itself has declined since 2022. Data from analytics company Similarweb suggested that search traffic to The New York Times sank from 44 percent to 35.5 percent in three years, the WSJ reported.

A report from Digiday pointed to similar dips at Digital Content Next (DCN), a trade association that represents outlets and media companies like Bloomberg, The Associated Press, The New York Times, Condé Nast, and Vox Media. Between May and June 2025, DCN says 19 of its members experienced a traffic loss on Google, ranging from 1 to 25 percent, Digiday reported. DMG Media, which owns Daily Mail and Metro, told the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority that click-through rates dropped by up to 89 percent between June and July 2025, citing impacts from AI Overviews. On top of all of this, Pew Research found that people are “less likely” to click on links to other websites when they see an AI Overview.

These numbers starkly contrast with Google’s claims that its AI search features are helping the web. Last year, Google Search head Liz Reid said click volume from the search engine remained “relatively stable,” adding that AI search is sending more clicks to different types of websites — especially those “with forums, videos, podcasts, and posts” from other users. Nick Fox, Google’s senior vice president of knowledge and information, told the BBC, “From our point of view, the web is thriving.”

In addition to scrutiny from regulators, publishers from around the globe have filed lawsuits against Google, claiming the company’s AI search features have negatively impacted traffic. Many lawsuits haven’t been successful. US District Judge Amit Mehta dismissed an antitrust case from Chegg and Penske Media, which owns The Rolling Stone, Billboard, The Hollywood Reporter, and The Verge. The same judge also rejected a proposed class action lawsuit surrounding AI Overviews filed by Arkansas newspapers.

Online publishers have had to adjust their strategies in the wake of falling search traffic, with many leaning on social media, newsletters, and subscriptions to promote and make money from their work. Others are using a toggle that allows them to opt out of appearing in AI Mode and AI Overviews without affecting their visibility in search — an option Google broadly rolled out following an order from the UK. But this still doesn’t fix sinking traffic.

Pushback from online publishers appears to have resulted in some changes to Google’s AI search features. The company has begun to make sources more prominent in AI Mode and AI Overviews, as hovering over a link in either feature will show a pop-up with a list of articles and accompanying images. Another AI search change puts in-line links “higher up in responses more frequently.”

Google will likely continue making changes to how it presents sources in AI search, while coming up with ways to compensate publishers that inform its results. The company says 400 publishers, including The Washington Post, CNN, Axios, and the Financial Times, are now part of its News AI pilot program, which licenses content to develop new AI features. It’s also testing a program that pays publishers for the use of their content in AI Overviews and AI Mode, according to reports from The Information and Digiday. Whether this program is enough to repair Google’s relationship with publishers remains to be seen.

items.title: The College of Magic turns ordinary kids into confident, top-hat wearing magicians
paragraphs: Lubelo Mthenjana, who's 11, performs a magic trick involving fire during the annual junior magic contest at the College of Magic in Cape Town, South Africa. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption

Dressed in a sharp black three-piece suit and a dapper yellow bow tie, Lubelo Mthenjana stands alone on a dark stage, taking in the last few seconds of quiet before the curtain opens. He takes a deep breath as his name is announced. Then he opens his arms wide and flashes a bright smile.
"Hello everyone! My name is Lubelo Mthenjana, and I will be performing for you … some magic!"

The audience of about 30 children and parents is spellbound. They laugh out loud as he makes a string of paper clips vanish into a plastic cup and gasp with surprise as the clips reappear inside a matchbox. Then comes his best trick: He conjures sweets out of thin air and tosses them into the crowd. The room erupts. As Lubelo takes his final bow to thunderous applause, his mom beams a proud smile at the 11-year-old apprentice magician.

On this cloudy Saturday morning in September, Cape Town's College of Magic is buzzing with energy as dozens of students are competing in the annual junior magic contest. Heading to their classrooms, children in top hats, crisp white shirts and ties dash up and down a staircase decorated with a riot of brightly colored posters. On every floor, display cabinets overflow with magic wands, sparkly hats, silk scarves, handcuffs, dice, Rubik's Cubes, toys, photographs and dozens of trophies earned by students in competitions all over the world.
Students examine a set of trick playing cards during a class at the College of Magic, whose pupils are ages 10 to 18. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
Aspiring magician Sibabalwe Sibaj, 17, juggles while riding a unicycle. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption

Outside the old red-brick Victorian mansion, framed by palm trees, two teenage boys zip around the car park on unicycles. Balls, clubs and diabolos shoot up into the air as a handful of kids practice juggling on the porch.

Tucked away in a peaceful suburb, this extraordinary school is a real-world Hogwarts: Africa's only school for youthful stage magicians and illusionists. Every Saturday morning, about 190 starry-eyed students ages 10 to 18 attend classes in everything from puppetry, mime and clowning to juggling, card tricks, illusions, mentalism, stage magic, theater production and escapology. "All the skills that will make a good magician," sums up David Gore, the school's founder.
In 1980, Gore was studying law and paying his way by performing at private magic shows when he and a friend came up with the idea of starting a magic school.

David Gore founded the Cape Town College of Magic in 1980, defying apartheid era laws by teaching multiracial classes. In the decades since, the college has trained thousands of magicians, illusionists and performers. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption

"We walked into our local newspaper house with our top hats and tails, told our story about how we were starting the College of Magic, did magic for the journalists in the newsroom, and they published an article," he recalls. "From that article, we had 34 young people who started attending formal weekly classes studying magic."

At the time, South Africa was still in the grip of apartheid, a brutal system of racial segregation that dictated almost every aspect of daily life. State schools were strictly segregated. Students of different races could not even share park benches, some building entrances or take the same public transport to school. Yet the College of Magic was multiracial from day one.
The College of Magic Students are entranced by a class on close-up magic. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption

"When we started out, our organization was illegal," says Gore, referring to its no-segregation policy. "This was an opportunity for young people from all backgrounds to come together around a common interest in magic, to learn about each other and understand each other."
Nearly 50 years later, the school continues to stand out in a city still deeply divided along racial and economic lines.

"Many of our young people remain siloed in their socioeconomic groups, very often along either language or racial lines," Gore explains. "Some arrive in very fancy cars, others have taken an hour in a collective taxi to get here. But when they're here, they work with the same equipment, the same classes, the same stages and get the same food."
Though the six-year course costs a fee, about 80% of the students cannot afford to pay and are sponsored, mostly through private donations.
How do you master the arts of juggling and spinning plates? Practice, practice, practice. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption

"Magic is such a wonderful companion for our young people here in South Africa," says Gore. "They're able to carry it in their pockets, into the communities and the marginalized areas where most of our students come from. It's an art form that can be performed without being wealthy or needing very expensive instruments."

Multiple studies have found that learning magic can help children develop self-esteem, curiosity, lateral thinking, fine motor skills and problem-solving abilities. A 2021 study conducted by researchers at the Universities of Hertfordshire and Edinburgh found that children who learned and performed a magic trick showed greater improvements in creative fluency and originality than those who completed a similar art activity.

Themba Van der Westhuizen, 12, practices a magic trick on a schoolmate at the College of Magic. Van der Westhuizen says he enjoys impressing friends and family with his tricks and that learning to become a magician has boosted his self-confidence. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption

Even watching a magic trick can challenge our assumptions about the world and stimulate more original thinking. In another study, researchers found that it stimulated areas of the brain associated with cognitive flexibility and processing unconventional information.

In this photo from 2021, Anele Dyasi, a former student and now teacher of at the College of Magic, reaches out to a white dove at the school's dove enclosure. The college has since stopped using animals in its performances. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption

"Many of our graduates don't become performers or magicians. But one of the skills that this young generation is most going to need for their careers is creativity," adds Gore. "That is what's so fantastic about magic: Nothing's impossible for us."

For 11-year-old Lubelo, magic has "opened up a new world." After watching a family friend perform a trick, he was determined to join the College of Magic. He had to wait until he turned 10 to enroll. Now, he's hooked.

At home in Makhaza township, about 40 minutes from the college, Lubelo spends his free time watching magic shows online and practicing tricks on his brothers and parents. He keeps his props, tools and other secrets in a box hidden away in his room. He's even chosen a stage name: Spade Boy — after his favorite card suit.
Aspiring magician Lubelo Mthenjana is clearly the family star as they stand outside their home in the Khayelitsha neighborhood of Cape Town. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
"If my mom is cooking and asks me to pass the potatoes, I'll start juggling with them," he says mischievously.
Lubelo has also persuaded several friends to join the school, becoming something of an ambassador in a community where magic is often frowned upon and associated with witchcraft.

"Many people are afraid of magic. But at the College of Magic, we don't do dark magic," he explains. "We just do the kind of magic that makes somebody smile, makes them happy and takes the stress away."
Sometimes, he says, other children ask whether he can turn people into pigs. "Then I just say: 'Let me start with you!' and they run away," he laughs.

Lubelo's mother, Yandiswa, says the magic lessons have boosted her son's confidence. They have brought another kind of relief, too. "It keeps him occupied and away from this environment and everything that's happening outside," she says.

With nearly 60 murders per day, South Africa has one of the world's highest crime rates, and several of Cape Town's townships are among the areas hardest hit by violent crime. From his home in Makhaza, Lubelo often hears gunshots. He says boys his age are drawn into using and selling drugs.

The magic community hasn't been spared. Just a few weeks before our visit, the school held a memorial service for Duma Mgqoki, a promising young magician, former student and volunteer teacher who was killed in a shooting in July. He was 22.

In this photo from 2021, Duma Mgqoki tries his hand at a card trick at the Cape Town College of Magic. In 2026, Mgqoki was killed in a shooting in the Philippi neighborhood of Cape Town. Many of the College's students come from neighborhoods marked by unemployment and violent crime. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption

"On a weekly basis, some of our young people come to us saying they've experienced crime on a firsthand basis," says David Gore. "These things need to change, and we're very hopeful that the younger generation of today are going to be the force of change to bring about the society which we all would like to live in."
Students from the Cape Town College of Magic do their magic trick homework in the Mfuleni neighborhood where they live. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
Back at the college, after finishing his show, Lubelo steps off the stage to a chorus of fist bumps and backslaps from his excited friends.
"He was so good! We're swimming in happiness!" one teenager beams. Without skipping a beat, the boys run outside, pick up colorful leather balls and launch into a juggling competition.
Lubelo Mthenjana begins his performance during the annual junior magic contest at the College of Magic. Spoiler alert: He won in his age class! Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption

By now, a light drizzle has set in, but the two unicyclists are still making their rounds in the car park, seemingly undeterred. "Even when the storm comes, even when the world ends, I'll never stop unicycling," declares 14-year-old Joshua Clyde as he whizzes past.

Inside the cafeteria, a wide-eyed crowd has gathered around a teacher showing off a magic trick. With a snap of his fingers and what seems like a touch of superhuman power, he makes a coin disappear from a student's closed fist. It reappears beneath the student's watch.
Others have opted for the puppeteering class, upstairs, where pairs of students are taught to bring their humanoid puppets to life.
Puppets are part of the curriculum at the College of Magic. Teacher Jesse Brooks shares his puppet mastery with 12-year-old Okuhle Ntshutshe. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption

Footsteps drum up and down the staircase as the remaining performers in this Saturday competition rehearse their routines, nerves and excitement mounting. "Why am I so nervous? I've got this!" says bubbly Kungentando Ndenetya, 12, repeating the mantra to herself.
Aspiring magician Kungentanda Ndenetya performs during the annual junior magic contest at the Cape Town College of Magic. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption

Once every child has performed, the jury retires to a quiet office to deliberate. All four judges are former students or teachers at the College of Magic. Twenty-five-year-old Caitlin Hutchison, who comes from "a long line of magicians," says the school taught her "resilience training." Monica Nyakatya graduated in 2009 and now works in logistics but has remained close to the institution that, she says, "shaped" her.
The judges at the annual junior magic contest applaud after a performance at the College of Magic in Cape Town, South Africa. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption

The deliberations are strictly confidential. When the judges return, everyone gathers in the small theater. The young magicians hold hands, waiting anxiously as the results are announced. Then comes Lubelo's age group.
Prestidigitation pupil Lubelo Mthenjana adjusts his bow tie. Many of the College's students sport traditional magician attire like bow ties and top hats. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption
Beaming, he strides onto the stage to shake each judge's hand — then runs into his mother's arms.
As soon as he gets home, he will practice his newest tricks.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.
Julie Bourdin is a freelance journalist based in South Africa and France. She covers human rights and climate-related stories across Africa and beyond.

Tommy Trenchard is an independent photojournalist based in Cape Town, South Africa. He has previously contributed photos and stories to NPR on the Mozambique cyclone of 2019, Indonesian death rituals and illegal miners in abandoned South African diamond mines and won a World Press Photo prize for the images in his story for NPR on clashes between elephants and people in Zambia.

items.title: Flight disruption and thousands without electricity after Storm Boelo
paragraphs: Thousands of homes across the island of Ireland are without power after Storm Boelo.
Northern Ireland Electricity (NIE) said 7,000 customers have been affected, while about 41,000 homes, farms and businesses across the Republic of Ireland are without electricity on Sunday morning.
The worst impacted areas in Northern Ireland include Springfield in County Fermanagh and Bushmills in County Antrim, where more than 1,000 homes near each village are without power.
Flights have also been cancelled at Belfast City, Belfast International and Dublin Airports due to the storm.

An NIE spokesperson said high winds and severe weather conditions during Saturday night and into the early hours of Sunday morning resulted in a "level of damage to the electricity network, leading to power outages for some customers".
NIE said customers can check estimated restoration times using its Powercheck tool, external.
A spokesperson for the Republic of Ireland's ESB Networks said properties in the north west of the country are primarily affected.
"As Met Éireann weather warnings remain in place, there may be further power outages this morning," they said.
Among the villages worst affected in the Republic of Ireland is Milford in County Donegal with more 1,600 homes without power and Aghagad in County Sligo with over 1,200 homes impacted.
ESB Networks said crews have been deployed to all impacted areas and they "expect the vast majority of impacted customers to have their supply restored by this evening".
A yellow weather warning for all of Northern Ireland is in place until midday while a yellow wind warning is also in place in County Donegal until 15:00 local time on Sunday.
At Belfast City Airport, flights departing to Edinburgh, Cardiff, Manchester and Kirkwall on Sunday morning have been cancelled.
Meanwhile, flights arriving from Edinburgh, Leeds Bradford, Cardiff, Manchester, Birmingham and Inverness have also been cancelled.
At Belfast International Airport, 17 flights have been cancelled this morning.
"Storm Boelo continues to cause some disruption to flights today. Please check with your airline for latest flight information as delays can be expected," a spokesperson said.
At Dublin Airport, strong winds continue to have an impact on flight operations on Sunday.
"Mainly due to weather issues in other countries, airlines have so far cancelled 12 inbound and 12 outbound flights," Graeme McQueen from the airport's operator daa has said.
He advised passengers to travel to the airport as normal and keep in contact with their airline, adding that further disruption is possible due to the wind warnings.
An amber warning across parts of County Antrim and County Londonderry ended at 10:00 GMT on Sunday.
On Saturday, Northern Ireland's strongest gust of wind reached 78mph and was recorded in Orlock Head, County Down.
Magilligan in County Londonderry recorded 73mph and Castlederg in County Tyrone recorded a wind gust of 70mph.
Westerly winds will continue to gust close to 70mph in exposed coastal areas until well into the afternoon.
Generally, though winds will gradually ease through the afternoon with a significant reduction this evening.
An orange wind warning ended in County Donegal at 09:00 local time on Sunday.
On Saturday, Malin Head in Donegal had gusts of 83mph recorded.
The last 24 hours also brought notable amounts of rain with Castlederg and Lough Fea in the Sperrins recording almost 40mm.
Over 30mm has been recorded at Killylane in the Antrim Glens and 30mm at Stormont in Belfast.
Sunday is due to be a drier day but still very windy with some sunshine and occasional passing showers.
The disturbed weather pattern will continue into the half term week as another deep area of low pressure will bring more strong winds later on Monday and through to Tuesday.
The Met Office has issued a yellow wind warning across parts of Northern Ireland for this system which may be updated later on Sunday.
The second half of the new week, however, looks somewhat quieter, drier, and less windy.

items.title: Lights out: the island that goes dark to save young seabirds – in pictures
paragraphs: Once a year, Corvo, the smallest and most northerly island of Portugal’s Azores archipelago, goes dark. Since 2019, the island’s 450 or so inhabitants have chosen to switch off the lights every autumn for five nights to tackle the disastrous effects of artificial light on Cory’s shearwaters, a seabird endemic to the Atlantic Ocean.
It began in 1991 when the community noticed huge numbers of deaths among young shearwaters.
The juveniles spend three months in their nests before attempting their first flight to the ocean, orienting themselves by the stars.
Unfortunately, many are fatally confused by the artificial glow of streetlights, and end up crashing into Vila do Corvo’s narrow streets.

Local people began rescuing them at night, roaming through the village in the dark. This inspired other communities, and in 1995, the Azorean government launched the “SOS Cagarro” [shearwaters] campaign to include the other eight islands.
In subsequent years, the Portuguese Society for the Study of Birds (SPEA) joined the project, helping it grow.
At nearly 2am, dedicated young volunteers remain engaged in their work, helping with the recovered birds

Leonardo Xavier is one of the young volunteers who helps to capture the disoriented birds around the village, top left. Top right, the webbed foot of a Cory’s shearwater. Rui Pimentel, left, is Corvo’s forest ranger, and on the frontline of Cory’s shearwater conservation. Cats, right, are the main predators of Cory’s shearwater chicks. The SPEA team has installed ultrasonic devices around nests to deter attacks
I discovered the initiative on my second trip to Corvo, in June 2024. I knew of the Cory’s shearwater because I had travelled to the Azores before and had the chance to observe them in the open sea.
But it was not until I saw a campaign sticker in a shop on the island that I found out about the blackout. When it was explained to me, I decided to come back and document it.
To me, the message of this story is that there is always hope, especially when we involve future generations and teach them to care about our planet and its beauty.
Today, Corvo is still the only island that performs a full blackout of public illumination to help the birds find their way to the ocean without interference from artificial lights.

A long exposure photograph of Vila do Corvo during the blackout, with only security lights on. People do not have to turn off their household lights, but many choose to do so. The island of Flores can be seen in the distance

Tania Pipa, left, a marine biologist from SPEA, checks each artificial and natural Cory’s shearwater nest on the island. A native of São Miguel Island, the largest of the Azores, she travels to Corvo every year to check on the birds. ‘To me, the day I don’t hear Cory’s shearwaters in the Azores, it will certainly not be the Azores,’ she says. Right, a Cory’s shearwater in its artificial nest

The island sinks into darkness and the stars can be seen clearly; the birds begin their journeys, hoping to find their way to the ocean, while people walk through Vila do Corvo, the only village on the island, to find and rescue any fallen birds.
Those rescued will be placed in cardboard boxes overnight to recover, and released the next day from a cliff close to the ocean, giving them a second chance to reach the water, their new home.
The campaign says more than 30,000 Cory’s shearwater fledglings have been rescued in the Azores since 2015 – about 6,000 of them on Corvo alone.
This collective effort is a powerful example of how reducing light pollution can restore ecological balance. It demonstrates that small changes can significantly affect biodiversity.

How can an action like this inspire global reflection? This intentional blackout is not just an act of conservation but a step towards developing the ability to coexist with nature without disrupting its rhythms.
The night sky above Caldeirão, the volcanic crater that shapes the island of Corvo
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

items.title: Arup creates arrow-shaped viewpoint for Fehmarnbelt Tunnel project
paragraphs: A zigzagging path tops the demountable Pilen viewpoint in Denmark, created by engineering firm Arup to give the public views of the construction of the vast Fehmarnbelt Tunnel.

Fehmarnbelt Tunnel is an 18-kilometre-long road-and-rail tunnel being built underwater between Rødbyhavn in Denmark and Puttgarden in Germany to improve links between continental Europe and Scandinavia.
Pilen, whose name means “the arrow” in Danish, offers views of its construction site to help the public gain an understanding of its scale.
According to Arup, its design is intended to symbolise travel, evoking an arrow or compass needle, and it points to the site where the tunnel emerges in Germany to orient users.
The ramped structure measures 217 metres in length, reflecting the size of each of the 89 individual concrete elements that will form the tunnel, which will be the longest of its kind.

“The arrow-shaped design points towards the location where the Fehmarnbelt tunnel emerges on the German side, acting as a large compass needle for visitors,” project architect Kristian Winther told Dezeen.
“At 217 metres long, the viewpoint also reflects the length of one of the tunnel elements,” Winther continued.

“We hope the viewpoint will create a closer connection between the tunnel project, the local community, and visitors, giving people an opportunity to experience the scale of the project more directly.”
Pilen was designed for contractors Femern, which is overseeing the tunnel’s construction and wanted to open up the construction site to the public.
The site was chosen for its proximity to the tunnel portal, maximising views of construction work, but also for the expansive views of the coastal landscape beyond.
Pilen’s structure is built from landfill timber and steel and designed to be demounted once the tunnel is complete.

To facilitate this, all the components, including the foundations, are engineered to be easily reused in other projects, “helping to give the materials a life beyond the viewpoint itself”, Winther said.
The main deck is formed from timber and landscaped with greenery and local vegetation, through which a fully accessible landscaped walkway zigzags as it rises 24 metres above sea level.
Fehmarnbelt tunnel is scheduled for completion in 2029. It is expected to reduce journey times between Hamburg and Copenhagen to 2.5 hours by train.
We recently reported on a 300,000 square metres land reclamation scheme in Denmark created as part of the project, which will be landscaped with ponds and planting.
Other viewpoints recently featured on Dezeen include the Titlis Tower in the Swiss Alps by Herzog & de Meuron and Lech Mountain Mirror in the Austrian Alps by Snøhetta.

items.title: Wind gust of 84mph recorded as Storm Boelo brings disruption
paragraphs: Hundreds of homes were left without power on Sunday morning after back-to-back storms led to flooding and felled trees in Wales.
A wind gust of 84mph (135km/h) was recorded in Capel Curig, Conwy county, on Saturday, which also saw 2.1in (54.6mm) of rain.

Police forces and councils said they have been dealing with flooding and trees down as Storm Boelo followed Storm Austen over the weekend, while there is also significant disruption on Wales' railways.
Four flood warnings were in place in south Wales on Sunday morning, while 555 homes in Rhayader, Powys, were left without power.
About 100 homes across south Wales were also without power on Sunday morning, while SP Energy said it was dealing with 14 separate power outages in north and mid Wales.
The National Grid said its engineers were working to restore power to the households affected "as quickly as possible" and apologised for the disruption.
Most of Wales was not covered by a weather warning during Storm Boelo, although a yellow warning for wind covers parts of north Wales until 21:00 GMT on Sunday.
A total of 2.2in (55.2mm) of rain was also recorded in Bute Park in Cardiff throughout Saturday.
Buses are running instead of a number of Transport for Wales train services due to flooding and poor weather.
A TfW spokesperson said incidents included the line being blocked between Cardiff Central and Bridgend and flooding on the railway between Bridgend and Maesteg.
Rhondda Cynon Taf council said it had been dealing with numerous reports of trees down.
Natural Resources Wales had four flood warnings for the River Ely in place at 09:20.
Cowbridge Road in Ely, Cardiff, has been closed due to high water levels.

items.title: More wet and windy weather to follow stormy weekend
paragraphs: The unsettled weather is set to continue into the start of the week, although conditions should be less severe than those seen across the country since Friday.

Another area of low pressure is expected to deepen as it approaches the UK from the south-west, bringing a further spell of heavy rain and potentially strong winds to much of the country on Monday and into Tuesday.

Rain is expected to develop from the west, with some areas potentially seeing heavy and persistent downpours. Combined with strong winds, this could lead to further travel disruption and difficult conditions, particularly in exposed coastal areas.

As with Storm Boelo, northern parts of the UK are likely to see the strongest winds and greatest impacts as Tuesday approaches. A yellow warning for wind is in place across Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and northern England from 03:00 on Tuesday until midnight.

However, uncertainty remains over the strength and exact track of the developing low-pressure system, meaning the areas likely to experience the most severe conditions could change as the forecast evolves.
It is also not yet clear whether the system will be strong enough to be named as another storm.
You can follow the latest updates on BBC Weather online and Instagram, as well as TV and radio.

items.title: When a teen posts a selfie, how much filter is 'too much' filter?
paragraphs: How much filter is too much filter for kids and teens posting selfies on social media?

That is the question state attorneys general across the country are grappling with following a landmark settlement with Meta this summer. As part of the agreement, the social media giant agreed to block some digital beauty filters for minors — specifically those mimicking extreme transformations like cosmetic procedures or heavy makeup.
Now, the burden falls on state officials to tell Meta where to draw the line. But defining where harmless fun ends and harmful manipulation begins is far from straightforward.

For teenagers navigating the digital landscape, the pressure of online perfection is a daily reality. Much of that pressure has been driven by online beauty trends like "Instagram face." Coined in 2019 by The New Yorker writer Jia Tolentino, the phrase refers to a look characterized by a small button nose, high cheekbones and pouty lips. While traditionally only achievable in real life through plastic surgery or extreme makeup, it can be applied instantly online using beauty filters.

Mia Lerner, a 17-year-old high school senior in California and a youth body image activist, knows the toll these digital tools can take. She told NPR experimenting with beauty filters contributed to her eating disorder and left her struggling with her self-image.

"I've even tried to fix my nose with AI," Lerner said. "My face looks a lot better, I think, in [the] photo that I manipulated with these beauty filters. But I'm still living with this nose that I see in the mirror."
Lerner welcomes the aspect of the Meta settlement that aims to restrict beauty filters for minors. "It's a very important step in the right direction," Lerner said.
However, the agreement reached in August between Meta and 47 U.S. states — plus Washington D.C. and three territories — does not institute a blanket ban on all digital effects.

Filters that transform users into playful characters, like elves or puppies, will remain available for young people. But so will filters offering subtle beautification effects — such as smoothing skin tone or adding a slight eye glow.
It is this category of relatively minor editing that particularly concerns Lerner.

"When I see something that has been so obviously AI-generated, it's very easy for me to logically say, 'Well, that's obviously been manipulated so I can't compare myself to that,'" Lerner said. "But when I see these videos of people who are just slightly edited, it's a lot easier for me to go down that comparison path."
Meta has previously implemented measures to manage beauty filters, which are increasingly powered by artificial intelligence.

The tech giant has already banned filters that explicitly promote cosmetic surgery, such as those overlaying pre-surgery marker lines onto skin. It has also shut down its platform for third-party creators of these tools, introduced mandatory labels for AI-generated content, and deployed automated AI detection systems. Despite these systems, harmful aesthetic filters and features that keep children trapped in an endless cycle of scrolling, clicking, and staying online persistently slipped past these guardrails, as a federal judge wrote in a summary judgement denying Meta's defense this summer.

Meta is not the only tech company grappling with teen access to beauty filters. TikTok also restricts users under the age of 18 from using them. Snapchat does not restrict teen access to filters. Neither company responded to NPR's request for comment. YouTube told NPR it does not have any filters. But there's nothing stopping users from posting images or videos made with third party filters to the platform — or onto TikTok and Instagram, for that matter.

Meanwhile, state attorneys general are reaching the end of a two-month window they set themselves to provide Meta with guidance in the form of a letter on what constitutes a bannable filter — and what does not.
They face a moving target, as digital beauty standards evolve rapidly.

"If the states want to define what is a beauty filter, they should define what is beauty," said Florencia Solari, a creative technologist who has spent years developing AI and augmented reality experiences for global brands.

Solari noted that trend cycles move quickly. "Instagram face" is already falling out of favor. "People are starting to move away from that because it's starting to look a bit clownish," Solari said. "Now it's going towards extreme thinness. So that's another problem."

As a result, the tools that are used to achieve the latest look are therefore also changing. So what might be branded by lawmakers as an "extreme" beauty filter in 2026 will likely be different in 2027.
While beauty standards are changing quickly, so is technology.

Instead of sitting in boardrooms debating pixel thresholds for cheekbones, Kelly Frasier, the co-author of a recent study highlighting the negative impacts of social media on body issues in adolescents, said legislators should consider the fact that teens will soon be able to use AI to create entire fake universes around themselves, not just change the way they look. So they should focus on broader AI regulation for minors.

"I think that legislators are asking the wrong question if they're asking where to draw the line for beauty filters," said Frasier. "And to be honest, filters will probably become completely obsolete within the next few years."

On top of the technological and cultural challenges, legal experts warn that individual states may struggle to reach a consensus on what does and does not constitute what the settlement agreement describes as a "cosmetic procedure filter."

"What we don't really have a sense of is what happens if the states disagree with each other?" said David Greene, senior counsel at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. "What if one state finds, you know, eyebrow lifting to be completely acceptable and another one thinks it's awful?"

NPR reached out to the attorneys general offices in all four plaintiff states that led the trial — California, Colorado, Kentucky, and New Jersey — for an update on the guidelines. But officials either declined to comment or did not respond.
Beyond the U.S., some international regulators are hoping to avoid discussions around beauty filter definitions entirely.
In Europe, the proposed KIDS Act — designed to regulate youth social media usage — takes a sweeping approach.

In that plan, "Beauty filters – not extreme beauty filters; beauty filters full stop – are forbidden for minors," said European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier. Regnier said EU legislators are closely watching the implementation of the U.S. settlement. "We want child-friendly services for our children. A beauty filter has nothing to do with a child-friendly service," Regnier said.
Meta says that it plans to enforce the ban on "cosmetic procedure filters" by early next year.

For youth activists like Lerner, the hope is that tech companies and regulators will include teens in these discussions. "So often it's just the government or these companies in these conversations," Lerner said. "The company should be asking us for our actual perspectives, like 'Are people actually using these extreme AI filters or is that not going to make a difference?' 'Do we need to target something else?'"
Meta said the company has partnered with teens over the years, but did not respond to NPR's question asking if it is doing so currently.

items.title: Five uncanny venues where guests are treated to frightfully unique interiors
paragraphs: With spooky season in full swing and Halloween rapidly approaching, this lookbook rounds up five venues featuring unusual decor, including faux body parts, dead insects and slaughterhouse machinery.
A London pub, a brewery in Copenhagen and a bar in Shanghai are among the selected projects.

This is the latest in our lookbooks series, which provides visual inspiration from Dezeen’s archive. For more inspiration, see previous lookbooks featuring billiard tables, wooden staircases and bookmaxxed interiors.
The owner of this Shanghai bar is interested in insects – local studio Atelier XY honoured this through the addition of over 1,000 preserved specimens.

A wooden grid covering the back wall and ceiling of the bar area features thousands of beetles housed in individual recesses, while a glass-brick wall containing 42 preserved Thai Black tarantulas acts as a partition. Pull-out drawers, containing yet more taxidermied creatures, double as slim side tables.
The atmosphere of being inside an oven was recreated in this Valencia nightclub by Spanish firm Clap Studio.
Red lighting, stainless steel, glowing ceiling grids and burnt-looking alpi wood cladding come together to create a blisteringly immersive interior.
Bar Far, Italy, by Clementine Keith-Roach and Christopher Page
Human legs support tables, disembodied hands hold candlesticks and torsos emerge from walls in this unsettlingly cave-like bar by artists Clementine Keith-Roach and Christopher Page.
The space, which was open on a temporary basis during early 2026, was described as being “at once church and tomb, prophecy and ruin, heaven and hell” by installation curator Vittoria Bonifati.
Dark wood panelling and chairs upholstered in tartan set the mood for The Scottish Room, which inhabits the third floor of The Audley, a pub in London’s Mayfair neighbourhood.

Designed by architecture studio Laplace, this room belies the rest of the comparatively playful interior, being dominated by a sprawling chandelier made from deer antlers hanging above a nine-metre-long oaken table.
A former butchery in Copenhagen’s Meatpacking District has been converted into a lofty brewery by local studio Pihlmann Architects, with an interior partitioned using translucent curtains.
The studio elected to retain the original system of hanging rails, which the abattoir would have once used to suspend up to 980 animal carcasses.

items.title: Just Eat's AI apocalypse raises a glaring question
paragraphs: Lots of gastronomy businesses have gone all in on unappetising AI food imagery, but surely even the most enthusiastic slop purveyor would baulk at the Just Eat AI fail. The food delivery app's implementation of very literal text-to-image generation saw restaurants' menus filled with grotesque fantasy creations.
Just Eat has apologised and said it was removing the images. But what was it thinking?

As reported by the BBC, images spotted on the Just Eat app in the UK include a bacon and egg soda bread cocktail at a Northern Ireland cafe and a 'jacket potato' represented by an actual jacket with pictures of baked potatoes on it.

Other gems included a plain garlic bread shaped like a plane because of a typo, a bowl of tiger cubs (tiger prawns, apparently), a literal toad in the hole and a 'lighter' breakfast depicted as a cigarette lighter.

If I found out a particular restaurant was using AI to create images for its food, I just wouldn't eat there. Actually, even the fact @JustEatUK are trialling this out is already making me think of avoiding the app from now on. #JustEat #AI #food https://t.co/5OV94zwUzKOctober 21, 2026

Just Eat is really late to this party. Its rival Uber Eats went through this embarrassment almost three years ago. The technology has advanced massively since then, but somehow Just Eat managed to roll out an even worse implementation. On social media, people have been asking how a $4bn company managed to mess up so badly and how it could roll out such a risky feature without properly testing it.

But there's also an even more obvious question: why? Even if the AI 'worked' as intended and generated an image of the perfect Platonic ideal of each dish, using fake product photography for food seems like a guaranteed way to cause disappointment and complaints from customers.

Users have already been sharing screenshots on social media, showing 'AI vs reality' comparisons, with some complaining that Just Eat has refused to issue refunds despite the actual product ordered not even remotely resembling the AI hallucination.

That's not the fault of the business making the food when the false impression was created by an AI image foisted on it by the app. They join the growing list of businesses suffering because of automatic AI-generated images pushed on their products on platforms as varied as Amazon and Reddit.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: The penguins are noisy, the people fantastic - what it takes to be an Antarctic postmaster
paragraphs: George Clarke is returning for his third stint at Port Lockroy

It is hardly a typical round for a postie, but for five months of the year George Clarke leaves behind his partner and friends in Bristol to become a postmaster at the world's most southerly post office - in Antarctica.
"I thought it sounded like an amazing experience - living away from home for a few months on a very small island with five other people and 1,000 penguins," says Clarke.
He takes up his role as Port Lockroy postmaster from late October to March, during the southern hemisphere summer.

The part-time festival worker and artist says his days are spent sorting postcards, processing letters and arranging for the post to hitch a ride north on passing ships before being distributed around the world.
"The penguins are noisy and smelly. The people are fantastic," he said. "I've fallen in love with the Antarctic wilderness."
Port Lockroy is home to a colony of about 1,000 gentoo penguins

When Clarke sets off with in a team of six on Monday, it will be his third voyage to Antarctica helping the UK Antarctic Heritage Trust (UKAHT) to conserve Port Lockroy, a former British science research facility.
Unlike a regular post office, there is no fleet of vans ready to whisk the mail away.

"When we collect up all the postcards and we've sorted through them, we've bagged them up, we've weighed them, we then need to look to see which ships are heading north towards the Falklands," he said.
"Then we get them on email or the radio and we say, 'Hello, would you mind taking some postcards with you?' And they're always very keen to oblige."
Unsurprisingly, running a post office for six people does not take up all of Clarke's time at Port Lockroy.
He is also the deputy base commander, helps with the cleaning and maintenance of the site, and helps with wildlife observations for the British Antarctic Survey (BAS).
"The primary objective of the charity is conservation of the heritage surrounding UK exploration in Antarctica," Clarke said.
Postmaster George Clarke says he has fallen in love with the Antarctic wilderness

The team of six is about to embark on the second term of a three-year plan to shore-up and restore the island's largest building, Bransfield House, which is home to a museum, the post office and a shop.
They will install beams in the roof and 30 steel and timber props in the floor to help it withstand rain and snow.
The site on Goudier Island was chosen in the 1940s to become a permanent British foothold in Antarctica because it was known as a safe place to anchor by early 20th Century whaling ships.
The remnants of that industry are still clear to see, with the bones of whales killed long ago for their oil littering part of the shore.
Port Lockroy operated until 1962, when British research was moved to larger and more modern sites in Antarctica.
Clarke (second from left) and the team have been training in the Brecon Beacons before heading to Antarctica
The journey from the UKAHT base in Cambridgeshire to Port Lockroy takes about a week.
"We fly to Ushuaia via Buenos Aires in Argentina and we'll probably have a couple of days to acclimatise slightly," Clarke said.
"We'll then jump on a ship that will take us south to the Antarctic Peninsula and it takes four or five days."
Clarke's colleagues are also excited to get the new season under way.
Base commander and RAF veteran Carole McCullough said: "I applied for the role looking for a bit of an adventure, and Antarctica is the ultimate adventure.
"The team work, the bonding, the appreciation of the place - it's all going to make for the most wonderful experience."
Wildlife monitor and museum manager Alice Parr added: "I actually applied for a role three years ago and was selected as reserve.
"I tried again - clearly persistence pays off! I'm incredibly excited to be managing the museum and counting penguins. It's the opportunity of a lifetime."

items.title: Signs suggest Thomas Markle Sr may be ‘sex offender of the grossest kind’, says Philippine minister
paragraphs: All signs point to Thomas Markle Sr being a “possible sex offender of the grossest kind” although a full forensic investigation will give a “definitive picture”, the Philippine interior minister has told the Guardian.

Authorities in the south-east Asian country are analysing digital images allegedly belonging to the estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex that were said to have been found at his former home in Cebu. Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, reported to authorities last week that he had apparently discovered a stash of child sexual abuse images.

“In these cases where family disputes are mixed up, we have to consider all the angles,” said Jonvic Remulla, the interior minister. “Right now all signs point to a possible sex offender of the grossest kind. We want to be sure before we release the findings. The forensics data will be complete in a week.”

Remulla said a statement would be released once the data had been analysed, without giving a specific date. “Please give us a week to determine the contents and to come up with a definitive picture,” he said. “We will release a statement then.”
Markle Sr has denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail the accusations were “sick lies”.
Philippine police are also investigating a laptop found at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr had been living until he returned to the US earlier this year.
In a statement given to Agence France-Presse, Remulla said the Philippine national police inspected Markle’s former home and found a “trove of child pornography materials as well as a laptop”.
“The PNP will coordinate with their counterparts to locate and take appropriate legal actions against Mr Markle if found that there is sufficient evidence to charge him,” he said.
Markle told the Mail the computers had not been in his possession since he left Mexico with his son in 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”.
He said: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.
“This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”

Meghan has said she is “deeply distressed” over the allegations, which were first reported in the Sun. She said she had broken off contact with her father to protect her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five. He has never met them.

On Saturday, the Metropolitan police confirmed they gave a letter to Meghan in 2019 concerning “alleged offending” involving her father, but said they did not pass it on to other law enforcement agencies. Scotland Yard is considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to review its actions.

In a statement, a Met spokesperson said: “Following a thorough review of Met police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019 we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom. It was sent to the MPS [Metropolitan Police Service] Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex.

“The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.
“The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach.”

In a statement on Friday issued through her spokesperson, the duchess said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”
She later said she had misremembered the year in which the Met had contacted her, and confirmed it had been 2019, not 2018 as she said on Friday.

A spokesperson for the duchess said: “In recalling events from more than seven years ago, without the benefit of a diary entry or contemporaneous record, it is understandable that she may have been mistaken by a few months.
“If the MPS holds a time-stamped record confirming that the letter was reviewed in 2019, that should be treated as the accurate reference point for when it was received and shared with the duchess.”

Sources said that although Meghan was made aware of the allegations in 2019, she had been unable to speak publicly to avoid jeopardising any future investigation and because speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her.

The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu. Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.

items.title: Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored
paragraphs: Elon Musk has said his company SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink internet service, after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to have been resolved.

The tech billionaire accused Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity - but denied being responsible for a simultaneous issue with its US-run, military-grade counterpart Starshield.
Kyiv has not officially commented on Musk's latest claim but Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said his post was "very strange".
Musk had earlier denied deliberately throttling Ukraine's connection, which it says hampered its ability to conduct defensive operations for more than a week.
The issue first emerged last week during a broader row between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.

Musk's latest comments, and the seeming restoration of the service, came after US President Donald Trump said he had told the Tesla and X owner to "put it back", having repeatedly denied instructing him to limit the service.
"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X on Saturday.
"Ukraine['s] military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

He went on to say that SpaceX had "done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth" and reiterated his stipulation that Starshield was a different system and controlled by the US government, adding: "What they decide to do is up to them."
He added in a later post: "[Starlink] can be used for infrastructure that is military, but it cannot be used for unequivocally offensive strikes that make it fair game to be struck back."
Reacting to Musk's post, Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram that Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine have a speed restriction of 70-90km/h and do not work on Russian territory.
"Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he said.
"It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine."
There was no immediate comment from Ukraine's defence ministry.

Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed, both of which run on networks of low Earth orbit satellites launched by SpaceX.

Starlink allows military units to co-ordinate, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield, while Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.
Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.

Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said earlier on Saturday that the military was now recording a "stable connection", with drones now able to reach speeds in excess of 400km/h (249mph). Kyiv previously said the connection would cut out above 161km/h.
"The speeds are now where they need to be," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
Musk did not disclose in his post why SpaceX had chosen to make the change to its service last week, when Ukraine's extensive use of Starlink had been known for several years.
The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic standoff between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.
While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.

Faced with midterm elections next month and domestic displeasure with rising fuel prices, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal with Moscow - criticised by European allies as funding Russia's war machine - to supply Russian diesel to the US and the global market.

Zelensky initially agreed to cease strikes targeting Russian oil facilities on the proviso that Moscow cease striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, before restarting the strikes after several instances of Russia disregarding this.

The Ukrainian leader said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.
Fighting and aerial attacks continue to be exchanged between Russia and Ukraine overnight.
Ukraine's emergency services said three people were killed and 15 others injured, including an 11-year-old girl, in attacks on the Dnipropetrovsk region, in the south east.
Another six people were injured when a Russian drone struck an apartment block in the central city of Vinnytsia, it said.

The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday that it had struck a cargo vessel it claimed was being used to supply the Ukrainian army while it was en route to the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk overnight.
It also said Russian forces hit a logistics centre, a distribution centre and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv.

Ukraine's defence ministry earlier said it struck a facility in the Russian city of Oryol run by a sanctioned heavy machinery manufacturer. Russian authorities said three people were killed in the strike.

items.title: More dads taking paid family leave for a new baby, sometimes as much as moms are
paragraphs: Karlo Campana plays Magnatiles with his daughters Gianna and Giselle, while his 5-month-old son Gianluca watches. Campana is one of the growing number of California men taking advantage of the state's paid bonding leave program. Dania Maxwell for NPR hide caption
Karlo Campana is usually outnumbered these days. He has three young kids under age 4.

On a recent Saturday, he played a mini-game of basketball with his two older kids in their Southern California home, shooting a ball into a hoop on the door, while his baby boy watched from his bouncy chair.
Campana took paid time off in May after the birth of his son — just as he did for his daughters.
It's sometimes called "bonding" or "family" leave, to distinguish it from the paid leave ("maternity" or "disability" leave) that mothers can take to physically recover from childbirth.

"You need that adjustment period," he said. Campana, who works at an ad agency, said having the time off not to think about work — or worry about losing income during that time — was crucial for him and his family during a sleep-deprived period.

"My wife isn't doing it on her own," he said. "She doesn't feel like she's alone on this journey. She feels like she has support." He jokes that by kid No. 3, he thought he had nailed diaper changes without too much mess — but he was wrong.

"The benefits are I get to spend time with each of them when they were in the infant stage, the baby stage, and I get to hold them and, you know, change the poopy diapers," he said. " It's like the funny moments of, like, being a parent, like, 'This is it right here, you're in the thick of it.'"

Karlo Campana plays with his daughter Giselle and his infant son Gianluca at home on October 12 in Santa Ana, Calif. With three children under 4, paid paternity leave gave him something invaluable: time to bond with his kids and support his wife in the thick of early parenthood. Dania Maxwell for NPR hide caption

Campana is among a growing number of fathers who take leave to bond with a new child in the states that offer paid family leave programs — and are part of a larger cultural shift that has seen dads handle more caregiving duties.

In California — as in several other states — men make up about half of bonding claim applications. Last year, men even surpassed women — as in Colorado and Washington — for the first time in the state's history. This trend comes at a time when the federal government has said it wants Americans to have more babies, and families report affordability is an obstacle in raising them.

There's no federal law guaranteeing paid parental leave, but California is one of 14 states, plus Washington, D.C., that have passed legislation to enact paid family leave programs — and in many of those places, more dads are opting in.

"We're in a very different place in terms of our understanding of gender roles, of paternity leave, of dads' roles than we were 20-plus years ago," said Molly Weston Williamson, policy director at Paid Leave for All, an organization that advocates for paid family leave policies.

California's program offers, within a year, up to eight weeks of paid bonding leave for parents after a birth, adoption, or foster care placement. That's on top of six to eight weeks of paid disability leave that moms get to recover after birth.

Karlo Campana at dinner with his wife Lily and their three children. His experience reflects a broader shift across California, where fathers accounted for 51% of paid bonding leave claims in 2025, surpassing mothers for the first time. Dania Maxwell for NPR hide caption
Campana said he initially wasn't sure if he should take paternity leave because of lingering gender stereotypes.
" I felt guilty, for sure," Campana said. " I think dads maybe feel they need to be the provider. They need to be the ones that are only helping their family by bringing money or working."

Campana said that when he was growing up, his father worked three jobs. "It was hard for him to be present, and I think that's the one thing now — it's like, 'No, be present. Be there for your kids.'"

Research has shown that paternity leave confers benefits beyond allowing a father extra time to bond with a new child: It has positive effects on the whole family, including better health outcomes for both parents.
Paid parental leave has also been linked to lower odds of postpartum depression and a decrease in infant mortality rates.
In California, men accounted for 51% of bonding claims filed in 2025. It's a massive shift from when the state program started in 2004, and men made up about 18% of claim applications.

States fund their paid family and medical leave programs with different combinations of employer and employee contributions; California is among six states where family leave is entirely funded by employee payroll deductions.
Karlo Campana poses for a portrait with his wife Lily and their three kids (from left to right) Gianna, Gianluca, and Giselle. Dania Maxwell for NPR hide caption

In addition to changing gender norms, Williamson said other factors are likely contributing to the increase in claims by men in the state: greater awareness about the program, and recent changes to the benefit.
In 2025, the state boosted the amount of income a worker can recoup while on family leave. Now, in California and in other states, the leave benefit can be as high as 90% of their regular salary.

"That makes it a realistic option for a lot more families, and I think we're seeing dads and moms responding to that change," Williamson said. Still, she said, there's a lot the new data about dads isn't telling us.

"We're getting one particular vantage point into this data, which is useful and valuable, but it's only telling us sort of part of the story, and we'd need other kinds of information to better understand the full picture," Williamson said.
"Is it that more dads are working and therefore are potentially eligible for these benefits? Is it that women are deciding not to take leave?"
While private employers can offer their own paid leave as a benefit, this data also reflects only people who took leave through California's paid family leave program.

Karlo Campana washes Giselle's hands after dinner on October 12 at home in Santa Ana, Calif. "My wife isn't doing it on her own," he said of his decision to take paid leave from his job after the birth of their third child. "She doesn't feel like she's alone on this journey. She feels like she has support." Dania Maxwell for NPR hide caption

A spokesperson for the California Employment Development Department, which administers the state's family leave program, said the department couldn't provide definitive reasons for the increase in male bonding claims.
One thing is clear: The growth in these states comes as more parents are feeling strained economically.
President Trump has said, "We want more babies," and has promoted policy initiatives like expanding access to in vitro fertilization and offering investment accounts for newborns.

"People really are very worried about the affordability of kids," said Jeremy Pope, a professor of political science at Brigham Young University, and a principal investigator of the American Family Survey.
Karlo Campana plays with his new son Gianluca as his wife Lily prepares dinner in Santa Ana, Calif. "You need that adjustment period," he said. Dania Maxwell for NPR hide caption

According to the latest survey in 2025, 7 in 10 Americans said raising children had become unaffordable, according to the survey. It was the biggest single-year jump since the survey started more than a decade ago.

"I don't think they want government involved in the decision to have kids," Pope said. "But they worry a lot about how much it costs and they would like to see ways of making those costs smaller or getting help with those costs."

The Pew Research Center found in a recent survey of full-time working parents who are not self-employed, 84% said paid parental, family, or medical leave would be "extremely or very helpful" to them, but only half said it was available to them.
This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with LAist and KFF Health News.

items.title: Independent candidates sense a moment in the West. Democrats are hoping they're right
paragraphs: Pins and bumper stickers supporting Dan Osborn's candidacy for U.S. Senate sit on a campaign table on Sept. 3, 2026 at Pals Brewing Company in North Platte, Neb. Osborn, a 51-year-old Navy veteran, is running as an independent. Austin Johnson/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
BURWELL, NEBRASKA – Tucked in the rolling Sandhills, the largest sand dune formation in America, sits Morgan Ranch, a 15,000-acre, family-run operation home to 1,000 cows and thousands of offspring.
"There's a lot of mouths to feed — both animals and two-legged," laughed Dan Morgan. His ranch has one of the largest privately-owned Wagyu herds in the U.S.
He said his job has given him a front row seat to what he calls the "uncertainty" of President Trump's policies.

"To raise a piece of meat takes me three years," Morgan said. "Well, look at the changes in the past two years: costs, tariffs, reciprocal tariffs because half of our business is export — it's just hell," he said.
