items.title: WHO reports six more polio cases in Afghanistan
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.
The World Health Organization has reported six new poliovirus cases in Afghanistan this week.
In a statement, the WHO said that the six cases of wild poliovirus type 1, or WPV1, were reported in the provinces of Kandahar, Nangarhar, and Kabul.
The WHO said so far this year, 48 positive cases of the wild poliovirus have been registered globally, 42 of which are in Afghanistan and six in Pakistan.
The number represents a sharp increase from last year.
In 2025, 52 positive wild poliovirus cases were reported worldwide, including 21 in Afghanistan and 31 in Pakistan.
Before the Taliban imposed a ban on house-to-house polio vaccination in Afghanistan, the number of positive poliovirus cases was low. There were only two reported cases in 2022 and six in 2023.
However, the Taliban, in September 2024, banned house-to-house vaccination campaigns, and the only through site-to-site, including vaccination at mosque and other designated locations.
Polio is an infectious viral disease that largely affects children under 5 years of age.
WPV1 is one of three original strains of wild poliovirus that attacks the nervous system and can cause irreversible paralysis or death.
Pakistan and Afghanistan are the two remaining countries where cases of wild poliovirus type 1 are still reported.
The wild poliovirus types 2 and 3 have been declared eradicated in 2015 and 2019.
New cases are being reported in Afghanistan as the world prepares to mark World Polio Day on Saturday, Oct. 24.
The day is celebrated to raise awareness of the importance of polio vaccination and honor the work of volunteers, health professionals and parents toward eradicating the disease.
Kamal Shah, a former UNICEF communications officer, told VOA that Afghanistan's polio eradication program faces serious challenges as cases rise.
“One of the main issues in implementing the polio eradication campaign is shortcomings in vaccination campaigns,” he said.
Shah added that the lack of public awareness about the virus and other factors, such as malnutrition in children, are compounding the country’s polio problem.

items.title: Tuesday Labs debuts "droid butler" Voxel
paragraphs: New York technology company Tuesday Labs has debuted its first semi-autonomous robot Voxel Series-1, designed to help with household chores and to avoid the appearance of an “uncanny valley” humanoid robot.
Voxel Series-1 (Voxel) performs tasks such as watering plants and sweeping crumbs, which it currently achieves with a combination of autonomous intelligence and teleoperation.

The robot is counter-height and covered in a colourful matte plastic shell with primarily “cuboid” body parts, LED eyes and 1-DOF grippers for hands. Tuesday Labs founder Rosalind Shinkle told Dezeen that initial designs were informed by home objects such as lamps, chairs and briefcases.
Working with former Pixar character designer Alonso Martinez, Shinkle said the finalised Voxel is a combination of “exceptional capability and charming character”.
“We deliberately didn’t build a humanoid,” Shinkle said. “We wanted to stay far from the uncanny valley, and far from robots that fill a human-shaped space in the home.”
“Instead, we made Voxel relatively small and cuboid, to signal his role in your life: a droid butler, not a human butler.”

“We know we don’t want him to feel almost-human, and we know we don’t want him to feel like a toaster,” she continued. “A believable character needs every element sitting at roughly the same point on that human–toaster spectrum.”
Shinkle said five key principles drove the design of Voxel, including easy integration into the home, a maximalist appearance, simplicity, luxury and playfulness.
Part of the strategy was also “affordance matching”, or that, when Voxel is perceived by a human, its capabilities can be inherently understood.

“When someone looks at a robot, they should be able to roughly predict what he’s capable of,” Shinkle said. “If you correctly match perceived and actual affordance, you can avoid that constant feeling of disappointment when a humanoid robot isn’t quite as good at doing things as a human.”
Voxel’s plastic shell and finishes are meant to keep it relatively lightweight, but Shinkle said the external design should also communicate its quality.

Like another home robot that is currently in production, Neo by 1X Technologies, Voxel’s initial customers are “early adopters” who opt in to help informally train the robot’s autonomous software at home.
“We’re starting with a limited number of robots for early adopters who are excited to experience and help shape this technology,” she said.

“Voxel’s estimated price is $20,000, so he will be a luxury product. But our ambition is much bigger – as the technology improves and production scales, we want to make household robots accessible to far more people.”
Shinkle said her own distaste for household chores was part of what drove Voxel.
“Robots will soon be a part of our homes,” she said. “I set out to build the robot that I would actually want to live with.”
“Also, I hate cleaning my apartment, and I’d much rather spend my time building something that solves that problem once and for all.”
Voxel is powered by a rechargeable battery and will charge in an at-home docking station as part of “his normal routine”.

Tuesday Labs is based in New York City and was founded in 2025 by Shinkle, who previously worked as an engineer at Boston Dynamics. The studio is focused on creating “robots that feel natural and delightful to live with”.
The combination of advanced technology and autonomous intelligence has made the creation of robots more possible than ever at this point in history.

This has allowed the field to diversify, and technology companies and studios have released a varity of different types of robots in recent years, including all the cute robots from CES 2025 and five that were displayed at Carlo Ratti’s architecture biennale.
Other recent home robots that debuted include Neo by 1X Technologies and CLOiD by LG.

items.title: Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit
paragraphs: A US judge has ordered President Donald Trump to answer questions under oath in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by 11 December.
Trump is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.
Charles Tobin, a lawyer representing the BBC, said in court that "we still haven't been able to depose the plaintiff" with two months left in the discovery period.
Trump cancelled a previous deposition on 16 October, citing "matters of national importance" while he was campaigning in Georgia.
In US law, a deposition is an out-of-court statement made under oath in response to questions, which is recorded for use in later proceedings.
The judge in the case, US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett, said that Trump must sit for the deposition by 11 December, unless the discovery period is extended.
Last week, attorneys asked that Lett compel Trump to face deposition after the last scheduled meeting did not take place.
On that day, Trump attended a midterms campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia and a fundraiser at his property in Mar-a-Lago in Florida.

In a separate filing on Wednesday, Trump's lawyers said that the president could appear for the interview between 11 and 22 January next year, and claimed that the BBC was "wrong to claim that President Trump is avoiding his deposition in this action."
Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.
The BBC apologised for the error and said that the broadcast gave "the mistaken impression that President Trump made a direct call for violent action".
The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US.

In July, Trump's lawyers conceded that they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service - as they originally claimed - or on the BBC's website, BBC select or through US broadcasters.
Trump ultimately agreed to drop the lawsuit against BBC Studios, its commercial arm, after the BBC argued that it had "no role in creating or producing the documentary.
Typically, depositions take place in a lawyer's office - rather than a courtroom - without a judge physically present.
Depositions, however, carry legal weight and take place under oath. They are recorded verbatim by a court reporter, and the transcripts can later be used as evidence during trials.

items.title: Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found
paragraphs: Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming language, PHP.

Websites around the world were taken offline on Wednesday and Thursday after the developers of PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" were found in the back-end language, used in web development for decades.
Researchers warned the "severe" flaws could expose millions of sites using it to potential hacks if left unpatched - and the UK government was among those to take some sites offline as a precaution.
There have been no successful attacks reported so far, but experts say any impact may take time - even months - to become fully apparent.
Downing Street said on Thursday "some" limited government services "may be offline" while security work was being carried out.
"The information I have is that 32 Government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra told the House of Lords.
She attributed this to having "largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied".
The government did not specify which services were taken offline - but it said no large UK public-facing critical services had been affected.

A spokesperson said work had already taken place across government to "identify and fix potential exposures to our systems and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue".
"But this does not mean they were hacked, and work continues to resolve any issues," they added.
Olly Whitehouse, chief technology officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), called the event "unprecedented".
"It will be universally felt, I suspect," he told BBC Radio 4's World At One.
But he said there were "no indications" of any successful breaches by hackers.
He said the NCSC was "starting to see positive confirmation" that advice sent to those affected, external had been received and was being acted on.
Cyber-security lecturer Rory Hopcraft told the BBC the government needed to make sure that its own infrastructure was up-to-date.
"Hacking has been around for many years," he said.
"The government are the ones who set the rules for other organisations... they just need to effectively be practising what they're preaching at this point."
Dean Presley, who has a garage in Chepstow, South Wales, told BBC Your Voice he had been unable to properly process MOTs online.
He said his computer system had been down since Wednesday morning, and while he has experienced outages before, they have not lasted this long.
"MOTs can be conducted and they're legal but none of the paperwork and certificates can be printed and they're not on the system," Dean said.
He said this has forced him to write everything on paper documents, leading to delays for customers.
PHP stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor.
It's a programming language which runs on a web server, behind the scenes of a website, and effectively lets you see the sites you visit.
When you go to a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read.
It was developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, but still powers lots of platforms today.

PHP has been used across a wide range of platforms including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites - as well as to write tools to build web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks.
According to cyber-security firm Wiz, external, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites.
And it said the flaws - now coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, affecting many past versions of it.

The PHP Foundation, the non-profit which maintains the programming language, warned this meant that, under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker would be able to remotely execute code on servers running PHP.
Some large organisations said they had seen a high volume of attempts to breach their systems.

Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, wrote on X, external on Thursday that the company saw "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced.
"That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he added.
Amazon also says it saw hackers attempt to exploit the flaws, but its websites were operating as normal.
While the impact of the PHP flaw remains to be seen, disruption continued for businesses and organisations after many sites were taken down on Wednesday.
The website of a Dutch agency specialising in cyber-security, Finland's government and parts of Wikipedia, taken temporarily offline, had returned to business as usual by Thursday.
But a number of sites appeared to have been taken offline on Thursday, as operators rushed to check if PHP might be running within their systems or if any patches were required.
In France, telecommunications company Orange also said, external it had suspended access to certain services globally while it deployed security fixes.

According to some cyber-security researchers using scans to check servers at risk of the PHP vulnerability, the rate of organisations implementing patches - but not as quickly as might be hoped globally.
"The window to respond has shrunk dramatically," said Matt Hull, VP of cyber intelligence and response at global cyber security company NCC Group.
"A few years ago, attackers might have taken weeks to exploit a vulnerability. Now, it can be days or hours."
Hull also highlighted the extent of the task facing developers and engineers working to deal with the issue.

"Several days into this incident, security professionals might already be dealing with significant burnout," he said, urging a need to "make time to rest, share the workload and look after each other".
"Resilience depends on people as much as technology."

items.title: Websites across world hit by millions of attempts to exploit PHP code flaw
paragraphs: Websites around the world have been hit by millions of attempts to exploit a recently discovered vulnerability in their code, cybersecurity companies have said, as the US warned the flaw could allow attackers to take control of web servers, steal data and disrupt services.

The problem in the PHP programming language, which underpins about 70% of the world’s websites, emerged on Wednesday causing governments and companies to pull their websites off the internet before they could be attacked and so they could patch the fault.

In the UK, 32 government services had been taken offline, the cybersecurity minister, Liz Lloyd, told parliament. She said this “largely resulted from precautionary measures” while updates were applied. Downing Street said no public-facing critical services had been affected and “some limited services may be temporarily offline” but this did not mean they had been hacked.

The website for the BBC’s Traitors was one of those that was down on Thursday, while the government declined to name the affected sites, saying services were being reviewed, updated and coming back online. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) sent out 50,000 alerts to affected organisations, but said it had no reports of successful hacks as a result of the flaw. Other sites reportedly temporarily affected included the Internet Archive, Wikipedia and 4Chan.

The vulnerability sparked particular concern about the ongoing vulnerability of systems used by schools, local governments and charities, which may not have dedicated cybersecurity support to execute the fix. The NCSC said the scale of the vulnerability was “unprecedented” and the patch would not work for some organisations running older systems, and these would have to be replaced. The British Chambers of Commerce, which represents thousands of employers, said it was not yet causing firms any significant difficulties.

Ciaran Martin, the former chief executive of the NCSC, described the flaw as “very bad”, saying that while most internet software vulnerabilities did not matter, this was “the most serious vulnerability discovered for five years”. The former GCHQ chief David Omand warned that Russia and China could look to exploit the bug.
However, Ryan Austin, a researcher at the cybersecurity company Calif, who was key to discovering the flaw, said: “At the moment it doesn’t look like exploitation has taken off or been widespread.”

The flaw prompted governments into action, with the US National Security Agency saying it could allow attackers to seize control of web servers, steal sensitive data, disrupt services and move deeper into a network. Government websites were quickly taken down so the patch could be installed with many coming back on line soon afterwards.

In an update overnight on Wednesday, and into Thursday, Matthew Prince, the chief executive of the cybersecurity business CloudFlare, said the company encountered tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the weakness in the 45 minutes after the problem was announced, rising to “hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now”.

Amazon Threat Intelligence, another cybersecurity company, said PHP2Shell, as the vulnerability is known, was “now being broadly exploited in the wild” and it had identified several attempts from multiple actors to test ways to capitalise on the vulnerability before the fix was released by the PHP developers on Wednesday.

CloudFlare also said that in the 10 hours before the vulnerability was publicly announced, it saw thousands of attempts to exploit it, amid concern over the handling of the alert. One cybersecurity expert, Prof Alan Woodward, said the flaw was revealed a day before the patch was released, and that “somebody let the cat out of the bag”.

The PHP vulnerability could allow hostile actors to “grab the resources” of exposed sites, said Michał Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert. A website, such as Slack or Wikipedia, has access to computing power, servers, and IP addresses which locate it on the internet. In many cases, this infrastructure is managed and mediated by PHP.

Criminal groups, state-sponsored hackers, or crypto miners might “nest” themselves into exposed sites using this PHP vulnerability, and then exploit those resources for their own aims. A hacking group could use an exposed site’s IP address to launch attacks that could not then be traced back to it. Crypto miners could use a server’s computing power to run their energy-intensive calculations for free.
It was unclear at what scale this has been done, said Woźniak, and many sites would not even be aware of it.

Wiz, one of the research organisations that uncovered the vulnerabilities, said it was arguably among the most severe software vulnerabilities ever discovered. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” it said in a blogpost. “Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”
“Cyber-actors are likely to weaponise PHP2Shell,” the NSA said. “These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across US government departments and agencies.”

The government of South Korea said on Thursday it was activating emergency response measures, raising its private sector cybersecurity alert level and issuing guidance to tens of thousands of companies on how to fix the problem.

China’s industry ministry urged organisations to immediately inspect their systems and upgrade to the latest secure version of PHP, and recommended strengthening cybersecurity monitoring, changing passwords and keys. The prime minister of Japan encouraged businesses and organisations to patch the vulnerability – or shut down their sites.

items.title: Dispatch's new Deluxe Edition lets you play the whole game as storyboard animatics
paragraphs: Game publishers rarely let you behind the curtain to see exactly how a game was made. So I’m quite taken with the fact that AdHoc Studio marked Dispatch’s first anniversary by letting you play through the whole thing using its original storyboard animatics. This means all those slick, TV-style superhero workplace scenes get swapped back for the rough drawings they started out as, timed against the dialogue, with all the awkward pauses and unfinished staging that implies.

It’s one half of a free update for Dispatch Deluxe Edition owners, out now on PC (Steam), PS5, Nintendo Switch/Switch 2, and Xbox Series X/S, and the other half is Commentary Mode, with more than 16 hours of cast and crew talking you through the episodes.
The commentaries include two tracks, one for the cast and one for the crew, with different choices unlocking different commentary, and you can switch it on over the top of Storyboard Mode.

So you can sit and watch a scene in its scrappiest form while somebody who worked on it explains why it ended up looking the way it did. Aaron Paul (Breaking Bad, BoJack Horseman), Laura Bailey (The Last of Us Part II, Critical Role) and Erin Yvette (Hades II, The Wolf Among Us) are among the cast voices, and they’re talking about bringing the characters to life, which is a nice thing to hear while you’re looking at the version of those characters that hadn’t been animated yet.

I’d be wary of expecting a full production breakdown, because the idea is the animatics themselves and playing them. But for anyone who draws, animates, or storyboards for a living, seeing where a gag gets its timing or a reaction shot gets an extra beat before anyone’s spent a fortune finishing it is a more dynamic way to see a game's scaffolding than doomscrolling ArtStation. We previously went behind the scenes of Dispatch, exploring how AdHoc used Unreal Engine, previsualisation and cinematic tools to bring its superhero workplace comedy to life.

Nick Herman, Co-Creative Director on Dispatch and COO of AdHoc Studio, put it this way: "Dispatch was only possible because of folks who believed in it enough to show up and do their best work. In our industry, it's often really hard to showcase those people and how the development process actually works, but fortunately our game is very weird and specific and affords us some unique opportunities."

Standard Edition owners aren’t left out and can access these neat extras, though the Deluxe upgrade costs $10.99 and includes a digital art book and four digital comics. I think that's good value. Herman says the idea was to give people more ways into a game that’s become part of their lives, "whether that’s playing alongside the cast and crew, experiencing the entire game in its original storyboards, or hanging out together IRL at the wildest version of a Dispatch concert our finance team would sign off on".

The rest of the celebration releases are for people who’d like something to take home. Those four digital comics are now getting a physical release as a complete set, with covers that join up into one big battle scene, and the first 1,000 orders on the AdHoc store get a numbered collector’s card. T-shirts and hoodies feature artwork by art director Derek Stratton, originally made for the three-record soundtrack vinyl set exclusive to Lost In Cult, and they also include 100 signed Stratton album-art posters.

Lost In Cult is also behind Dispatch: Design Works, a hardcover making-of book and collectable box with interviews from the cast and developers, though there’s no date yet, only an alert sign-up on the Lost In Cult site. For another look at the thought that goes into building a game's visual identity, read how the team behind Dustborn created its comic-book-inspired art style, turning a deliberately stylised look into part of the storytelling.

If you haven't played Dispatch, there’s a new phone version releasing on iOS and Android on 9 December, rebuilt for touch and vertical play, with PC support via Google Play Games. The first four episodes are free, and the full game is $19.99, with Google Play pre-registration and App Store pre-orders coming soon. If you're still looking for something new to play, our pick of the best hidden-gem indie games of 2025 also features Dispatch, alongside other games worth seeking out.

And the music is going live too: on Thursday, 3 December, AdHoc and Banter Events are putting on a one-night soundtrack show at AVALON Hollywood in Los Angeles, featuring composer Andrew Arcadi and the SDN Company Band, joined by THOT SQUAD, Bershy, Primer, Caroline Kingsbury, and Fartbarf. Tickets go to AdHoc email subscribers first, and Herman describes it as “the wildest version of a Dispatch concert our finance team would sign off on”, which tells you most of what you need to know about the tone.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

items.title: Prime Minister swaps dispatch box for Gogglebox
paragraphs: Appearing on the edition with the prime minister will be comedian Joe Lycett and Sugababes singers Mutya Buena, Keisha Buchanan and Siobhan Donaghy.
A Channel 4 spokesperson said nothing would be "off limits as Gogglebox continues to celebrate the simple joy of watching television together".
"They'll be sharing hilarious, honest and often unexpected reactions to the week's biggest television moments as well as poignant stories all in aid of Stand Up To Cancer," they added.
Burnham and Rotheram have been friends for many years, serving together as Labour MPs before they both left Parliament to become regional mayors in 2017.

They remained close allies, writing a book together on their vision for Britain's future, and Rotheram was a visible supporter of Burnham's successful campaign to become the MP for Makerfield in June.
The Liverpool City Region mayor said while filming their contributions, he and Burnham had struggled with one particularly cerebral TV quiz show and found themselves flummoxed by its music round.
"We're both big into our music but we couldn't get it," he said.
He added that while their television tastes were largely similar, he and the prime minister disagreed over what snacks to eat while watching.
"I'm more of a cheesy puffs-type guy, but he's more into the hard, crunchy stuff," he said.

items.title: Kenya and plastics – level 1
paragraphs: Kenya’s biggest landfill is called Dandora. It is in Nairobi. It is one of the biggest landfills in the world.

Dandora is full of throwaway plastics. People use most of these plastics only once. Then they throw it away. Kenya is trying hard to be cleaner. Kenya wants a strict global rule on plastics. Countries are talking about it now. In 2017, Kenya makes tough laws about plastic bags. People can go to jail or pay a lot of money if they use plastic bags.

Now, a new law says that companies must handle their products’ waste, not consumers. A Kenyan milk company changes its bottles to clear ones. It is easier to recycle these bottles. People like this change. It shows that Kenyans care more about this problem than before.

Difficult words: landfill (a place where people put things which they do not need anymore, and it looks like a mountain), waste (things which people and companies throw away), consumer (a person who buys things).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Russell Brand accuser said alleged rape 'really hurt', court hears
paragraphs: Warning - this report contains graphic content
The friend of a woman claiming to have been raped by Russell Brand told a jury the complainant had told her after the alleged attack that it had "really, really hurt".

The witness who spoke via video link at his trial said she had attended the Hammersmith Apollo theatre in London with the alleged victim in 2009, where they had been invited to the defendant's dressing room after his comedy show.
Statements from the woman's parents were also heard in court, saying their daughter had told them about the alleged attack, and that she had been "very worried about HIV".
Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.
The allegations span a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009 and involve six female complainants.

The witness said the woman had told her she had visited Brand's house in London soon after meeting at the theatre, and that he then sent a car to collect the woman, which took her to his place in Hampstead.
She said when they spoke about it "quite soon after", she said she "was just crying - really upset".
The witness said Brand had forced her into having anal sex at the end of an encounter that started off consensually.
"He was quite aggressive," she said her friend had told her.
"He forcibly put it in my bum and "it really really hurt".
The witness says she remembers specifically asking the complainant if she had said no to Brand when the alleged attack started.
She said the woman replied "lots of times".
"She told me that she was in a lot of pain" and that "she couldn't sit down".
Another friend of the same complainant also gave evidence to the court.
From the witness box, she told the jury her friend had told her that she had told him to stop during the alleged rape.
She said her friend had said the worst moment had been after the act, and "she said that Brand told her she'd been dirty and had to clean up her mess".
"She said he was quite cold and keen to get her gone".
The witness said she had given her friend advice after she had confided in her.
"I told her that she should go and get checked out because she had anal tears and a lot of discomfort and to seek guidance from her parents and to go to the police.
"She just wasn't sure - it was all a bit chaotic in her head. She felt like it wasn't worth it."
She told jurors: "She didn't think she would be believed, and she didn't think it would be worth it to go.
Statements from the alleged rape victim's parents said their daughter stayed with them for about two months after the alleged incident with Brand.
Her mother's statement said: "I just remember her saying 'he raped me'.
"She was very worried about HIV," she said, adding that her daughter had started talking about it during a car journey.
"She said she went to his place, went to see him, as she had always admired him."
Her father recalled their daughter being "very upset and very unwell", during the stay, that that she was "upset by something that had happened to her."
The father said in his statement that his daughter told him: "They were having sex, she asked him to stop, she kept saying she had been assaulted.
"I turned to her in the car and asked if she asked him to stop, and she said 'no' several times.
"I said 'you have been raped, that's rape'."
He said his daughter got a sexual health check, and he said he had only recently learned his daughter is accusing Brand of anal rape.

items.title: ‘The tech bro fight club is real!’ The titans of AI get the Succession treatment in a wild new TV show
paragraphs: Showrunner Jonathan Glatzer wanted the tagline of his latest TV creation to be: “We’re so fucked.” He laughs. “Sadly it got rejected by the network. Hey, maybe I can use it for season two!” The show in question is The Audacity, his darkly comic drama about AI tech titans. Instead, it went with the more PG tagline “Move fast and break people” – a twist on “Move fast and break things”, the Facebook motto coined by Mark Zuckerberg. The Audacity promises to do for tech bros what Succession did for legacy media. Considering Glatzer is a former writer on Succession, that is no empty threat.

This acerbic and all-too-timely Silicon Valley satire follows CEO Duncan Park (played by Billy Magnussen), the obscenely wealthy founder of a data analytics company. He’s a self-proclaimed “inventor of the future” who also happens to be a morally bankrupt man-baby. “Duncan is worth about half a billion,” says Glatzer. “Naturally, that’s not enough. He desperately wants to be a billionaire and ascend to what we call ‘God Mountain’. But he’s no God.”

Like Succession, The Audacity’s scripts are liberally spiced with baroque swearing. Park boasts about keeping investors “moist” and “Viagra-ing the share price to keep it up”. Magnussen delivers such juicy dialogue with relish. “Jonathan has a way of painting a picture with words while also getting nasty with it,” he grins. “My favourite line in season two is: ‘I pulled it out of my ass and it came out clean.’ You’ll have to wait and see what it refers to.” It’s a measure of The Audacity’s whip-smart relevance that the second season was commissioned before the first had even aired.

“Unquestionably, there’s a tech bro mentality that is sexualised,” says Glatzer. “Silicon Valley is such a male-dominated culture. It’s also very white or south Asian. When I first came here, I didn’t see a person of colour for two weeks. That struck me as very odd in a major US city. Hiring practices are dictated by algorithms. The algorithms say that if you went to these universities, you’re our man. If you came from someplace else, and are maybe not a man, the algorithm says you might be problematic. And you could end up writing a book about us.”

The Audacity pulls no punches on how the tech sector is wrecking the planet. “It sure is,” says Glatzer. “Generative AI is environmentally ruinous. Datacentres are tremendous suckers of energy. Worryingly, it doesn’t take too many rampantly ambitious entrepreneurs to fuck up an entire planet for the rest of us.” When Park is warned about the huge carbon footprint of his “algo”, he shrugs: “I’ll sponsor a penguin.”

Zach Galifianakis plays billionaire genius Carl Bardolph, who “basically created spam”. He’s rich enough to retire but becomes a disruptor out of boredom. “I’ve always been very concerned about the people running tech,” says Galifianakis. “They have math minds, but that sometimes comes with a lack of empathy. About 12 nerds are controlling our lives and designing our futures. And they all tend to have the same profile. Most come from Stanford University. I don’t know what they’re teaching there.” He laughs. “It’s weird and kind of evil.”

Did Galifianakis base his portrayal on anyone specific? “He’s pulled from one dude I’ve watched over the years. I won’t give his name but he’s a real piece of shit. A major jerk. The guys running Silicon Valley are damaged. Carl has a giant hole in his heart and a ton of anger because of his dad. I’ve seen a lot of men like that in Hollywood, so I drew on them too. Most of the puppet masters are egomaniac weirdos and I wouldn’t mind saying that to their faces. Zuckerberg has something missing. Elon Musk is bizarre. They’re little boys. You almost feel sorry for them.”

“Duncan also deals with daddy issues and a lack of love,” says Magnussen. “A lot of tech bros are trying to fill voids. The great irony is that the most antisocial people work in social media. Those who don’t know how to be personable are controlling how we communicate. It’s nuts.”

Both actors view the show as a howl of protest. “I’ve done some cool shit in my career,” says Magnussen. “I’ve been in Bond [he played a CIA agent in No Time to Die]. I’ve been in fun, escapist movies. But this feels different. It’s a call to arms. People need to wake up to the audacious behaviour of this handful of people. Their decisions affect 8.3 billion people. That’s scary, man. I just hope our show opens some conversations. We’ve got to start making a difference.”

Galifianakis agrees. “It’s a warning. I’ve never felt this way before with my work – come on, I was in a movie with a baby wearing sunglasses [The Hangover] – but this show’s important. This industry has no guard rails. You can’t sue them, you can’t do anything, so of course they’re going to take advantage of the population. That’s exactly what they’ve done. The destructive environmental impact alone is enough reason to take to the streets and protest. Sure, there’s all this darkness online but also, we’re going to take your water and electricity from you, too.”

Park blackmails his therapist – sorry, “performance psychologist” (played by Barry’s Sarah Goldberg) – into giving him insider-trading tips from her other powerful clients. The pair are soon engulfed in a scandal over fraudulent stock pumping. It’s a familiar-sounding storyline. “Elon got into trouble for market manipulation,” says Glatzer. “It’s like Duncan says in the show: ‘It’s not a felony in Silicon Valley, it’s good hustle.’ That’s the mentality here. Laws are for morons, not us.”

Real world echoes are everywhere in The Audacity. The search engine of choice is called Spookle (slogan: “You Agreed to This”). A corporation called Cupertino is a thinly veiled reference to Apple, while its mythical boss “Big Tim” nods to Tim Cook. Are any of Glatzer’s characters directly based on real-life figures? “The truth is, I don’t find any of them worthy of a three-dimensional character that could go the distance of multiple seasons,” says Glatzer. “They’re interesting enough for a film like The Social Reckoning but not much more.”

Indeed, Magnussen can currently be seen in The Social Reckoning as a Meta spin doctor. Is this his tech bro era? “AI is the most pressing issue of our time,” he says. “It affects our planet, our politics, our mental health, everything. Technology can do wonderful things but once it starts dividing us or swaying elections, it’s deeply damaging.”

“I don’t understand why people get on board with social media,” sighs Galifianakis. “We fed these machines for years. Now these machines are going to find us. I don’t believe the promises of AI because I don’t trust the people doing it.”

The Audacity’s protagonist has been described as “highly punchable”. Magnussen concurs: “You’ve seen these guys in front of Congress. They’re pretty fucking punchable.” An early episode includes a sequence at a Palo Alto fight club, where nerds whack each other with keyboards and strangle each other with cables. “That’s real!” laughs Magnussen. “The tech bro fight club is an actual thing.”

Despite the plentiful real-world parallels, Glatzer has never met a tech mogul. “That’s fine by me,” he says. “I don’t imagine the conversation would be anything other than stage-managed and dishonest. They have people workshopping their handshake and smile, so what am I going to get from that? But I have talked to a number of people who work in the tech world. The first thing they say is: ‘I’m not like that. That’s those other guys. I’m one of the good ones.’”
“Me too,” says Magnussen. “The response I get is: ‘I know that guy!’ It’s always someone else. You want to go: ‘No, it’s you. You’re that guy.’”

In America’s richest enclave, hi-tech goes hand-in-hand with hippy-dippy. The Audacity lampoons heath fads like ayahuasca ceremonies, microdosing and bio-hacking. “Tech titans feel as if they’ve got the golden ticket,” says Glatzer. “They want their prime to last as long as possible, perhaps for ever. Maybe the singularity comes when they upload themselves into an AI consciousness and become gods. I don’t have proof of that being the reason why so many datacentres are being built by these guys – but I don’t think it’s uninvolved.”
“There’s no limit to these people’s overreach,” agrees Magnussen. “They truly believe their life is more valuable than anyone else’s.”

The show also skewers the hypocrisy of execs who ban their own offspring from smartphones, reasoning that “arms dealers don’t give their kids landmines”. “It’s like how a lot of Hollywood don’t have TVs in their houses,” says Galifianakis. “Because they know the poison they’re selling.”

“They know the dangers,” nods Glatzer. “It’s a classic case of capitalism gone haywire. I don’t think they’d live next door to a datacentre either. None of them do what they’re telling us to do. It used to be that people in public life had to practise what they preached. That has quietly gone away. US congresspeople invest in the same tech companies they’re supposedly regulating. Look at what Trump’s doing. It’s a kleptocracy.”

He’s equally concerned by “screenification” in schools. “The amount of information gathered on our kids is frightening,” says Glatzer. “Shopping habits, medical history, exam grades. When schools get given tablets in the States, the law says it’s OK for the provider to track that student. We’re handing our kids these screens with the patina of being an educational tool but they are data-collecting devices. Just like everything is.”

“I can’t believe how much information people give up,” says Galifianakis. “If you go to LA, there’s all these cars that say Google on the side, taking pictures of everything. If those cars said US Government, people would lose their minds. But because it’s a corporation, we all sit back and go: ‘I guess this is the future.’ I think people are starting to wake up but maybe it’s too late.” He laughs. “What do I know? I’m just a dumb actor trying to alarm people. But our children are the new oil. They’re being mined for data.”
“I’m most scared for the kids,” agrees Magnussen. “They’ve been digital since they were born. They’re being manipulated without even knowing.”

In The Audacity, even seemingly benign tech is sinister. Eccentric inventor Martin Phister (The Big Bang Theory’s Simon Helberg) is developing an empathetic bot to be a digital “friend” for alienated teens. US viewers have likened him to OpenAI’s Sam Altman, who initially presented as a sympathetic mogul.

“Martin’s trying to do something good,” says Glatzer. “You later learn that he’s compensating for something very bad. Carl has a speech about his generation coming to a crossroads: ‘Leave a legacy of good or go full Dr Evil.’ Most choose the latter. They are drawn to doing something positive but they are Hungry Hungry Hippos. They can’t resist the allure of a good deal.”

“Carl knew the internet could have been a good thing for society if we’d done it right,” adds Galifianakis. “But greed and old-fashioned American competition, the need to win, became more important than human beings.”

Geeky idealism is long gone. “It began as a desire to change the world for the better,” says Glatzer. “A bunch of nerdy engineers wore hoodies rather than suits and put ‘Do No Evil’ slogans on their office walls. That’s all in the rear-view mirror.”

Glatzer freely admits that his work on Succession informed The Audacity. “There’s no way that it didn’t. But that was about institutional, dynastic wealth, whereas our characters are self-made. They are Logan Roy as a young man, if he had decided to be a tech guy rather than a media baron. What I certainly gleaned from Jesse Armstrong was finding a tone that enables you to give the establishment some real gut punches. Sarcasm might be the protest of the weak, but that’s all we’ve got. Speaking as a weakling.”

The invasive cyber-surveillance and data-mining in The Audacity are deeply chilling. “We consulted experts but all the information is out there,” says Glatzer. “The Guardian and New York Times do some terrific reporting on AI. It always feels like the journalists secretly want to headline their articles: ‘Wake the fuck up! This is happening!’”

items.title: How tech became the villain of the US midterms
paragraphs: The campaign ad begins with a clear, idyllic stream that suddenly turns sludge-brown as two concrete datacenters slam onto its banks. Another facility thuds down on a peaceful suburban park, and two more crush-green pastures as an ominous soundtrack to a disaster movie blares overtop.
“They’re coming for our rivers. Our neighborhoods. Our farmland,” a deep-voiced narrator says. “Because Brent Taylor wrote the law allowing datacenters to take over Tennessee.”

The attack ad, paid for by the Democrat-aligned Three Star Pac and targeting a Tennessee Republican congressional candidate, is one of more than 150 midterm election campaign commercials across the US focused on datacenters or the artificial intelligence industry. At debates and at rallies, in mailers and online ads, the burgeoning AI industry has taken center stage, as both Republican and Democratic candidates try to convince voters that their opponents will put the unpopular facilities in voters’ backyards.

And it’s not only datacenters – the public anxiety over AI and distaste for the billionaires developing it, as well as backlash over encroaching tech like surveillance cameras, has turned the tech industry into a ubiquitous villain this election cycle. As with big pharma before it, candidates are straining to distance themselves from big tech.

The stigma of the tech industry has even forced prominent Republicans to break with Donald Trump’s pro-AI party line, with candidates like Ken Paxton, campaigning for US Senate in Texas, calling for a slowdown. In Tennessee, Taylor’s campaign ran its own television spot that claimed he was tough on tech and datacenters.

The campaign ads focused on tech have sprung up alongside an ecosystem of pro- and anti-AI political action committees, which have collectively spent hundreds of millions of dollars to influence elections and back candidates. The breathtaking amount of spending has pushed tech into the forefront of the midterms, even as polls show issues like the economy, democracy and healthcare still rate as more important among voters.

Super Pacs funded by tech billionaires are among the top spenders in this election cycle. Leading the Future, formed by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, has raised more than $75m to back tech-friendly candidates. Elon Musk has sunk $366m into Republican causes, more than he spent on the 2024 presidential election. AI money has also been funneled into pro-regulation Pacs seeking to counteract the influence of deregulation groups.
Including Musk’s contribution to various Republican-aligned Pacs, the tech industry and its leaders have spent more than half a billion dollars to influence elections and ballot proposals in 2026.

The cumulative effect of such vast spending, lobbying and advertising is that tech issues and the tech industry have become far more pervasive in the midterms than previously seen in US elections, marking the first major test of how American voters will react to the AI boom.

Concern over AI’s potential effect on society has grown over the last year, and the backlash has been most intense where there is a physical target for voters’ ire. None of those targets have loomed larger than the sprawling datacenter facilities that are part of the tech industry’s multitrillion-dollar infrastructure build-out. Although campaigns have nodded to AI regulation and fears over the technology’s risks, it is datacenters that candidates have repeatedly and specifically called out as a real, tangible threat to constituents.
“Datacenters are now a campaign question in nearly every race in the nation,” said Brad Carson, the head of a pro-AI-regulation group Public First Action and a former congressman.

The growing animosity toward datacenters has also been reflected in nationwide protests and polling. A Pew Research poll from last month showed that the percentage of US adults who believe that datacenters are bad for the environment, energy costs and quality of life has spiked upwards across demographics since January. Only 4% of respondents believe the facilities will be good for the environment or home energy costs.
Datacenters have become toxic enough that some candidates have even begun using the facilities as an epithet to tar their rivals.

“Data Center Derek gave the billionaires and greedy corporations a $2bn tax break. Driving up our electric bills, destroying Ohio farms,” declared a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee attack ad against Ohio Republican candidate Derek Merrin.

At least 20 candidates for governor across the US are calling for moratoriums on datacenters, according to policy tracking firm MultiState, while fewer than 10 candidates across 36 gubernatorial races are backing the projects without any calls for increased regulations.

Along with datacenters, the public backlash against AI-enabled Flock surveillance cameras that automatically scan license plates has also bled into campaigns, including in key battleground races. In Michigan, Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed ran a Flock-focused ad that accused his Republican opponent Mike Rogers of pushing a surveillance state by backing the cameras. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico has similarly spoken out against the company and its data collection.

“Flock cameras have no place in Texas,” Talarico said last month at a rally. The state’s Republican governor, Greg Abbott, surprisingly agrees with him, blocking state agencies from spending on Flock cameras in August.

Elsewhere, legislation has targeted not just tech infrastructure but the billionaires behind it. In California, voters are considering a ballot measure that would levy a one-time 5% wealth tax on any resident of the state worth more than $1bn. The state’s ultra-rich have feverishly mobilized against it, raising more than $340m and spending more than $1m a day to fight the measure. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone has contributed at least $102m to oppose the tax.

The collective backlash against the tech industry has put its leaders in a bind. Companies are facing internal and external criticism of their products and politics, but accepting more intense government regulation or halting datacenter construction would threaten their growth.

The pushback has caused a shift in at least one company’s calculus – OpenAI has distanced itself from Leading the Future in recent months, and Brockman backed out of a planned $25m donation to the Pac.
Musk, Brin and other tech moguls, however, have doubled down on their efforts to swing votes their way.

“They have never met a problem that they didn’t think they could solve by throwing more money at it,” said Charles Blaettler, political director of pro-AI-regulation Pac Guardrails Alliance. “They’re realizing there’s an intense backlash to their ideas.”

The political landscape of the tech industry is vastly different from the last time the US held midterm elections. Anthropic, now potentially set to go public at a more than $2tn valuation, was just one year old in 2022. OpenAI had not publicly released ChatGPT. Musk had not yet allied himself with Donald Trump’s campaign.

The tech industry has become increasingly entrenched in government and determined to shape regulation in the period since. Tech leaders have simultaneously built up immense campaign finance and lobbying arms that have come into full force in this year’s midterms.

Meanwhile, Americans feel negatively about how AI will affect a range of issues from personal relationships to the economy to elections, multiple polls show, as well as broadly opposing datacenters in their communities. More Americans oppose a datacenter being built in their area than oppose a nuclear power plant, according to a Gallup poll from earlier this year.

The public distaste for the AI industry also extends to its leaders, with polls showing that the US generally views executives such as Musk, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei as untrustworthy and unlikeable.

“There’s this very deep-seated sense of anxiety people have about the direction this technology is taking and who’s in control of it,” Blaettler said. “People just feel like they don’t have any agency in their lives anymore.”

The enormous spending from the tech industry has largely flowed to Republicans, but it has also inspired a new category of pro-AI-regulation Pacs that have formed to counter groups like Leading the Future. Some of these pro-regulation Pacs have received money, counterintuitively, from AI companies and workers with different views on how government should oversee the technology. Anthropic contributed more than $40m to Carson’s Public First Action, while the Guardrails Alliance and its associated non-profit have raised more than $11.5m.

One of the early tests for this type of battle was in the Democratic primary for New York’s 12th congressional district in June, where pro- and anti-AI groups, including Carson’s, cumulatively spent $24m on the race – largely targeting candidate Alex Bores, who was running on a pro-regulation platform. The result of all the spending was hard to determine, with Bores coming second in a crowded field and losing to similarly pro-regulation candidate Micah Lasher. After the vote, Lasher sought to distance himself from both Anthropic and OpenAI’s spending.

“I have some news for the two big AI companies who’ve taken such an unusual interest in who won this congressional seat,” Lasher said in June. “I won’t be taking my cues from either of you when it comes to protecting our kids, our jobs, our environment.”

While the spending frenzy on pro- and anti-AI campaigns has helped fund some of the fights over tech in the midterms, leaders of pro-regulation Pacs say these are issues that voters already organically care about and are mobilizing around. The message from the AI industry has for years been that their products will usher in a utopian era of abundance and affluence, but this election cycle has shown there is deep skepticism from everyday voters that they will benefit from the boom.
“It’s now a world where most people on the street have a view about AI,” Carson said. “And it’s mostly negative.”

items.title: Prest Vale Architects extends historic stone rectory in the Cotswolds
paragraphs: London studio Prest Vale Architects has extended a Grade II-listed rectory in the Cotswolds, continuing its gabled roofline with a pale stone volume topped by a sundial.
Located close to Blenheim Estate in Oxfordshire, the rectory was originally constructed in the 17th century and is neighboured by a stone barn dating from the mid-18th century.

Prest Vale Architects was tasked with uniting and expanding this historic ensemble, extending the main home, converting the barn into a guest annexe and flattening out a banked garden that had previously blocked daylight and views.

“The starting point was really about reconnecting the house with its landscape, while introducing a new gable that feels like a natural next chapter within the existing ensemble of buildings,” studio co-founder Richard Prest told Dezeen.

“This also enabled us to rethink the relationship between the house and the landscape, so we embedded the extension into the topography and used changes in level to bring the planting up to the windows,” he added.
The existing rectory’s southern facade was defined by a row of three Cotswold stone gables, which are topped by a weathervane, chimney and a belfry window.
Continuing this formal language, Prest Vale Architects housed the extension within an adjoining gabled form, topped by a stone sundial.

This extension contains a kitchen attached to an expanded dining area, flanked by a store and rear entrance to the north, and a study that projects to the south with a large sit-in window surrounded by planting.

A steep bank that had blocked views from the rectory’s southern windows was flattened as part of a garden scheme by landscape architect Todd Longstaffe-Gowan, with a ha-ha – or sunk fence – introduced to separate the garden from the adjacent field.

“The extension reaches out towards the barn, bringing the two buildings into a closer relationship, whilst also creating an informal courtyard on the south side of the house for evening dining,” Prest explained.
“The existing silhouette has evolved over 300 years, so we wanted the extension to add to that evolution,” added fellow co-founder Michael Vale.
“The new gable offers continuity in the building’s story, while the sculptural sundial above it offers a playful nod to its South-facing perspective,” he told Dezeen.
To match the existing building, the extension is finished in local Cotswold stone, with fenestration and a gable end in crisp white Portland stone marking it out as a contemporary addition.
In the neighbouring barn, an expansive, double-height living, kitchen and dining space sits beneath the exposed structure of a new Douglas fir roof, overlooked by a mezzanine balcony.
Both this barn and the main home share access to a pool created at the rear of the site, surrounded by a stone terrace and overlooked by a small oak poolhouse.

“We wanted the extension to feel rooted in its place, so we took materials from the existing buildings – Portland stone, locally quarried Cotswold stone and oak – but used them with contemporary precision to give the new building its own character,” said Prest.
Other projects recently completed in the Cotswolds include a leaf-shaped home by Michaelis Boyd and a home by DeDraft raised above a parkland site on a plinth of local stone.

items.title: Zoe Kleinman: PHP is the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb
paragraphs: I once worked opposite a site where a shopping centre was being built.
We were warned there might be unexploded bombs from World War Two unearthed during the construction.
In the end, there were none, but procedures were put in place as a precaution and we all had to practice filing into designated safe zones inside our building.
The PHP story feels like the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb - I have never seen such a dramatic, public and global response to a cyber event that hasn't happened yet.
There has been no painful attack like the ransomware we saw knock out M&S and JLR in 2025.
But the potential threat is so serious that websites around the world have been taken down as a precaution.
Less than two months ago, 100 tech companies wrote an open letter warning the world to adopt a new level of cyber resilience in the age of AI.
It turns out we didn't have to wait very long to find out what they meant.
The weaknesses found in the PHP programming language, which is used by millions of websites, had been quietly resting there for years and are not easy to exploit.
One cyber security researcher told me he'd been up all night trying to do it as an experiment, but it was proving very difficult.
However, things that are very difficult for humans are increasingly very little trouble for AI.
The tech is getting a lot of credit here for assisting researchers in finding the bugs, and the PHP foundation, which oversees the programming language, was on the case and issued a fix.
It was supposed to be kept quiet until everyone had a chance to fix their sites - but the news was leaked.
From that point the clock started ticking.
As I write this, there are no reports that anyone or anything has succeeded in using the flaws to attack a site.
"There's a real dilemma," said Prof Alan Woodward from Surrey University.
"How do you alert people they need to be ready, and then that a patch is urgently required, whilst not alerting attackers?
"Basically you're telling everyone about the problem at the same time and hoping the defenders aren't awake enough to act as soon as the patch is out."
But we do know from large web companies like Cloudflare and Palo Alto Networks that millions of attempts have been made.
We probably won't know for a while whether it has worked for any criminals, because the companies affected might not be aware yet either.
As far as we know the unexploded bomb remains intact for now, and for some experts this is a success.
Gina Neff, Professor of Responsible AI at Queen Mary University, described this as a good news story.

"We've seen how a team of people supported by the large AI company have used AI to find the problem, work for months together to solve it and get everybody ready to be safe and secure," she told the Today Programme on BBC Radio 4.
"We have enormous capability to handle these risks."
But the baddies can use AI too, and those same tools are probably churning away right now trying to get in.
Cyber security authorities are warning website owners to fix the weaknesses immediately, but the patch only works on the latest version of PHP, so older sites will need to upgrade first.
For many it may be a significant repair job, so if there's a web developer in your life you may want to send them thoughts, prayers and maybe a strong coffee.
