items.title: AI firms say UK has a year to head off datacentre protests before construction is threatened
paragraphs: AI companies have told ministers they have 12 months to head off public opposition to datacentres in the UK or risk US-style protests that could threaten their construction.

Successive dry summers and rising energy bills are increasing public scrutiny of plans for the huge computer warehouses that are used to train and run AI models, says a submission to the Labour government from a group including the AI infrastructure companies Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco.

Amid increasing anti-datacentre activism in the US and Europe, they are calling on ministers to create a “compact” that would show how communities can benefit from hosting datacentres, including allowing councils that host them to retain more tax revenues.

The move by the Sovereign AI Leadership (SAIL) taskforce reflects rising concern among tech companies that arguments that have blocked datacentre developments in parts of the US are taking hold in Britain. Microsoft has promised to invest $30bn (£22bn) in UK AI infrastructure.

Microsoft has built a datacentre in Acton, London and another is under construction in Newport, but wants to build several more facilities and is engaging with local and national leaders, including the prime minister, Andy Burnham, over the balance between the potential benefit of AI to the economy and public opposition to datacentres.

The SAIL group said: “In the United States, organised local opposition has stopped fully permitted datacentre projects, and moratoriums have been announced even in states that are otherwise pro-growth.

“Reporting from those places shows that AI itself is only a surface-level concern; distrust of corporate and government promises, fear of stranded assets and electricity costs run deeper. The same arguments have begun to appear here.”
It added: “Britain has a window – we think of roughly 12 months – to build a compact that earns public consent before that pattern takes hold.”

The taskforce is calling for the government to create a clear framework for councils and mayors to follow that will set out recommended terms for local benefit, including an indicative contribution – likely to be financial or in terms of facilities – scaled to a site’s size.

Opposition to datacentre construction is being fuelled by widening public concern about the safety of AI systems, after a summer in which some of the largest companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google appeared to lose control of some of their most cutting-edge AIs. Some protesters have begun resorting to direct action and the membership of anti-AI campaign groups has been growing rapidly.

The datacentre companies are determined to head off that opposition. The chair of the SAIL taskforce, Steve Rigby, said: “By establishing a clear prosperity compact between government, industry and local communities, we can build the infrastructure we need, equip our workforce with future-ready skills, and ensure Britain’s digital destiny. This taskforce’s goal isn’t another strategy document, but high-impact actions that materially accelerate the UK’s transition to an AI-enabled economy.”
It has not calculated the cost to central government finances if councils that grant permission to datacentres are allowed to keep all of their business rates.

Responding to the proposals, Joseph Miller, the director of PauseAI UK, which campaigns for a global pause to datacentre buildout, said: “People are going to feel it is undignified to be bought off by huge tech companies who do not share their interests.”

He said tech companies were “absolutely right to be worried” about US-style public opposition to datacentres growing in the UK. Kat Jones, the director of Action to Protect Rural Scotland, which campaigns against datacentres, said tech companies had already “missed the boat on containing community opposition to hyperscale AI datacentres”.

“In Scotland, we have 15 community campaigns already working incredibly hard opposing these environmentally destructive developments locally, and a growing national campaign,” she said. “Even the titanic lobbying efforts of US big tech are going to find it a real challenge to change the winds of public opinion, which have already shifted solidly against hyperscale AI datacentres.”

Donald Campbell, the director of advocacy at the tech equity campaign Foxglove, said: “Big tech firms have spent years trying to force vast, highly polluting datacentres through the planning system under a blanket of secrecy and misleading information. Now, with the public waking up to the fact that these facilities plunder resources and wreck the climate, the US tech giants have decided that there’s a problem.”

He warned that incentivising councils to back datacentres by allowing them to keep more of their business rate revenue would mean “these wealthy tech giants would not pay a penny more” while boosts to council funding would “come from the pocket of central government services like the NHS”.

A government spokesperson said datacentres “should create British jobs and supply chains, and provide investment to the communities in which they are built, as well as prioritising clean power, using water responsibly”.

“For most proposed datacentre developments, community benefits are considered through the relevant local planning processes,” they said. “We have already announced measures which will enable local authorities hosting datacentres in AI growth zones in England to keep all the additional business rates they generate.”

items.title: “Hydrofeminism” and leaky saints feature in Everything Moist Seems Alive installation
paragraphs: The technical minimalism of artist Boris Acket and the maximalism of fake fashion house Maison the Faux come together in the installation Everything Moist Seems Alive at MU Hybrid Art House during Dutch Design Week.

The multidisciplinary creatives worked with MU to devise the large-scale installation, which fills a dark, cavernous room with kinetic water structures connected by clear pipes and running on a continuous cycle of containment and deluge.
They are overlooked by towering video installations of glistening, oozing humanoid figures called the “leaky saints”.
These are surrounded by marshy candlelit altars and wishing wells, and, several times a day, brought to life by ritualistic choral performances from the Dutch National Opera and Ballet.

Everything Moist Seems Alive was the product of two years of discussion between the creatives on the topic of water, during which they were particularly drawn to cultural theorist Astrida Neimanis’ concept of “hydrofeminism”.

In her 2012 essay Hydrofeminism: Or, On Becoming a Body of Water, Neimanis considered the philosophical, ecological and sociological implications of conceptualising one’s human body primarily as water.
“In this hydrofeminist approach in the sense, we are all bodies of water,” said MU director Angelique Spaninks. “The world is made out of water, and so are we, for at least 60 per cent of our body.”

“Water is like: we need it. We tend to hide it. We want to control it. We use it as something that we need instead of thinking that we are part of it,” she continued. “And all these ideas have culminated into this total installation.”
The leaky saints serve as the most overt visual embodiment of Neimanis’ theory, dripping with shimmering fluid from their eyes, pores and other orifices.
“We lactate. We sweat. We have blood,” Spaninks summarises.
Greek myths and their powerful rivers also influenced the design of Everything Moist Seems Alive, which is broken up into five water structures.
Dubbed “water bodies” by the creatives, they each represent a different form of or interaction with water. There’s The Well, The Womb, The Whirl, The Wake and The Waterfall.

The Womb is a large circular tub in the centre of the space, and represents how everything “gets born in water, some way or another”, said Spaninks – an image that is evocatively conjured in the performance.

The Well is a series of three pumps that draws water from the tub and guides it into the rest of the system, in preparation for a climax that sees the usually dripping Waterfall, representing a dam, turn into a torrent.
The Whirl holds a white cloth that spins and dances with the movement of water, and the Wake slowly drips water onto a hot plate, emitting bursts of steam.

The pipes connecting the structures nod to the sanitation systems that underlie our daily interactions with water, while the gothic 3D-printed metallic ornaments on the pipes were inspired by Paris’ gargoyles, traditionally used to redirect rainwater flow away from buildings.
“We are big believers of ornamentation and the beauty of ‘a lot’ to give some sort of a reaction to mundane bareness,” Maison the Faux co-founder Joris Suk told Dezeen.

“What I like [in Everything Moist Feels Alive] is that it’s a collision of aesthetics. Studio Boris Acket is well known for its quite technical and stylish and minimalistic visual approach to things. We are very maximalist. So just bringing those two worlds together has created a lot of the aesthetics that you see here.”
Acket is best known for his mechanical fabric canopy Einder, which featured on the world tour of music producer Fred Again.
The Everything Moist Seems Alive installation is accompanied by a water bar at the entrance, where visitors can gather and sample three types of water – or choose to feed it to the installation.

The darkened water bar also features a suspended mixed-material sculpture by the artist Roni(a) Johansson that resembles abstracted flesh, with dozens of moist “egg sacs” setting the tone for the installation.

Maison the Faux was founded in 2012 by Suk and Tessa de Boer, both fashion design graduates who have gone on to build a cross-disciplinary practice involving performance art, fashion and costume design and set and interior design.

The conceit at the heart of their practice is that they are “a creative studio posing as a grand couture fashion house”, playing with the aesthetics of fashion and the boundaries between the real and the fake.

This Dutch Design Week also saw students protest against overcrowded facilities at Design Academy Eindhoven. Ahead of the week, we rounded up ten things to have on your radar during Dutch Design Week.
Dutch Design Week 2026 takes place from 17 to 25 October 2026 at various locations across Eindhoven, the Netherlands. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.
Photography by Hanneke Wetzer and Nikola Lamburov

items.title: Carminati lift-and-slide windows frame Dubai skyline at Bvlgari Hotel and Resort
paragraphs: Minimalist timber windows from luxury brand Carminati’s Skyline Minimal Frames collection were chosen to frame views from the Bvlgari Hotel and Resort in Dubai.

Designed to make the “least possible visual impact”, Carminati‘s Skyline Minimal Frames range includes both windows and doors defined by minimal profiles, natural materials and modern, patented technology.
The frame’s slimness is the result of Carminati’s patented Skyline Minimal Frames construction, where the timber sash is structurally bonded to the glass pane, which reinforces the whole frame.

“With a front-facing profile of just 37 millimetres for lift-and-slide systems and 50 millimetres for all other opening types, Skyline Minimal Frames combines outstanding thermal and acoustic performance with a minimal visual impact, making it the world’s slimmest wooden profile,” said Carminati.
The collection was selected by Milan-based studio ACPV Architects to be integrated into their design for the Bvlgari Hotel and Resort, which reached completion on Dubai’s Jumeirah Bay Island in 2017.

“Our Skyline Minimal Frames range, personally selected by the architects, possesses all the characteristics required for the project,” Carminati said. “The frames provide the perfect setting for enjoying a breathtaking panorama while feeling at the centre of Dubai’s vibrant social life and exclusive luxury.”
“The new resort is the result of refined Bvlgari style, professionalism and taste of its design team,” the brand added.

Carminati’s Skyline Minimal Frames collection offers a range of windows and door products, including Skyline Sliding, Skyline Bifold, Skyline Pivot, Skyline Drive, Skyline NoForce and the Skyline Handle.

Each of the collection’s products is available in a range of styles, from Skyline Modern to Skyline Classic, which can be manufactured entirely from wood or paired with an external aluminium cladding.

For the 158,000-square-metre Bvlgari hotel, ACPV Architects opted for Carminati’s Skyline Sliding lift-and-slide system – combining its sleek 37-millimetre profile with pale oak on the inside and a bronze-coloured aluminium cladding on the outside, chosen for its resistance to coastal environments.
This offered expansive views throughout the hotel, intended to create “continuity between the indoors and outdoors”, along with access to adjacent terraces.

“Large lift-and-slide doors connect the living rooms with expansive shaded terraces, while full-height glazing gives guests the feeling of being outdoors, conveying a sense of luxury associated with greenery, privacy and the tranquillity of the interior,” Carminati said.
The Skyline Sliding system operates through a lift-and-slide mechanism and is available in configurations with two sliding leaves – one fixed and one sliding – among other combinations.
Integrated into the product is the brand’s patented bottom track, designed exclusively for the Skyline Minimal Frames collection.
Its carriages are set entirely into the floor and covered by a flexible belt, which protects the mechanism from dust and allows for “maximum sliding smoothness”.

According to Carminati, the large-scale commission for the Bvlgari hotel involved the development of a bespoke product to meet the project’s specific technical requirements and local building regulations.

With glazed panels reaching up to four metres in height and subject to significant wind loads, the project required a bespoke system: a concealed steel structure between the lift-and-slide doors and the fixed transoms above.
Built around a composite beam, with three welded steel tubes set within the cavity between the frames, it allowed the profiles to stay slim while meeting the structural requirements.
“The structure takes on the challenges of the environment and combines its contrasts in an original and sophisticated solution,” Carminati said.
Carminati was founded in 1894 near Bergamo, Italy, and is still run by the founding family.

The company specialises in architectural timber windows and doors, holds patents on its Skyline Minimal Frames system, and develops bespoke solutions for each project through its in-house technical office.
To learn more about Carminati’s Skyline Minimal Frames collection, visit its website here.

items.title: Trump's green card curbs test Indian tech workers' American dream
paragraphs: For millions of Indians, the road to the ultimate career aspiration had a familiar script - an engineering degree to get a tech services job, then a posting in the US, repeated visa renewals and then the green card that gave them permanent residency in the country.

Earlier this month, the US announced it would suspend eight technology firms, including Microsoft, India's Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL Technologies, from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa pathway.

New and pending applications under the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, have been frozen. This is a big blow to Indians who hold a majority of H-1B visas - a temporary visa for specialists - which they used to work in the US while relying on PERM to get a green card and, ultimately, citizenship.

The latest announcement is in line with Trump's push for stricter skilled-worker immigration rules, which tech firms have been adapting to and, therefore, the impact on businesses may be minimal, experts say.
Nasscom, the trade association of India's $300bn (£226bn) technology industry, says that Indian companies have reduced the dependence on H-1B visas and are hiring more locally.
"Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited," the association adds.

Wipro said in a statement that more than 80% of its workforce in the US is locally hired. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), said its PERM applications were in single digits in the last two years. Microsoft said in a statement that it has filed for H-1B visas mostly to retain existing staff, not to import new workers.

A report in Business Standard newspaper, citing PERM Tracker, said, TCS' applications filings fell to two in 2025-26 from 513 in the previous year and 1,804 in the year before that. The report said no records were found for Infosys and Wipro for 2025-26.
BBC's email to all eight companies asking questions about the impact of the restriction and how they were supporting affected employees in the US remained unanswered.
Brokerage firm HDFC Securities said the impact on tech firms would be minimal, as PERM-linked jobs make up only a small share of revenue, even if higher-paid American workers replace them.
But the US government's decision has an impact beyond business.

A US-based senior executive with one of these eight firms told the BBC on condition of anonymity that the new PERM restriction will "not break the business", but the impact is more "intense" at a human level.

"A good number of people we know are stuck in a space where they have spent some years in the US but their green card application hasn't moved. Even if they are ready to move back to India, their children don't want to because they grew up here," he said.
Recent policy moves have deepened uncertainty and amplified online hostility towards Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders.

Researchers at Stop AAPI Hate, a US non-profit that combats anti-Asian and Pacific Islander discrimination, have reported a sharp increase in anti-South Asian online sentiment since the 2024 US election, with Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders being frequent targets.
While barring the eight tech companies from PERM, US Vice President JD Vance too referred to foreign professionals holding H-1B visas as "foreign indentured servants".

While he later acknowledged that it was an "imperfect" rhetoric, his remark drew sharp criticism from India's foreign ministry which called it "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive" for the colonial connotation.

Poorvi Chothani, founder and managing partner of global immigration law firm LawQuest, said many came to the US for better prospects, borrowing heavily to study and build careers. But as rules tighten now, they have fewer options and less ability to absorb the costs.
Immigration experts believe that as pathways for residency become limited, some may reconsider their future in the US, while others may choose not to move at all.
Ahmet Gulek, Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford's Immigration Policy Lab, told BBC that despite alternate ways to get residency, not many may be feasible.
While moving to another firm not covered by the suspension is an option, he flags that it's unclear if those firms would be open to hiring immigrants given "the fear of retaliation".
Besides, it's also a tough time to change jobs.
The technology industry has already been reshaped by layoffs, cost-cutting and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), making career moves tougher.

But there are other routes to a US green card. People with exceptional accomplishments or whose work advances national interests may be eligible for categories that bypass the PERM labour certification process.
Applicants can also qualify for permanent residency by investing at least $800,000 in eligible US enterprises.
Gulek warns some of these categories "may be targeted next."
While Chothani says some are so keen to stay in the US that they are considering the EB-5 investor route but may not have enough capital to invest.

Nearly one million Indian nationals were waiting for employment-based green cards as of December 2025, representing 79% of the total pending applications, according to the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP).

Their report projects wait times ranging from five to 179 years for highly skilled Indians filing labour certification or employment-based immigration petitions from January 2026, depending on the visa category.

Like other recent immigration measures, the PERM suspension may face federal court challenges. But together, these moves signal a more restrictive climate for those hoping to study, work or settle in the US.

Earlier, the Trump administration imposed a $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B visa petitions, a measure that was later struck down by federal courts. More recently, it has also proposed a $70,000 fee for universities recommending international students for a programme that allows graduates to work in the country after completing their studies.

"This trend is not changing anytime soon," said an Indian professional, who spoke to BBC on condition of anonymity and has transitioned to an H-1B visa recently after a "long wait". He says both the Republican Party and the Democratic Party agree immigration laws need reform, even if they disagree on how.

Some research suggests that restrictions could shift jobs to India rather than to American workers. This is supported by industry players saying that they are already witnessing an increase in companies offshoring work.

"Companies benefit from cost arbitrage when they move work offshore. Post Covid, there is also greater acceptance and appreciation for remote work from clients," the executive from the tech firm earlier quoted says.

Experts believe America's appetite for Indian tech talent is unlikely to disappear. What may be changing is how it taps that talent. For Indian professionals, that could mean rewriting the script about building a future in the US.

items.title: The four locations in the running to be UK City of Culture 2029
paragraphs: Blackpool is one of four shortlisted locations to be the next UK City of Culture
Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham have been shortlisted to become the UK's City of Culture in 2029.
The winning location will be announced in May and will be the fifth holder of the title - following Derry-Londonderry, Hull, Coventry and Bradford.
A different location is given the City of Culture title every four years. Each shortlisted city will now receive at least £125,000 from the government to do further work on their bid.
The eventual winner will receive £10m to deliver a year of cultural events and activities drawing on its "local strengths and stories".
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said the shortlisted cities "have shown the pride that exists in their places with the incredible culture on their doorsteps".
Three of the contenders are in England and one in Wales. They were chosen from a longlist of nine, which also included Inverness, Ipswich, Middlesbrough, Portsmouth and Swindon.

What is it known for? Its landmark Blackpool Tower, Pleasure Beach and Illuminations. It also hosts a major dance festival and an annual visit from Strictly Come Dancing. The Showtown museum celebrates Blackpool's history as a showbiz and comedy hotspot.

What have they said? Lynn Williams, leader of Blackpool Council, said: "Blackpool has been entertaining people for generations, and now we have the chance to show the country exactly what our town is made of."
She added: "Blackpool has never been a town that stands still. It is proud, working-class culture that has always been about bringing people together, having fun and making something happen."

What is it known for? Constructed in the 1960s and 70s, Milton Keynes is known for its US-style grid road system and numerous roundabouts. It is home to historic World War II codebreaking centre Bletchley Park, now a museum, and the National Bowl, an amphitheatre that has hosted concerts by Oasis, Queen and David Bowie.
What have they said? Milton Keynes' bid described it as "a city built on imagination – a place where innovation, diversity and creativity thrive side by side".

Councillor Jane Carr, leader of Milton Keynes City Council, said: "We're now on the cusp of the 60th anniversary of our founding and have so much to look forward to during this landmark year and beyond."

What is it known for? The traditional centre of steel and cutlery manufacturing, Sheffield has since become known for musical exports like the Arctic Monkeys and Pulp, for its annual documentary film festival, and for the Crucible - one of the leading theatres outside London.
What have they said? The city's bid put its spotlight on Sheffield's "world-renowned creative heritage, as well as our ambitious future plans".

Celebrating its place on the shortlist, councillor Fran Belbin, leader of the city council, said: "Sheffield is a city built on creativity, innovation and community spirit... Culture is part of who we are."

What is it known for? North Wales's largest city was a powerhouse of the industrial revolution, and most recently hit the headlines when its historic football club Wrexham AFC was bought by Hollywood actors Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney.
What have they said? The bid said: "Our ambition is simple but bold: to make Wrexham the world's most playful place."

Joanna Knight OBE, chair of the Wrexham bid, styled as Wrecsam2029, explained: "There's a real sense that something very special is happening here. Just imagine what becoming the first Welsh UK City of Culture could mean... the opportunities are enormous."

items.title: US adds wrongful detention warning to China travel advisory
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

The U.S. State Department has added a wrongful detention warning to its travel advisory for mainland China, cautioning that Americans face a serious risk of being detained without a fair legal process.
The advisory, updated October 19, keeps China at Level 2 — “Exercise Increased Caution” but adds a “D” risk indicator for wrongful detention.
The advisory warns that Chinese authorities may enforce local laws arbitrarily and impose exit bans without a fair and transparent legal process.
In an emailed statement to VOA, the State Department said it had determined that “Americans are at serious risk of wrongful detention in China.”

“The Trump Administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans,” a State Department spokesperson told VOA, adding that the administration was committed to securing the release of Americans wrongfully detained overseas.

The department identifies several groups that may face heightened risks, including Americans of Chinese descent, people involved in business disputes, and those with current or past ties to U.S. law enforcement, the military, intelligence agencies or the federal government.
The House Select Committee on China called the new “D” indicator “a serious warning to all Americans” in a social media post Tuesday.
The State Department has formally designated two U.S. citizens detained in China as wrongfully detained: Chinese American seismologist Chen Youlin and Myanmar-born American scholar Min Zin.
Chen had worked with Chinese researchers on a U.S. government-funded public research project examining seismic signals from underground nuclear tests in North Korea.

Chinese authorities arrested Chen on November 5, 2024, as he prepared to return to the United States after visiting family in China. On May 1, 2025, China accused him of espionage. The State Department designated his case as wrongful detention in March 2026.

Min Zin, who studies Myanmar politics and China-Myanmar relations, was detained by Chinese authorities after traveling to China’s southern Yunnan province for a conference in June this year. Beijing accused him of suspected espionage that endangered China's national security. The State Department designated his case as wrongful detention on August 20.
The designations make securing the release of both men a U.S. government priority.
President Donald Trump said he raised the cases of detained Americans and Chinese political prisoners with Chinese President Xi Jinping during their White House meeting at the end of September.
The State Department also confirmed to VOA that Washington had directly raised Chen's and Min Zin's cases with Beijing.
Chen's wife, Rong Yufang, welcomed the updated travel advisory in a written statement sent to VOA through Global Reach, a nonprofit organization working to secure her husband's release.

“I am grateful to Secretary Rubio for taking this action,” she said. “He has tried for months to quietly resolve my husband’s wrongful detention in China, and President Trump has even asked President Xi twice about Youlin.”

Aung Maw Zin, Min Zin’s brother, told VOA on Wednesday that “we are glad to see this small but important step that could help ensure that no other American family has to endure the nightmare our family has been living through since June.”

The United States previously placed China at Level 3, with a “D” indicator for wrongful detention. The advisory was downgraded to Level 2 and the indicator removed on November 27, 2024, after three Americans detained in China for years were released in a prisoner exchange between Washington and Beijing.
Upcoming summits could bring renewed pressure
Eric Lebson, chief strategy officer at Global Reach, told VOA that the espionage allegations against Chen were fabricated.
Lebson said Trump could press for a resolution when he meets Xi at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen and the G20 meeting at Mar-a-Lago over the next two months.
“President Xi can expect President Trump to continue raising the need to resolve this case while the State Department increases the costs associated with holding two U.S. citizens,” Lebson said.

Beijing has rejected allegations of wrongful detention, maintaining that its judicial authorities handle cases in accordance with the law.The Chinese Embassy in Washington has yet not responded to VOA's request for comment.

items.title: US says wartime command transfer to South Korea remains conditions based
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

The United States has reiterated that wartime operational control, or OPCON, of allied forces on the Korean Peninsula will transition to South Korea only after mutually agreed conditions are met, despite renewed calls from Seoul to accelerate the process.

“The transition of wartime operational control (OPCON) remains a conditions-based process mutually agreed upon by the United States and the Republic of Korea,” a U.S. Department of Defense official told VOA on Monday, speaking on background.

“Both nations remain committed to ensuring that the necessary conditions are met before any transition occurs,” the official said. “We will not prejudge decisions or outcomes of this bilateral process.”
Wartime OPCON refers to the authority to direct military operations during a conflict.

Under the current U.S.-South Korea combined defense structure, a U.S. general serves as commander of the Combined Forces Command, which would oversee allied military operations in wartime. CFC was established in 1978 with a goal to "deter, or defeat if necessary, outside aggression against" South Korea. It unified U.S. and South Korean forces under a single war-fighting command.

Although South Korea regained peacetime OPCON in 1994, plans to transfer wartime OPCON were repeatedly postponed before the allies adopted a conditions-based approach in 2014, leaving the timing of the transition undecided.
The comments come as South Korean President Lee Jae Myung pushes for a faster transition of wartime command authority.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Lee said South Korea should “swiftly” regain wartime OPCON, arguing that the country possesses sufficient military capabilities to assume greater responsibility for its own defense. According to South Korean media reports, Lee suggested that “regaining” or “restoring” wartime OPCON would be more appropriate terms than “transferring” it.

The issue gained renewed attention last week after Gen. Xavier Brunson, commander of U.S. Forces Korea, said the conditions surrounding the transition had evolved since the allies established their original framework.

“Because the conditions have changed, because we’ve changed our plan, we have new standards which we have to uphold,” Brunson said at a policy forum in Washington, citing an evolving security environment that includes North Korea’s continued weapons development and recent missile activities.
The Pentagon did not say whether the formal criteria for the transition had been revised.

The two allies have agreed to a conditions-based process that includes assessments of South Korea’s military capabilities and its ability to lead combined operations. While the Lee administration has expressed interest in completing the transition before the end of its term in 2030, Washington and Seoul have not publicly announced a target date.
Patrick Cronin, chair for Asia-Pacific security at the Hudson Institute, told VOA earlier this year that the OPCON transition carries both political and military significance.

Politically, the transition symbolizes “regaining full sovereignty” for many South Koreans, Cronin said. Militarily, however, he argued that the focus should remain on how the change would affect deterrence and the alliance’s ability to respond effectively to regional threats.
Sungwon Baik from VOA's Korean service contributed to this report.

items.title: Former Afghan soldiers fear deportation from Iran
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.
“We are in a very difficult situation in Iran,” said a former Afghan soldier, adding that “there is always the fear of being deported to Afghanistan.”
The 37-year-old former soldier, who requested not to be named for security reasons, told VOA that he fled Afghanistan soon after the Taliban returned to power in 2021.
Remembering his forced deportation and brief detention by the Taliban, he fears being deported again as Iran continues the forcible expulsion of Afghans.
The United Nations said on Oct. 12 that Iran deported nearly half a million Afghan nationals back to Afghanistan in 2026.

In 2025, about 1.9 million Afghans returned from Iran, including 1.26 million who were deported. Iran hosts the largest Afghan refugee community in the world. According to the U.N., there are 4.4 million Afghan nationals living in Iran. This includes 1.4 million undocumented Afghans.

“I live in hiding, with no documents. I go to work in the morning and come straight back home. I don’t go out at all anywhere,” the former soldier said, adding that he fears being arrested and deported.
He added that he would rather endure the difficult situation living in Iran than be forced to return to Afghanistan, where his life would be in danger.
His story is just one of the many involving former Afghan security personnel who live in fear of being deported to Afghanistan and arrested by the Taliban.

In its latest report released last week, the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan said that it documented at least four killings and 14 arbitrary arrests and detentions of former Afghan security personnel between July 1 and Sep. 30, 2026.
The report said that despite the Taliban’s announcement of a general amnesty, former Afghan officials who return to the country remain at risk.
Under Taliban rule, harassment, detention and killings are not limited to former security personnel, as activists are also at risk.
Khalid Qaderi, an Afghan writer and journalist, was arrested in 2022 and accused “of spreading anti-regime propaganda and committing espionage for foreign media outlets.”

Qaderi, who was in the Taliban’s prison for 10 months, told VOA that after he was transferred to the Taliban’s Intelligence prison, he got to know that his Facebook posts and private conversations were used as evidence against him.

“There I realized that all my Facebook posts that I had written against the Taliban, and a collection of my voice messages in which I spoke against the Taliban in very private settings, were used against me, calling it propaganda against the regime," said Qaderi.
He added that the Taliban’s officials in the detention center in the western city of Herat tortured him.
After his release, Qaderi left Afghanistan.
“We either had to be quiet, or we had to leave the country, and I obviously chose to leave the country, at least not to be silenced,” he said.
In its quarterly report, UNAMA documented at least 443 arbitrary arrests and detentions and 97 incidents of ill-treatment of Afghan women and men.

items.title: Iran steps up pressure on Kurdish opposition in Iraq
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdi article.
With a lull in the U.S. Iran conflict and the September completion of the withdrawal of American forces from Iraq, Iran appears to be increasing pressure on Iranian Kurdish opposition groups.

The actions against Kurdish groups based in Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan Region are a test of Baghdad's independence and analysts are warning Tehran retains considerable influence over Iraqi political decisions.

Iranian news agencies reported that Iraqi and Iranian officials agreed during talks on Monday to relocate members of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups from the Kurdistan Region. Iranian Ambassador to Iraq Mohammad Kazem al-Sadegh said Tuesday that both countries had agreed to expel groups Tehran describes as separatist terrorists or hand their members over to Iran.
Iraqi officials confirmed the meeting, attended by representatives of the Kurdistan Regional Government, but made no mention of an agreement to expel or extradite opposition members.
Iraq's National Security Advisory Agency said the discussions, chaired by National Security Advisor Qassim Aboudi, focused on resolving outstanding issues under a bilateral security agreement.
The conflicting accounts highlight the political sensitivities surrounding Iranian Kurdish groups, which have maintained bases in northern Iraq for decades.
Hazhar Barnji, U.S. representative of the Kurdistan Democratic Party of Iran (KDPI), told VOA that the party had received no official notification of any relocation decision.
"To date, we have not received such official communication or indication from either the Iraqi federal government or the Kurdistan Regional Government," Barnji said.
He said the party respected Iraqi sovereignty and international law, while its principal political activities remained focused on Iranian Kurdistan.

Washington-based Iraqi political figure Entifadh Qanbar said Iran's influence over armed factions continued to constrain Baghdad's decision-making despite American efforts to weaken Tehran's regional reach.
"In reality, Iraq is currently governed by armed groups and the will of those forces," Qanbar told VOA, arguing that Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had little ability to restrain them.
"Iraq will not emerge from Tehran's control unless a fundamental political change takes place," he said.

Political analyst Isam Fayli told VOA that Tehran's concerns extended beyond border security to fears that Kurdish opposition movements could gain broader support inside Iran and emerge as a more significant political challenge.

Fayli warned that Iraq handing opposition members to Iran could raise serious legal and humanitarian concerns. He suggested international assistance in finding safe resettlement arrangements, citing the relocation of members of the exiled Iranian opposition group Mujahedin-e Khalq.
Sheikh Ghaith al-Tamimi, head of the Iraqi Citizenship Project, said Iraq's own history demonstrated the limitations of military approaches to Kurdish political demands.

He said Baghdad's security cooperation with neighboring countries must respect constitutional and international obligations rather than become an instrument for settling another government's political disputes.

The changing U.S. military presence, Tamimi argued, presents a crucial test of whether Iraqi institutions can make independent security decisions or remain vulnerable to foreign influence and powerful armed factions.

For Iranian Kurdish opposition groups, the immediate question is whether Tehran's reported agreement with Baghdad will translate into concrete action, given that previous agreements between the two governments have failed to result in the expulsion of these groups from Iraqi Kurdistan.

items.title: Pupils who designed a badge sent to space meet NASA astronaut
paragraphs: Pupils at the school in Cemaes got the chance to ask question to a NASA astronaut
Pupils at a school on Anglesey were "very excited" when they met virtually with a NASA astronaut.
Students at Ysgol Cemaes were able to put their questions to Frank Rubio on Wednesday, who is set to be part of the crew for the Artemis III mission.
Rubio also spent more than a year aboard the International Space Station (ISS) after a fault with the spacecraft that was due to bring him and his fellow astronauts back to Earth.
During the virtual session, pupils asked him about his experiences of living and working in space, as well as the challenges and excitement of space travel.
Astronaut Frank Rubio was stranded on the ISS for 371 days
This is not the first time pupils at the primary school have had the chance to speak with astronauts.
Earlier this year, they took part in a project to design a badge that was sent into space, later seeing it float in zero gravity aboard the ISS.
The opportunity was made possible by former pupil Dr Melanie Coathup, a scientist who works closely with astronauts and has helped inspire the school's growing links with the space industry.
Guto Rhys, acting headteacher, said the students were "extremely excited" ahead of the meeting, and had "been looking at videos of life on the ISS and life in space".
The school's headteacher says the pupils were very excited to talk to an astronaut
The pupils had prepared many questions to ask Rubio.
Harry, 9 and his friend Sofia, 8, were among those listening to the astronaut talk about his experiences.
Harry said: "The most interesting thing I've done today is learning about NASA and Frank Rubio."
The pupils had been busy preparing in the classroom ahead of the meeting, according to Sofia.
She said: "In the school today, we've been learning about Frank Rubio. We learned that if you're sick in space, there are medical kits to help.
"We've been watching some videos about how to brush your teeth and sleep in space."
Harry and Sofia were both delighted to meet Frank Rubio
Lola, 9, was also in the hall for the talk on Wednesday. She was delighted to see Rubio holding a badge that one of the pupils at the school had designed.
"We've been learning about Frank Rubio and that he was supposed to stay in space for six months, but he ended up staying there for a year," she said.
"We got to design a badge to go up to space and it was my cousin who won and her badge got to go up to space."
Lola and Ruby say they're lucky to be able to have such a close connection with NASA as a school
Speaking to a real astronaut was "very cool" according to Ruby, 10, "because no other schools in Wales will get that experience".
"The most interesting thing that I learned today was that there is a space station up in space," she said.
The school plans to design a new badge very soon, with the plan to send another one up to space next year.

items.title: Olivier Mourgue obituary
paragraphs: Olivier Mourgue always wanted to design the future. Growing up in Paris in the 1950s, he took against the ornate antique furniture of his parents’ apartment, the formality of a dining room with a table surrounded by elaborately uncomfortable chairs and a living room dominated by a sofa used only on special occasions. “Furniture like that has nothing to do with life,” he would suggest later. “One is never at ease in such rooms.”

Mourgue, who has died aged 87, set out to design furniture that belonged to the modern world, and blurred the boundaries between furniture and architecture. In his view, that meant that it should be flexible, informal, affordable and as close to the floor as possible. He succeeded in a way that he could not have expected.

The film director Stanley Kubrick made Mourgue’s designs an essential part of popular culture’s expectations of how the future would look, even though Mourgue’s work was produced by the thousand rather than in millions. Kubrick used a cluster of Mourgue’s Djinn armchairs to equip the lobby of the Hilton hotel orbiting the moon on Space Station V for one of the key scenes of 2001: A Space Odyssey. The Djinn seemed to float almost weightless, like a colourful bubble of air. There were no conventional arms or legs to be seen. Instead there was a lightweight steel structure and some sturdy rubber webbing to support the foam upholstery, all hidden inside a seamless surface.

Kubrick had a preternatural gift for finding what might be called “real” objects, such as Djinn, from his own time, that seemed to belong to the future. He used them to give a sense of authenticity to his sets. Kubrick filmed A Space Odyssey in 1968, when Djinn looked entirely at home in a plausible version of 2001 that did not yet exist. Almost 60 years later, Djinn still looks like a version of the future, fluid and colourful, covered with a specially made stretch fabric that was available in 15 different bright colours and light enough to carry under your arm.

Mourgue wanted to do more than change the way that things looked. He believed in designing furniture that reflected the way that people want to live. He created a low-cost range of mass-produced designs for the department store chain Prisunic, in the days when it was a French version of Ikea, selling through its catalogue as well as its network of stores. The 1969 Prisunic edition launched a collection that Mourgue described as “bringing beauty at the price of the ugly”. It included bookcases, beds, tables, and seating made from lightweight chipboard that could be easily dismantled if required. One piece was a floor-cushion seat with raised edges that formed a place to sit.

Mourgue was born in Paris, to Denise (nee Lesieur), a physiotherapist, and Jean, who owned an art supply store. His uncle, Pierre Mourgue, was a successful illustrator, working for Vogue and Harper’s Bazaar in the US. Olivier’s younger brother, Pascal, also became a successful furniture designer.

Mourgue was influenced by the radical spirit of 1968, and impatient with tradition. But he was also the product of one France’s historic institutions. At the age of 14 he went to the École Boulle, a school named after Louis XIV’s cabinet maker, André-Charles Boulle, and set up to train apprentices in the art of marquetry.

After graduating, he studied at the École Nationale Superieure des Art Decoratifs. He also went to lectures at the Conservatoire National des Arts et Metiers by the architect and designer Jean Prouvé, whose ideas about prefabrication would have a lasting impact on Mourgue. He spent six months interning as a furniture designer for the Stockholm department store Nordiska Komaniet. His travels in Sweden and Finland, in those days Europe’s leading centres for innovative design, gave him an important new perspective.

Mourgue was still a student in 1959 when he designed Joker, his first chair to go into production. One of his teachers at the Boulle school introduced him to the Bernard family, founders of the Airborne furniture company. He caused something of a stir at Airborne’s factory in Montreuil, on the outskirts of Paris, when he arrived on his Solex moped carrying a full-scale prototype. It was the beginning of a long collaboration. Airborne launched Joker in 1964 and made the Djinn range, which included a two-seater sofa and a chaise longue. The company also manufactured a version of Montreal, the lounge chair that Mourgue designed for the French national pavilion of the 1967 Expo.

In 1966 Mourgue had set up his own studio in Paris. His projects included a consultancy for the motor manufacturer Renault for a low-cost version of the Renault 4 and lighting for the French company Disderot.

Despite Mourgue’s radical approach, he was part of the teams that designed the French national pavilions for both the Montreal Expo in 1967, and the one in Osaka in 1970. He designed the Bouloum chaise longue for Osaka and gave it a playfully anthropomorphic human form. But then the French state has always been determined to present itself as modern and forward looking. It was the Mobilier National, the state-run foundation originally set up in 1663 as the Royal Furniture Depository, that made the Montreal chair from fibreglass.

The Mobilier National was also responsible for Mourgue’s most radical project, an experimental scheme to equip 500 flats in the prefabricated Grand’Mare social housing development in Rouen with a furniture system. The architect was Marcel Lods, one of Prouvé’s collaborators. Mourgue used factory-made steel and glass components for the project; Lods designed the 80m² floor-plan. Mourgue came up with a series of prefabricated units that could in theory be used to take the place of internal walls to equip it. There was a sleeping pod on wheels, a kitchen that could be shifted as required and an integrated bathroom unit that could be plumbed in where needed.

Mourgue had a personal fondness for mobility. In the 1970s he built himself a series of travelling studios, one based on a Land Rover, another on a VW van. By now married with children, he took his family on an extended tour of central Europe on a specially adapted Saviem truck made by Renault for military use. In the 1970s he began to teach, first in Paris at the École Nationale Supérieure des Art Décoratifs, then, after moving to Brittany, at the École des Beaux Arts in Brest, where he was a charismatic and inspiring presence for 30 years, retiring in 2004.

Alongside his design work, Mourgue pursued painting and sculpture. He created a series of what he called “Imaginary Gardens and Little Theatres”, exhibited in 1992 at the Sainsbury Centre at the University of East Anglia, among other places. They can be seen as a more personal exploration of possible futures.
Mourgue is survived by his wife, Anne Turlan, a kindergarden teacher, and their five children, Thomas, Mikael, Armel, Gaetan and Maria.

items.title: Controversial US-backed vaccine trial in African newborns halted
paragraphs: The US-backed hepatitis B vaccine trial in African newborns that drew global backlash was halted, the lead researcher said on Wednesday.

It was “now clear” that the study “will not move forward in Guinea-Bissau”, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Danish researcher, wrote on LinkedIn, adding, “we were not given the necessary governmental approval.”
The minister of health in Guinea-Bissau, Quinhin Nantote, previously denied that the project would move forward. “This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese last week.

The study was to be funded with $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with another $1.6m from private partners like the Bill Ackman-backed Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.

“The solution is clear here: take the money and vaccinate as many kids as you can,” said Paul Offit, a vaccines expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, who sharply criticized the proposed study as unethical.
The government of Guinea-Bissau now has control over the researchers’ vaccines, which they apprehended when they searched the offices of the Bandim Health Project on Monday.
It was vital to support Guinea-Bissau in rolling the immunizations out to all newborns as soon as possible, Offit said. Guinea-Bissau currently plans to offer the universal birth dose in 2028.

The Danish researchers, led by Schaltz-Buchholzer, Christine Stabell Benn and Peter Aaby, hypothesized giving live vaccines, like the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), may have an overall mortality benefit beyond simply preventing illnesses like tuberculosis – but giving another vaccine like hepatitis B alongside it could dampen that effect.
Such a hypothesis was “fanciful” because the hepatitis B vaccine is a single protein among billions encountered by the immune system each day, Offit said.

“There’s no evidence for that, and it doesn’t make biological sense,” he continued. He also added that there was a very clear benefit to giving the vaccine to babies as soon as possible, because of high rates of hepatitis B in the country and the possibility of lifelong illness and death from infection.

The Danish researchers did not respond by press time to questions about the study or to this criticism. The CDC did not respond by press time to questions about whether the funding, which was appropriated through its global health work, would now be used to roll out the vaccine to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO).

“WHO recommends that all infants receive a first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth – preferably within 24 hours – followed by at least two additional doses,” said Tarik Jašarević, a WHO spokesperson. “WHO remains committed to working with national authorities, researchers, and partners to ensure that all newborns – in Guinea‑Bissau and worldwide – receive timely, evidence‑based protection against hepatitis B.”
Those who declined participation in the study would not have received the vaccines – making true informed consent impossible, experts say.

“Imagine you’re a mother. You want to do the best for your child,” said Henrik Støvring, a Danish researcher who has co-published research raising questions about previous research from the Bandim project.

“If they decide to participate in the trial, they have a 50% chance of getting the vaccine for their children. But if they stay out, they have a 0% chance of getting the vaccine. So how can you say that’s a non-coercive informed consent?” Støvring asked.

The proposed trial led to distrust among Bissau-Guineans, who wondered if the vaccine – which has a decades-long record of being safe and effective – was being tested on Africans because it was dangerous, Schaltz-Buchholzer said in his post.

It “should be clear” that both birth vaccination schedules – with or without hepatitis B – are not “dangerous to anyone”, he wrote. There is a clear benefit to giving hepatitis B vaccines at birth, and not doing so can lead to lifelong danger, experts say.
Conducting a study like this “makes the case that there’s something that’s worthy of study, for which they have no evidence”, Offit said.

“We have millions and millions, arguably hundreds of millions, of children in this world who have gotten that vaccine as a birth dose or haven’t. If there was any evidence that this was problematic, you would know this by now,” Offit added. “We eliminated hepatitis B in the United States in children virtually within years of starting that program, so the benefits are clear.”

Schaltz-Buchholzer also cast doubt on the effectiveness and safety of the hepatitis B vaccine at birth, noting that he believes the study was canceled because it challenges “prevailing medical assumptions, such as that HBV0 does not have non-specific effects”. The study, in addition to looking at mortality, would have also examined side-effects such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. Dozens of studies have shown no link between vaccination and autism.

“All newborns should be given a birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine,” Offit said. “Guinea-Bissau is a country that suffers a high incidence of chronic hepatitis B. That country, more than any other country, arguably, needs to launch this program.”

items.title: Johnston Marklee unveils designs for Bass Museum expansion
paragraphs: California architecture studio Johnston Marklee has unveiled designs to expand the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach, USA, including elevated galleries and courtyard spaces.
The project will extend the Museum of Art (the Bass) into the 22,000-square-foot area at the southwest corner of the museum’s campus with indoor and outdoor space.

Renderings show two rectangular pavilion structures that sit on a thin concrete plane, elevated off the ground to meet “resiliency guidelines”, likely in reference to Miami-Dade County’s stated floodwater risks due to sea-level rise. Courtyards will pass underneath the structure.

This elevated structure also keeps the corner of the property open and increases public access, according to Johnston Marklee founding partner Sharon Johnston, who called the project “transformative”.

“Through careful analysis of light and shadow, space and volume, and the surrounding park and urban context, we are planning a transformative project that will increase public access to the museum’s programs and artworks,” said Johnston.
Formally, the expansion will feature sheer white walls for the upper structures, with more texture on the walls at ground level, underneath the elevated structures.
At the centre of the project, a backlit oculus will illuminate the passage under the structure at night.
The passages will also lead to landscape garden areas, with the blank face of one of the pavilions providing a screen for screenings.
This space will connect to the trees that are part of Collins Park, which extends from the east face of the museum.
Facade perforations will be placed at the top of the rectangular pavilions and on the walls separating the covered courtyards from the street.
The expansion builds upon the original art deco building designed by Russell Pancoast as a library in the 1930s before the Bass opened in 1964 and the Arata Isozaki expansion.

Primary exhibition space will be held in the rectangular pavilion structures, with renderings showing white-wall galleries, rectangular windows and a skylight placed on top of the one nearest to the Isozaki building.
“We are thrilled to reimagine the southwest corner of Collins Park for The Bass,” said Johnston Marklee founding partner Mark Lee.
“This project continues the storied architectural heritage of the museum, preserving Russell Pancoast’s 1942 Art Deco design while honoring Arata Isozaki’s vision of a porous campus.”
Other recent projects by Johnston Marklee include a green-metal skyscraper in Phoenix and a minimalist pavilion for Danish furniture brand Vipp in Upstate New York.

items.title: Sir Donald Insall obituary
paragraphs: Donald Insall, doyen of conservation architects, who has died aged 100, was very clear about the distinction between preserving buildings and conserving them. “Preservation,” he pronounced, “is what you do for marmalade.” Though Insall could see the value of preservation, he was an adroit conservationist rather than a stodgy marmalade maker, always seeing how historic buildings could be revived and put to new uses.

Marshalling teams of architects, craftsmen and builders, he brought Windsor Castle back from the brink following the devastating “annus horribilis” fire of 1992. The exacting rescue scheme encompassed a range of strategies, from complete restoration to renewal in spirit. “As well as keeping things as they were, or putting them back as one thinks they were – which is chancy and not the main aim – we had to find new solutions to parts that had been irreparably destroyed,” Insall told Country Life in 2018.

Other high-profile projects included the renovation of Kelmscott Manor, the Oxfordshire country home of the writer, designer and socialist William Morris, following its acquisition by the Society of Antiquaries in 1961, and the restoration of Kedleston Hall in Derbyshire, Robert Adam’s Palladian masterpiece, now in the care of the National Trust. “Kedleston was our first big job,” Insall recalled. “I used to take a scooter on the train, hop off at Derby and go to the hall, where I was met by the butler and the dogs. Once or twice, Lord Scarsdale, the owner, came on the back of the scooter for a ride around the estate.”

Insall was also involved in the lengthy rebuilding of Wotton House in Buckinghamshire, which had previously been remodelled by John Soane following a fire in 1820. Derelict and teetering on the brink of destruction, it was bought in 1957 by the enterprising Elaine Brunner, daughter of King George V’s valet, who had first arrived there, chauffeured by an antique dealer friend, to scavenge columns to adorn her swimming pool and then embarked on a decades-long programme of restoration.

Commissioned by custodians of the country’s most significant historic buildings, from town halls to royal palaces, Insall changed the scope and ambition of conservation practice, shaping pioneering approaches to heritage management at a time when historic buildings were widely seen as impediments to progress rather than assets to be cherished. In deftly addressing issues of heritage, sustainability and contemporary use, his approach has a renewed resonance and relevance. When Insall once worked for the College of Arms, he was granted a personal coat of arms. Aptly, he chose the motto “Bring Forth the Best”.

The son of Phyllis (nee Hill) and William Insall, he was born in Bristol into a family of long established manufacturers of traditional luggage, such as trunks, cricket bags and portmanteaux. He attended Bristol grammar school, and his interest in architecture was piqued when his father commissioned and built a new family home at Henleaze, in the north of the city. During the blitz, Insall witnessed the wartime destruction of Bristol’s ancient churches and historic buildings, and in 1942 started architectural studies at the Royal West of England Academy School of Architecture. He saw wartime service from 1944 in the Coldstream Guards, completing his education after being demobbed in 1948.

Insall studied civic design in London at the Royal Academy Schools and later at the RA’s School of Planning. In 1951 he was a Lethaby scholar with the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings, the organisation founded by William Morris in 1877 in response to the activities of Victorian architects, whose misconceived enthusiasm for restoration often caused calamitous damage. As a Lethaby scholar, Insall worked with and learned from an array of traditional craftsmen, including thatchers and lime plasterers, going on to spend 18 months measuring and surveying Winchester college for the medieval historian John Harvey.

It proved a formative education in which he got to know and understand historic buildings from different periods. He claimed to have no favourites. “I love them all,” he said, relishing how social change was reflected in architecture. “It’s all part of a lively continuity.” What also mattered to him was not just the quality of individual buildings, but their wider contextual relationships with streets, towns and cities. The role of conservation architects was, Insall believed, to help make “every place to be truly more itself”.

Insall initially joined Phillimore and Jenkins, a London-based practice specialising in the restoration of country houses in the greatly altered postwar milieu. In 1958, together with a fellow Lethaby scholar, Peter Locke, he founded Donald Insall Associates, working from the kitchen table in his flat in Belgravia. His father and then his wife, Libby (nee Moss), a lawyer, whom he married in 1964, did the accounts. From these tentative beginnings, the practice is now over 100 strong, operating out of eight offices across England and Wales.

With modernism then in the ascendancy, it was a bleak time for historic buildings. Country houses that did not find a saviour were all too often demolished, as were urban swathes of Victorian and Georgian terraces. While conservation fired Insall’s imagination, taking an interest in old houses was regarded as perplexingly antiquarian, as he recounted to Country Life. “Nice to meet you, but when will your father be coming?” asked the builder on one early job.

Insall’s 1968 study of Chester was a landmark for urban conservation and town planning. Undertaken as a part of a government pilot project surveying four historic towns (the others were Bath, Chichester and York), it recognised for the first time the importance of groups of structures with historic or architectural value. Insall and his team “crawled in overalls” over some 400 buildings, evaluating their merits and advocating that the best ones should be retained.

This led to his appointment as conservation consultant for Chester, and, ultimately, to the establishment of municipal conservation officers in local councils across the country. It also helped formulate many of the principles that underpin today’s conservation management plans and historic building appraisals.

Over time, Insall became a driving force in the workings of the Ancient Monuments Board and the Historic Buildings Council for England. There he befriended the architectural historian John Summerson, and the historians and conservation activists Nikolaus Pevsner and John Betjeman. These liaisons seeded the formation of English Heritage in 1984, of which Insall was a founding commissioner.

Conservation techniques are continually evolving and Insall kept abreast of developments. In the decade-long restoration of Westminster Hall completed in 2020, for instance, nanolime (nano-sized particles of calcium hydroxide dissolved in alcohol) was used to consolidate weathered limestone, and latex poultices employed to remove staining. Insall was also a thoughtful writer, summarising his philosophy, principles and practice in Living Buildings (2008), reprinted a decade later with a foreword by the then Prince of Wales.

For the last three years, Insall projects have won the Europa Nostra award, Europe’s highest accolade for heritage conservation: for the restoration of Westminster Hall (2024), the saving from dereliction of the 18th-century Camellia House at Wentworth Woodhouse, in South Yorkshire (2025) and the revitalisation of Rochdale’s imposing neo-Gothic Town Hall (2026).

Whether resplendent in elegant tweed suits on Instagram, commuting to the office on a BMW 750 motorbike, or vertiginously face to face with Nelson at the top of his column, Insall cultivated a suavely swashbuckling persona, laced with charm and humour. Though he retired as practice chairman in 1998, he continued to work as a consultant until his death.

“Buildings are so very much like people,” he observed. “They all have their own characters, their own strengths and weaknesses, their own message, their own background in terms of the influences that have made them. People change throughout their lives – so does a building.”
Insall was knighted in 2010. He is survived by Libby and their three children, Robert, Christopher and Hilary.

items.title: Severely ill ICE detainees face imminent deportation to unknown African states, advocates say
paragraphs: Relatives of gravely ill detainees at two Florida immigration jails say authorities are about to deport their loved ones to unknown countries in Africa despite worsening medical conditions.

Flights are scheduled as early as Wednesday, according to the families and the immigration advocacy group the Workers Circle, which has been monitoring conditions and speaking with detainees inside two Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facilities in south Florida.
The group said multiple sick detainees with varying conditions had been targeted for imminent deportation, and learned about the operation only in the last few days.

“I received a call from several detainees letting me know that men were being pulled in to interviews with deportation agents, where they were being informed that because of their medical conditions, Mexico would not be accepting their entry, and they will be sent to Africa,” Arianne Betancourt, the group’s immigrant rights organizer, said at a Tuesday night press conference.
“We know that once they are deported and sent to these third countries, they are not receiving medical care in detention. They have difficulties getting medicine.”

The affected detainees are at the Krome North processing center in Miami, which was found to be experiencing severe overcrowding by a government inspector’s report last month, and the Broward transitional center in Pompano Beach. Both facilities are privately run on behalf of ICE.

Anisley Cortés, the wife of Noslén Sendra, a 41-year-old Cuban national, said her husband had been incarcerated since last November, first at the now closed “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration jail, and at Krome since April. She said he has uncontrolled diabetes and acute pancreatitis that resulted in a weeks-long hospital stay earlier this year.

“He lost over 50 pounds. They wouldn’t give him his medication, and they would not give him enough food. It was a nightmare of a time for all of us,” she said. “He is very sick and needs the right healthcare.

“Cuba will not accept him as a deportee, and we now have proof that Mexico will not accept him as a deportee because he is so sick. And so they told him that because he could not be accepted at either of those two countries, ‘Oh well, we’re going to have to send you to Africa.’

“They told him that Mexico would not accept him because he has too many medications that he requires, and so they said, ‘Well, we have to deport you anyway.’ We’re left with the uncertainty of not knowing how he is, or if we’ll see him again.”
Shalyn Fluharty, an immigration rights attorney, said information from the detainees indicated deportation flights were imminent.

“We understand that just this week, within a couple of days, likely Thursday and Friday, there will be two flights going to Africa, in particular to the Central African Republic, and we also believe Burundi,” she said.
Fluharty said previously deported immigrants were shackled at their hands, ankles and waists during lengthy flights, and some who complained were placed in full body wraps with no ability to move.
“This is what we anticipate will be happening this week for these individuals, based upon what we’ve seen in the past,” she said.

“Travel can last sometimes up to 24 hours. What if you’re somebody who has a heart condition? Who has a high risk of stroke? Who is experiencing diabetes and requires regular access to food or insulin? These conditions take your already vulnerable medical state and make them, unfortunately, often life-threatening.”

Responding to a request for comment, a spokesperson for the homeland security department demanded to know the affected detainees’ personal information. The department did not respond further when provided with Sendra’s details.
Betancourt said families risked retaliation for their relatives by coming forward. “This is not a single one-off story,” she said.

“The inspector general’s report confirmed that there is a lack of medical care inside of the Krome detention facility. Families have been demanding oversight, and every day they are experiencing real fear to speak up and advocate for their loved ones.”

During two unannounced visits to Krome in May, government inspectors found multiple violations of noncompliance with detention standards, including severe overcrowding. Holding 1,102 detainees in a facility with a maximum capacity of 882, the report said, “jeopardizes the safe and orderly operations within the facility”.

Other listed violations included an inadequate number of operational toilets, sinks and showers, and previous complaints included female detainees made to use toilets in full view of men, and arriving detainees held for more than 24 hours in a bus in the parking lot because of a lack of space.

Advocates say Donald Trump’s sweeping second-term immigration crackdown has caused overcrowding in detention centers nationwide that the DHS has attempted to alleviate by ramping up deportation flights to so-called third countries.
The controversial practice, approved by the US supreme court last month, has seen hundreds of detainees deported to at least a dozen African countries where they have no ties.

A Human Rights Watch report earlier this month found countless examples of abusive treatment during and after the flights, and detainees subjected to persecution, arbitrary incarceration and torture following their arrival.

items.title: Why has a crumbling bottle plant been rebuilt in Paris? The stunning show suggesting the future is Ghana-shaped
paragraphs: Ibrahim Mahama has dug through the ruins of post-colonial Ghana, sorted through the ashes of its ancient history, picked through the industrial detritus, the corporate waste, the piles of rubbish, and found something pretty unique: hope.

Sit on one of the Asante stools in his circular Parliament of Ghosts and you can almost feel a new future being worked out right in front of you. It’s the first installation in this huge exhibition at the Fondation Cartier in Paris, and it sums Mahama up pretty neatly. He’s looking at the collapse of the Ghanaian government in 1966, the way the hope of the post-colonial project was crushed in a military coup, and he’s looking at ancient Ghanaian history, at the empires that fell centuries ago and the way colonialism tore them to shreds. But he’s not lamenting any of them. He’s not mourning. Instead, he’s reclaiming them, asking how things can be rebuilt, how we can move forwards by learning from the past.

And he does it over and over. In 2024 he bought an old bottle factory – a symbol of industry and its collapse. He’s rebuilt it here, in the centre of Paris. Its steel roof beams, rusted and crumbling, reach up to the ceiling, its walls are lined with thousands of green bottles in Coca-Cola, Schweppes, Kool and Club Minerals crates. It’s a whole history of manufacturing, of commerce in West Africa post-independence. Not left to rot, but rebuilt and reconfigured into something new.
Nearby, he’s taken some of those bottles and piled them around a collection of local pottery. The industrial meets the artisanal, two lost arts creating a new one.

But this huge show isn’t really about Mahama, it’s about the people around him. Most of the work here is by nine other artists and collectives. Mahama runs three art centres near Tamale in Ghana, giving time, space and opportunities to local artists. Their work is given priority here, alongside art by his mentors and collaborators. He’s taken this massive exhibition opportunity and used it as a chance to celebrate his community. It’s almost as if he’s trying to make the rest of us feel bad.

Way up on the top floor, a long scroll of jute and bark by Dorothy Akpene Amenuke undulates across the floor. If it looks like Mahama’s work, it should: she was his art teacher back in 2013. Knowledge, and the past, gets reconfigured and reshaped once again.

Nearby, the wall of a farmhouse has been built by artist and architect Courage Dzidula Kpodo out of red earth clay, a material lost as modernism brought in concrete. Now, historic methods become a kind of resistance, a symbol of tradition’s ability to endure.

Those core ideas get repeated through pretty much every presentation here. Influential 97-year-old photographer James Barnor captures the communities around Mahama in large format, grainy Polaroids. Gideon Appah’s hazy, dream-like paintings imagine fictional Ghanaian youths staring out to sea, congregating on beaches in utopian, idealised visions of the country’s past. Some of the works are absolutely stunning, like Peter Doig and Noah Davis transported to Accra.

The best work, appropriately enough, isn’t by one artist but a collective. On the top floor, a bunch of lumpy, surreal sculptures of birds, bodies and men wrestling bulls is by the Congolese Plantation Workers Art League (CATPC). Each one is made of chocolate, sculpted in the DRC but poured into moulds in Amsterdam. Everything they make from selling the art goes towards buying back land confiscated in the early 20th century by the Lever Brothers, who we now know as Unilever. The work is a whole conversation about global trade taking place in sculptural form, an act of resistance and reclamation through chocolate.

This exhibition is essentially an ambitious, ultra-idealistic group show of West African art. It is art exhibition as political utopianism. Which is great, even if not everything in it is good. And the real draw is Mahama, with his archival approach to monumental installation art, and it’s a shame to not get a load more of it.

Mahama has sacrificed himself for the greater good, basically. But this collaborative approach is the point: he’s saying collective action, community, togetherness, that’s how we’ll build a future. It might sound a bit cloying and earnest, but then you see the results, you see the art and the ideas, you see the community and the hope and the idealism and you eventually say: “Get me a one-way ticket to Accra. I’m in.”

items.title: Astronaut surprise video leaves pupils starstruck
paragraphs: Primary school children have been left amazed after receiving a personal video message from British astronaut Tim Peake.
Pupils at Thornbury Primary School in Plymouth, Devon, were sent the message after teacher Emily Trevarthen's father met Peake while working on a cruise ship over the summer.
Trevarthen explained that her father and the astronaut got chatting and her father mentioned she was a teacher. "We didn't expect to get what we got really," she said.

Peake told pupils, external: "I hear you've been studying all about space, a subject very close to my heart, something I love, so I'm very pleased that you enjoy it too. Stay curious. Keep looking up at the stars."
Trevarthen said that some children had previously assumed all astronauts were American, but learning about a British astronaut had helped them see that such ambitions were possible.

items.title: Dezeen launches "richer and more versatile" new website
paragraphs: Dezeen has updated its website for the first time in 10 years. Dezeen’s co-CEOs Benedict Hobson and Wai Shin Li explain the changes.
You might have noticed that things look a little different around here. Yes, after many years, we have redesigned our website!
It has been 10 years, in fact – the last major revamp of Dezeen was in 2016. And as with our previous redesign, evolution, not revolution, has been the aim.

Dezeen was launched by Marcus Fairs from his spare room as a basic WordPress blog in 2006. When it started to take off, he brought designer and typographer Micha Weidmann on board to design a logo and layout for it, and this has been the foundation upon which Dezeen has been built ever since.
We really like it, and millions of readers around the world seem to like it too.
So our ambition for this redesign was to bring the site up to date while staying true to the core identity that has helped Dezeen become what it is today.
Underneath the bonnet, there’s been a complete overhaul
We have worked with creative technology studio Made by On to refresh the look and feel of the site and improve the user interface to make it more useful and enjoyable to use.
Underneath the bonnet, there’s been a complete overhaul.
